# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2024, question Q5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (40 marks)

QUESTION 5: MACROECONOMICS

- Discuss in detail the reasons for international trade. (26 marks)
- Analyse the impact of a weaker currency (rand) on the South African economy. (10 marks)

(Section C essay: candidates answer ONE of the two 40-mark essay questions. Essay rubric: introduction maximum 2 marks — lower-order response, define the main concept, do not include any part of the question or announce what will be discussed; body main part maximum 26 marks — a maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples; body additional part maximum 10 marks — a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; conclusion maximum 2 marks — higher-order summary, opinion, additional support information, contradictory viewpoint with motivation, or recommendations.)

## Method

essay

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

INTRODUCTION (maximum 2 marks)

International trade refers to the exchange of goods and services between two countries or more. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

BODY MAIN PART (maximum 26 marks) — REASONS FOR INTERNATIONAL TRADE

Demand reasons:

1. Size of population: If there is an increase in population growth, it causes an increase in demand, as more people's needs must be satisfied. Local suppliers may not be able to satisfy this demand and consumers will be forced to import from other countries.
2. Income levels: Changes in income cause a change in the demand for goods and services. An increase in the per capita income of people results in more disposable income that can be spent on local goods and services, some of which may then have to be imported. Local supply may be insufficient to satisfy the demand, thereby creating a demand for imports.
3. Changes in the wealth of the population: An increase in the wealth of the population leads to greater demand for goods. People have access to loans and can spend more on luxury goods, many of which are produced in other countries. In case where luxury goods and services cannot be produced locally, people will have to import them from other countries.
4. Preferences and tastes: Preferences and tastes play a part in the determination of prices. Customers in Australia prefer a specific product which they do not produce and need to import, and it will have a higher value than in other countries. People's taste and preferences evolve and are often influenced by social media and globalization. Changes in preference create markets for goods and services that are not always manufactured domestically.
5. Difference in consumption patterns: The difference in consumption patterns is determined by the level of economic development in the country. In countries where the level of disposable income is high, demand for luxury goods is high, which creates a larger market for imports. A poorly developed country will have a high demand for basic goods and services but a lower demand for luxury goods.

Supply reasons:

1. Natural resources: Natural resources are not evenly distributed across all countries of the world. They vary from country to country and can only be exploited in places where these resources exist. South Africa has large deposits of gold while Nigeria has crude oil. The availability of natural resources creates a platform for specialisation and an opportunity to earn valuable export revenue.
2. Climate conditions: Every country has a unique climate which allows it to grow specific crops. Specialisation is promoted in production which empowers countries to produce at lower cost per unit. Climate conditions make it possible for some countries to produce certain goods at lower price than other countries. Brazil is the biggest producer of coffee in the world because its climate conditions are favourable for coffee production.
3. Labour resources: Labour resources differ in quality, quantity and cost between countries. Some countries have highly skilled and well-paid workers with high productivity levels, such as Switzerland. Some countries have bigger or smaller labour force, where minimum wage may be higher while others have no regulations regarding remuneration. Some countries have specialized labour force in the production of certain goods and services. Germany has the most skilled labour in the production of BMW, VW, Mercedes Benz cars, which gives it the capacity to export to other countries.
4. Technological resources: Technological resources are available in some countries that enable them to produce certain goods and services at a low unit cost. Some countries have access to advanced technological resources such as machinery and equipment. Japan and Singapore are considered to be technologically advanced which gives them a competitive advantage on the global markets.
5. Specialisation: Specialisation in the production of certain goods and services allows some countries to produce them at a lower cost than others (comparative advantage). Japan specializes in the production of electronic goods and sells these at a lower price. Specialisation ensures that mechanization, division of labour and economies of scale are associated with mass production are achieved. Countries therefore earn international reputation for specializing in the production of certain products.
6. Capital: Capital allows developed countries to enjoy an advantage over underdeveloped countries. Developed countries are usually highly industrialized and have well-developed infrastructure which promotes higher levels of productivity. Due to a lack of capital, some countries cannot produce all the goods they require themselves.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for headings/subheadings/examples)

ADDITIONAL PART (maximum 10 marks)

A weaker currency (rand) may positively impact on the South African economy as follows:

- Imports will become relatively more expensive which may discourage importing and increase demand of local products.
- Demand for South African exports such as base metals and mineral products will increase as they become relatively cheaper.
- Tourism activities will increase as more tourists visit the country due to the weaker rand.
- Balance of payments deficit will decrease as less goods are imported while more goods are exported.

A weaker currency (rand) may negatively impact on the South African economy as follows:

- Importing production inputs such as crude oil, agricultural chemicals and vehicle parts will become expensive fuelling cost-push inflation.
- Higher cost of importing production inputs may decrease domestic production which will slow down economic growth.
- Foreign investors may withdraw their investments in the economy because a weaker rand reduces the returns on their investments.
- Import payments will increase which may reduce welfare as more resources are used to produce more exports to finance higher cost of import.
- Export earnings will decrease, resulting in a decrease in trade balance.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples)

CONCLUSION (maximum 2 marks)

As a developing country, South Africa should encourage international trade to achieve higher economic growth. (Accept any other higher-order conclusion)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2025, question Q2.2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Use the information above to determine whether there is an increase or decrease in the reserve assets (A). Show ALL calculations. (Refers to the Q2.2.1 table, FINANCIAL ACCOUNT OF BALANCE OF PAYMENTS (BOP) – 2024, items in R millions: Net direct investment 68 622; Net portfolio investment -23 348; Net financial derivatives 4 311; Net other investment 13 481; Reserve assets A; Balance on financial account 62 869; memo item: balance on financial account excluding reserve assets 63 066. A note states that an increase in reserve assets is indicated by a negative sign and a decrease by a positive sign.)

## Method

bop calculation

The reserve assets figure is the missing piece that makes the financial account add up. The quickest route: the balance on the financial account includes reserve assets, and the memo item excludes them, so subtracting the one from the other isolates reserve assets. Alternatively, start from the balance on the financial account and strip out each listed item one by one. Either way you land on -197, and the note under the table tells you how to read the sign: a negative sign means reserve assets increased.

## Memo working

Method 1: Balance on financial account less balance on financial account excluding reserve assets -> 62 869 - 63 066 = -197.

Method 2: Reserve assets = 62 869 - 13 481 - 4 311 + 23 348 - 68 622 = -197.

The value of A is -197 (R millions); per the sign convention in the table, the negative sign indicates an increase in reserve assets.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

There is an increase in the reserve assets because the value of reserve assets has a negative sign (-).

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2025, question Q2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

How can the appreciation of the rand impact the South African economy? (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: the verb is 'how can it impact', so both positive and negative effects earn marks — any four points, two marks each. Positive channels: imported production inputs such as crude oil, agricultural chemicals and vehicle parts become cheaper, curbing cost-push inflation; cheaper inputs can lift domestic production and lower prices; a stronger rand raises foreign investors' returns and attracts investment; outbound tourism becomes cheaper for South Africans. Negative channels: exports such as base metals become relatively expensive, so foreign demand falls; exporters' profits shrink as their products lose competitiveness; producers may cut production and jobs; inbound tourism declines; and the trade balance can deteriorate as imports rise while exports fall.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

**Positive impact**

- Importing production inputs such as crude oil, agricultural chemicals and vehicle parts will become less expensive curbing cost-push inflation
- Lower cost of importing production inputs may increase domestic production which will stimulate economic growth and lower prices for goods and services
- Foreign investors may be attracted to invest more in the economy because a stronger rand increases the returns on their investments
- Import payments will decrease which may increase welfare as more resources may be used to produce more exports to finance higher cost of import
- Export earnings will increase, resulting in an improvement in trade balance.
- In the short-term, the terms of trade will improve as the prices of exports will be higher than import prices
- Outbound tourism activities will increase as more South African tourists will visit other countries due to the stronger rand

**Negative impact**

- Demand for South African exports such as base metals and mineral products will decrease as they become relatively expensive
- Local businesses will suffer in terms of profits due to their products becoming less competitive in global markets
- Unemployment levels may increase as local businesses will be forced to reduce their production due to reduced exports
- Inbound tourism activities will decrease as less tourists visit the country due to the stronger rand
- Balance of payments deficit will increase as less goods are exported while more goods are imported due to a stronger currency

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

**Note on a source anomaly:** the official memo lists the bullets 'Import payments will decrease which may increase welfare as more resources may be used to produce more exports to finance higher cost of import' and 'Export earnings will increase, resulting in an improvement in trade balance' under the impacts of an appreciation, where they appear internally inconsistent (they describe effects usually associated with a depreciation). They are transcribed verbatim above.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2024, question Q1.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

The players trained hard during the season. At the end of the season, the coach reported that each player was able to do 5 more push-ups per minute than they did at the beginning of the season. How does the increase in the number of push-ups influence the standard deviation of the data?

## Method

effect of constant shift on spread

## Memo working

Adding the same constant (5) to every data value shifts the whole data set up by 5 but leaves the distances between the values unchanged, so the spread does not change.

residual from regression line

An increase of 10 push-ups

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Show the amounts for the transactions below in the appropriate columns for the Cash Budget and the Projected Statement of Comprehensive Income for December 2024 in the ANSWER BOOK.

Example: Monthly insurance premium for December 2024, R5 000, will be paid.

3.1.1 Expected cash sales for December 2024, R132 000. Cost of sales, R101 000.

3.1.2 Drawings by the owner budgeted for December 2024, R40 000. This includes R34 000 cash and the remainder for merchandise.

3.1.3 A fixed deposit of R245 000 will mature on 31 December 2024. A direct deposit of R264 600 (inclusive of interest) will be made into the current banking account of the business on this date. Interest is not capitalised.

## Method

classify budget vs income statement

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

The test for each item: the Cash Budget records only actual money flowing in or out, while the Projected Statement of Comprehensive Income records only incomes and expenses.

Example: the insurance premium is both a cash payment and an expense, so it appears in both: Cash Budget payment 5 000; Projected Statement expense 5 000.

3.1.1: Cash sales bring in money, so the Cash Budget shows a receipt of 132 000. The Projected Statement shows the sales income of 132 000 and the matching cost of sales expense of 101 000 (or the net effect of 31 000).

3.1.2: Only the cash portion of drawings, R34 000, is a cash outflow for the Cash Budget. The R6 000 merchandise portion is not a cash flow, and drawings never appear in the Statement of Comprehensive Income — they reduce equity, not profit.

3.1.3: The full deposit of R264 600 lands in the bank, so it is a Cash Budget receipt. But only the interest portion, 264 600 - 245 000 = 19 600, is income in the Projected Statement — the R245 000 is the return of the fixed deposit capital, not income.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

3.1.1: Cash Budget receipt 132 000; Projected SOCI income 132 000 and expense 101 000 (OR net effect 31 000, two marks). 3.1.2: Cash Budget payment 34 000. 3.1.3: Cash Budget receipt 264 600; Projected SOCI income 19 600. (Example: Cash Budget payment 5 000; Projected SOCI expense 5 000.) -1 per line for superfluous entry (max -2); only if a mark is earned on that line.

Because stock is replaced through monthly purchases and all merchandise is bought on credit, credit purchases equal the cost of sales: 137 600. (Memo option 2: work in the other order — [103 200 x 100/125] = 82 560 (two marks) x 100/60 (one mark). Workings in square brackets constitute one part, cannot be separated.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

137 600 (one part correct)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.1b

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q3.2.1b.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

**Note (source discrepancy):** The November column total in the memo (133 412) does not match the Payment to creditors figure printed in the paper's Cash Budget extract for November (207 012). Both figures are transcribed verbatim from each source; the memo arithmetic (36 800 + 96 612 = 133 412; 33 200 + 100 104 = 133 304) is internally consistent, and the December total of 133 304 is the accepted answer.

## Question (5 marks)

Complete the Creditors' Payment Schedule for December 2024. (Information: creditors are paid 75% in the month after the date of purchase to qualify for a 3% discount, and the balance is paid in the month thereafter; credit purchases were R147 200 for September, R132 800 for October, and R137 600 for November — as calculated in question 3.2.1a.)

## Method

creditors payment schedule

## Memo working

Each month's credit purchases are settled in two slices: 75% in the following month, but only 97% of that slice is actually paid because of the 3% discount, and the remaining 25% in the month after that. For the December column: October purchases contribute their final 25% slice, 132 800 x 25% = 33 200; November purchases (137 600, see 3.2.1a) contribute the discounted slice, 137 600 x 75% x 97% = 100 104 (must be x [75% x 97%]; three marks if credit purchase not shown). December payment total: 33 200 + 100 104 = 133 304. (For reference, the memo's November column is: September 147 200 x 25% = 36 800; October 132 800 x 75% x 97% = 96 612; total 133 412. A December entry for September purchases would be superfluous and loses the method mark on the total.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

December column: October purchases 33 200; November purchases 100 104; total December payment 133 304 (one part correct)

2 800 (one part correct)

budget vs actual comment

Any two of these points, each supported with figures, earn the marks. Comparisons must be against the October budget, not September.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Any TWO valid explanations with figures: The number of customers grew (from 540) to 729 / by 189 / by 35%; Gross profit has improved (from R60 000) to R82 875 / by R22 875 / by 38,1%; Total sales has improved (from R160 000) to R221 000 / by R61 000 / by 38%. # Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.3c

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q3.2.3c.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Comment on the control over delivery expenses and packing materials for October 2024. Quote figures. (Information I compares October 2024 budgeted with October 2024 actual: total sales R160 000 vs R221 000; delivery expenses R24 000 vs R33 150; packing materials R14 400 vs R26 520.)

## Method

expense control comment

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) — Because these are variable costs, judge control by comparing each expense to sales, not by the rand overspend alone. Delivery expenses: budgeted at 24 000 on sales of 160 000, which is 15% of sales; actual 33 150 on sales of 221 000 is still 15% of sales — the increase of R9 150 (38,1%) simply tracks the 38,1% rise in sales, so control is effective. Packing materials: budgeted at 14 400 on 160 000, which is 9% of sales; actual 26 520 on 221 000 is 12% of sales — the overspend of R12 120 (84,2%) far outstrips the 38,1% sales growth, so this cost is not well controlled.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Delivery expenses (2 marks; must be compared to sales; do not accept comparison to September figures): Effective control — budgeted at 15% of sales, actual is 15% of sales (100% utilised); OR overspent by R9 150 / (from R24 000) to R33 150 / by 38,1%, while total sales also increased by 38,1% only / actual sales of R221 000 exceeds the budgeted sales (R160 000). Packing material (2 marks): Not well controlled — actual exceeded budgeted by 33,3% / budgeted for 9% on sales and 12% has been spent; OR overspent by R12 120 (from R14 400) to R26 520 / by 84,2%, while total sales increased by 38,1% only.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q4.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

VIVAN TRADERS: Information is provided for the budget period ending 31 January 2026. Complete the Debtors' Collection Schedule for January 2026. (The ANSWER BOOK pre-prints the schedule with credit sales October 2025 R1 417 500, November 2025 R1 443 750, December 2025 R1 496 250; the December 2025 collection column is completed as 198 450, 721 875 and 430 920 with total receipts 1 351 245; the January 2026 credit sales row and collection column are to be completed. From the information: total sales are November R1 925 000, December R1 995 000, January R2 030 000; credit sales account for 75% of total sales; debtors pay 30% in the month of sales subject to a 4% discount, 50% in the month following the month of sales, and 14% two months after the month of sales; the remaining amount is written off as irrecoverable in the third month after sales.)

## Method

debtors collection schedule

## Memo working

Work down the January 2026 column, one sales month at a time. From November 2025 credit sales of 1 443 750 (1 925 000 x 75%), January is two months after the sale, so collect 14%: 1 443 750 x 14% = 202 125. From December 2025 credit sales of 1 496 250 (1 995 000 x 75%), January is the month after the sale, so collect 50%: 1 496 250 x 50% = 748 125. January 2026 credit sales are 2 030 000 x 75% = 1 522 500; of these, 30% pay in the month of sale and receive the 4% discount, so the cash received is 1 522 500 x 30% x 96% = 438 480. Receipts from debtors for January = 202 125 + 748 125 + 438 480 = 1 388 730. (Memo cautions: if the credit sales of R1 522 500 are not shown but the R438 480 is correct, award three marks; a collection entered against October 2025 in the January column is superfluous — October's 198 450 was already collected in December — and loses the method mark on the total.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

January 2026 column: collections from November 2025 sales 202 125; collections from December 2025 sales 748 125; January 2026 credit sales 1 522 500 with collections 438 480; Receipts from debtors R1 388 730 (one part correct)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q4.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (13 marks)

Calculate the amounts denoted by (i) to (iv) in the extract of the Projected Statement of Comprehensive Income: (i) Bad debts in January 2026; (ii) Salary: sales manager for January 2026; (iii) Salaries: assistants for December 2025; (iv) Advertising for December 2025. (From QUESTION 4.1, Vivan Traders. Extract from the Projected Statement of Comprehensive Income — December 2025: sales 1 995 000, bad debts 78 600, salary: sales manager 29 000, salaries: assistants (iii), advertising (iv); January 2026: sales 2 030 000, bad debts (i), salary: sales manager (ii), salaries: assistants 88 000, advertising 182 700. Additional information: October 2025 credit sales were R1 417 500; debtors pay 30% in the month of sales, 50% the next month, 14% two months after, and the remainder is written off as irrecoverable in the third month after sales. The sales manager is paid for 20 days per month at a fixed daily rate and will take four days' unpaid leave in January 2026. All assistants will receive a 60% bonus in December, and their annual salary increase of 10% on 1 January 2026. Advertising is budgeted at a fixed percentage of the monthly sales.)

**Note (documented paper/memo conflict):** The paper's Information C states that the assistants receive the 60% bonus "in December 2026", although the budget period ends 31 January 2026 and the statement extract covers December 2025. The memo applies the bonus to the December 2025 salaries — its primary answer for (iii) is 128 000 (80 000 + 48 000) — while also accepting 80 000 for one method mark. The paper wording appears to be a misprint for December 2025.

## Method

projected income statement amounts

## Memo working

(i) Bad debts written off in January 2026 come from October 2025 credit sales: the collection pattern accounts for 30% + 50% + 14% = 94%, so the irrecoverable remainder is 6%. Bad debts = 1 417 500 x 6% = 85 050 (OR 1 417 500 - 1 332 450). (ii) The sales manager earns a fixed daily rate for 20 days: daily rate = 29 000 / 20 = 1 450; four days' unpaid leave costs 1 450 x 4 = 5 800, so January salary = 29 000 - 5 800 = 23 200 (OR 29 000 x 16/20). (iii) January's 88 000 already includes the 10% increase, so the December base salary is 88 000 x 100/110 = 80 000; adding the 60% December bonus of 80 000 x 60% = 48 000 gives 128 000 (OR 80 000 x 1,6 OR 88 000 x 160/110). (Memo alternative answer: 80 000, one method mark — see the note above.) (iv) Advertising is a fixed percentage of sales: 182 700 / 2 030 000 = 9%, so December advertising = 1 995 000 x 9% = 179 550.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

(i) R85 050 (one part correct); (ii) R23 200 (one part correct); (iii) R128 000 (one part correct) OR R80 000 (one method mark); (iv) R179 550 (one part correct)

## Question (3 marks)

Calculate the following for January 2026: Cash purchases of trading stock. (From QUESTION 4.1, Vivan Traders: total sales for January 2026 are R2 030 000; the mark-up is 60% on cost; stock is replaced in the month of sales and a fixed-base stock level is maintained; 20% of stock is bought for cash.)

cash purchases of stock

Because stock is replaced in the month of sale at a fixed base level, January purchases equal January cost of sales. With a mark-up of 60% on cost, cost of sales = sales x 100/160: 2 030 000 x 100/160 = 1 268 750. Cash purchases are 20% of that: 1 268 750 x 20% = 253 750. In one step: 2 030 000 x 20/160 [100/160 x 20/100] = 253 750 (OR 1 268 750 - 1 015 000, total purchases less the 80% credit portion).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R253 750 (one part correct)

## Question (4 marks)

Calculate the amount of the fixed deposit which will mature on 31 January 2026. (From QUESTION 4.1, Vivan Traders: a fixed deposit, including the quarterly interest, matures on 31 January 2026; the interest rate is 8% p.a., receivable quarterly; interest is not capitalised; the Projected Statement of Comprehensive Income shows interest on fixed deposit of R5 440 in January 2026 and R0 in December 2025.)

## Method

fixed deposit from interest

## Memo working

The R5 440 received in January is one quarter's interest (interest is receivable quarterly and is not capitalised). Convert it to a full year's interest: 5 440 x 12/3 (or x 4) = 21 760. The annual rate is 8%, so the capital is 21 760 x 100/8 = 272 000. Equivalently, one quarter at 8% p.a. is 2% of the capital, so 5 440 / 2% = 272 000. (Memo alternative: treating 5 440 as one month's interest, 5 440 x 12/1 x 100/8 = 816 000 — one part correct plus one method mark.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R272 000 (one part correct)

- Public positive campaigns may be used to inform the public about the benefits of merit goods to increase demand

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

How can a lack of information by various market participants lead to the misallocation of resources? (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: work through the market participants one by one — consumers, workers, businesses, investors and the government — and for each, state what information they lack and then link it to a wasteful outcome. The link is what earns the second mark each time: a fact alone only lists, an explained consequence discusses. Give FOUR developed points for 2 marks each. **Marking note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Market participants do not always have the necessary information at their disposal to make rational or informed decision
- Consumers may pay higher prices due to lack information about the prices of goods and services charged by different suppliers
- Consumer buy products that are harmful to their health because they do not have enough information about the ingredients
- Workers may earn less income because they are unaware of other jobs opportunities outside their current employment
- Potential workers may stay unemployed due to lack of information about the available job opportunities in different industries
- Businesses incur higher cost of production due to lack of knowledge about new technologies that are more cost effective
- Producers may experience disruptions in their operations because they do not have information about the availability of production inputs such as raw materials
- Lack of accurate information about the productivity of labour may result in entrepreneurs employing incompetent workers
- Investors may venture into business opportunities that are less profitable as result of lack of full knowledge about market opportunities
- The government may implement policies that do not improve the efficiency of market due to lack of information about the actual prevailing market conditions
- Producers who know more about the market than buyers may create a situation where buyers are exploited.
- Some producers may even use their knowledge of market conditions to block entry of new participants into the market.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q4.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, explain the effect of maximum prices on the market. (2 x 4)

## Method

graph drawing explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: start with an ordinary demand-and-supply diagram in equilibrium at price P and quantity Q. A maximum price is a legal ceiling, so to have any effect it must sit BELOW equilibrium — draw a horizontal line at P1 under P. At that lower price, consumers want more (quantity demanded rises to Q2) while producers offer less (quantity supplied falls to Q1). The horizontal gap between Q1 and Q2 is the shortage, and shortages invite black markets where goods change hands above the legal price. Marks: correct labelling of the axes = 1; correct drawing and labelling of the demand and supply curves = 1; correct indication or labelling of the maximum price = 1; correct labelling on the axes = 1 (max 4 for the graph, max 4 for the explanation).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Graph titled MAXIMUM PRICES: PRICE against QUANTITY; downward-sloping demand curve D and upward-sloping supply curve S intersecting at equilibrium price P and quantity Q; a horizontal maximum price line at P1 below P; at P1 quantity supplied is Q1 and quantity demanded is Q2, with the gap between Q1 and Q2 labelled 'Shortage'.

Explanation (Max 4):

- The government sets a maximum price of P1 below the equilibrium market price P to allow consumers to afford basic products
- The quantity demanded increases from Q to Q2 and the quantity supplied decreases from Q to Q1.
- A shortage of Q1 to Q2 is created in the market, as demand is more than supply.
- Product shortages can lead to the creation of black markets, where the goods may be sold at higher prices

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q1.3.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Give ONE term: A technique used to evaluate the social costs and benefits associated with public projects.

## Method

terminology recall

A technique that weighs the social costs of a public project against its social benefits — used by government to decide on projects such as dams and highways — is cost-benefit analysis.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Cost benefit analysis

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q2.3.5.

## Question (4 marks)

How can producer subsidies positively influence the economy? (2 x 2)

(Refers to the TAXES ON PRODUCTION graph in Q2.3.1.)

## Method

explanation

A producer subsidy works in the opposite direction to the production tax shown in the stimulus graph: instead of shifting supply left and raising the price, a subsidy lowers producers' costs and shifts supply to the right. Trace the chain from lower costs outwards — lower production costs ease inflation, more output means economic growth, more output needs more workers so unemployment falls, and lower prices leave consumers with more spending power. Any two chains, fully explained, earn the 4 marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Producers will incur lower cost of production which may reduce inflation in the economy
- Businesses may be encouraged to produce more goods and services which stimulates economic growth
- Increase in production may create more job opportunities thereby reducing unemployment in the economy
- Consumers may pay lower prices for goods and services leading to higher consumers spending.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q2.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Briefly discuss the immobility of factors of production and lack of information as factors that may lead to misallocation of resources in markets. (2 x 4)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: handle the two causes of market failure under separate headings, up to 4 marks each. For immobility of factors of production, the core idea is that markets cannot adjust quickly because the factors themselves are slow to move: labour needs retraining before it can change occupation, relocating is costly and breaks social ties, and physical capital like factory buildings simply cannot be moved to follow demand. For lack of information, the core idea is that rational decisions need information that consumers, workers and entrepreneurs often do not have: consumers cannot maximise utility without knowing products, workers miss job opportunities they never hear about, and entrepreneurs misjudge the cost and productivity of inputs. **Marking note: a maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Immobility of factors of production (Max 4):

- Most markets do not adjust rapidly to changes in supply and demand due to immobility of factors of production.
- Labour may take time to move into new occupations due to skills that may need to be upgraded / The supply of skilled labour cannot be increased immediately because of the time it takes to be trained.
- Labour may take time to move geographically to meet the changes in consumer demand due to high relocation cost and social ties.
- Physical capital, such as factory buildings and infrastructure cannot be moved to fit a change in demand.
- Other physical capital, such as machinery and equipment, may be moved from one place to another at higher cost.
- Technological applications change production methods, but it takes time for most industries to adapt. For example, the use of robots rather than physical labour.
- Greater technological change requires workers to be flexible and update their skills to change employment, occupations and work patterns which may take time.

Lack of information (Max 4):

- Consumers, workers and entrepreneurs do not always have the necessary information at their disposal to make rational decisions.
- Despite the advances in technology, consumers still lack information about products and producers to maximise their utility.
- Workers may be unaware of job opportunities outside their current employment to ensure that they use their labour effectively.
- Entrepreneurs may lack information about the costs, availability and productivity of some factors of production which may lead to productive inefficiency.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q4.2.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Why do markets undersupply goods that generate positive externalities?

(Refers to the IMPERFECT DISTRIBUTION OF INCOME AND WEALTH cartoon in Q4.2.1.)

## Method

explanation

A positive externality means part of the benefit goes to society, not the buyer or seller. Because businesses are not paid for that external benefit, goods like education look less profitable than they really are to society — so the market produces too little of them.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Goods that generate positive externalities, such as education, are often not highly rated by the market which leads to undersupply.
- Businesses do not fully account for the benefits that accrue to the society, as a result they may not be incentivised to produce enough of the goods leading to undersupply.
- Goods with positive externalities are not profitable because businesses are not rewarded for the external benefits.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q4.2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

How can the government use redress methods to redistribute wealth in South Africa? (2 x 2)

(Refers to the IMPERFECT DISTRIBUTION OF INCOME AND WEALTH cartoon in Q4.2.1.)

## Method

explanation

Redress methods correct historical disadvantage directly. Pair each instrument with what it redistributes: the Employment Equity Act redistributes job opportunities through affirmative action; BBBEE redistributes business ownership, management and control; RDP housing and property subsidies redistribute residential property; land restitution returns land or compensates those dispossessed after 1913; land redistribution transfers agricultural land to previously disadvantaged persons. Two fully explained methods earn the 4 marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- The Employment Equity Act can be used to promote affirmative action to give first preference to previous disadvantage in employment opportunities.
- Broad Based Black Economic Empowerment (BBBEE) can be used to significantly increase the number of black people who own, manage and control businesses.
- Property subsidies and free housing (RDP) can be used to help the previously disadvantaged groups to own residential properties.
- Land restitution aims to return land or pay cash compensation to those who lost their land because of discriminatory laws and practices after 1913.
- Land redistribution aims to redistribute the country's agricultural land to previously disadvantaged persons.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

multiple choice

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

C

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: An electrolytic cell is set up to electroplate an iron rod with nickel. [Diagram: electrolytic cell with a battery, a nickel electrode and an iron rod in a solution.] Consider the following statements: (i) The iron rod is the negative electrode. (ii) The metal ions in the solution undergo reduction. (iii) The anode is pure nickel. Which of the above statements are TRUE? A (i) and (ii) only B (i) and (iii) only C (ii) and (iii) only D (i), (ii) and (iii)

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) In electroplating, the object to be plated (the iron rod) is made the cathode, connected to the negative terminal of the battery — statement (i) is TRUE. At this cathode the Ni2+ ions in the solution gain electrons and are reduced to nickel metal, which deposits on the rod — statement (ii) is TRUE. The anode is pure nickel, which is oxidised and dissolves to replenish the Ni2+ ions in the solution — statement (iii) is TRUE. All three statements are true — option D.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Study the reactions below. Reaction 1: CH3CH2CHOHCH3 --(H2SO4 conc.)--> Compound P (major product) + H2O. Reaction 2: Compound P --(hydrogenation)--> Compound Q. Which ONE of the following combinations is the CORRECT IUPAC names of compounds P and Q? A But-1-ene; Butane B But-2-ene; Butane C But-1-ene; Butan-2-ol D But-2-ene; Butan-2-ol

multiple choice

By Zaitsev's rule the major product P is the more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, not but-1-ene. Reaction 2 is hydrogenation: adding H2 across the double bond of but-2-ene saturates it to the alkane butane, so Q is butane. That combination is option B.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q1.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: The potential energy diagram is for the hypothetical chemical reaction X + Y ⇌ Z. [Diagram: potential energy versus course of reaction; the products lie LOWER than the reactants (exothermic) and the activation-energy hump for the forward reaction is smaller than that of the reverse reaction.] Which ONE of the following combinations of values for the heat of the reaction and the activation energies can be obtained for this reaction? (ΔH(forward); EA(forward); EA(reverse), all in kJ·mol⁻¹) A -400; 300; 100 B -200; 300; 100 C +400; 100; 300 D -200; 100; 300

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The products lie lower than the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH must be negative — this eliminates option C. The forward activation-energy hump is smaller than the reverse one, so EA(forward) must be less than EA(reverse) — this eliminates A and B, which both have EA(forward) = 300 greater than EA(reverse) = 100. Check option D for consistency using ΔH = EA(forward) − EA(reverse) = 100 − 300 = −200 kJ·mol⁻¹, which matches the stated ΔH of −200.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Initially, an equal number of moles of hydrogen gas, H2(g), and iodine gas, I2(g), are mixed in a closed container. The reaction reaches equilibrium at a constant temperature according to the balanced equation H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Which ONE of the following is ALWAYS TRUE at equilibrium? A [H2] = [I2] B [HI] = [I2] C [HI] = 2[H2] D [H2] = [I2] = [HI]

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) H2 and I2 react in a 1:1 mole ratio. The container starts with equal moles of each, and every bit of reaction removes them in equal amounts, so their concentrations stay equal at every instant — including at equilibrium: [H2] = [I2]. The HI concentration depends on how far the reaction has proceeded before equilibrium is reached, so the relations in options B, C and D are not always true.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q1.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Consider the following reaction at equilibrium: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), ΔH = −188 kJ·mol⁻¹. Which ONE of the changes to the reaction conditions below will increase the yield of SO3(g)? A The addition of O2(g) B The addition of a catalyst C An increase in temperature D An increase in the volume of the container at a constant temperature

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Apply Le Chatelier's principle. Adding O2(g) (option A) increases a reactant concentration, so the equilibrium shifts toward the products and the yield of SO3 increases. A catalyst (option B) speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally and does not change the yield. Increasing the temperature (option C) favours the endothermic reverse reaction, because the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −188 kJ·mol⁻¹). Increasing the volume (option D) decreases the pressure and shifts the equilibrium to the side with more gas moles — the reactant side (3 moles versus 2) — decreasing the yield.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q1.7.

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: The table shows the ionisation constants, Ka, at 25 °C: butanoic acid 1,5 x 10⁻⁵; ethanoic acid 1,8 x 10⁻⁵. Consider the following statements for these two acids when they have equal concentration at 25 °C: (i) Both are weak acids. (ii) Butanoic acid is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid. (iii) The butanoic acid solution has a lower concentration of hydronium ion, H3O+(aq), than the ethanoic acid solution. Which of the above statements are TRUE? A (i) and (ii) only B (i) and (iii) only C (ii) and (iii) only D (i), (ii) and (iii)

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Statement (i): both Ka values are very small (order of 10⁻⁵), so both acids ionise only partially in water — both are weak acids. TRUE. Statement (ii): butanoic acid has the SMALLER Ka (1,5 x 10⁻⁵ versus 1,8 x 10⁻⁵), so it is the weaker acid, not the stronger one. FALSE. Statement (iii): at equal concentration, a smaller Ka means less ionisation, so the butanoic acid solution has a lower concentration of H3O+ ions. TRUE. Statements (i) and (iii) only — option B.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q1.8.

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Which ONE of the following pairs of acids and bases, all of the same concentration, react to give the highest pH at the equivalence point in a titration at 25 °C? A HCℓ and NH3 B HCℓ and NaOH C HNO3 and KOH D CH3COOH and NaOH

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) At the equivalence point the solution contains only the salt formed by the acid and the base. A strong acid with a strong base (options B and C) gives a neutral salt solution with pH 7. A strong acid with a weak base (option A) gives a salt whose ammonium ion hydrolyses to make the solution acidic, pH below 7. A weak acid with a strong base (option D, CH3COOH and NaOH) gives the ethanoate ion, which hydrolyses as a weak base, making the equivalence-point solution basic — the highest pH of the four.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: A standard galvanic cell is set up. [Diagram: voltmeter V connecting a Cd electrode in Cd2+(aq) and an Ag electrode in Ag+(aq), with a salt bridge between the half-cells.] Which ONE of the following combinations of the metal used as cathode and the electron flow direction is CORRECT? A Cd; Cd to Ag B Ag; Cd to Ag C Cd; Ag to Cd D Ag; Ag to Cd

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Compare standard reduction potentials from the table of standard electrode potentials: E°(Ag+/Ag) = +0,80 V is higher than E°(Cd2+/Cd) = −0,40 V, so Ag+ is reduced and the silver electrode is the cathode, while cadmium is oxidised at the anode. In the external circuit electrons always flow from the anode to the cathode, that is from Cd to Ag. Cathode Ag with electron flow from Cd to Ag — option B.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q9.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q9.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle. K, T and P lie on the circle (K at the top, T lower left and P lower right; chords KT and KP and radii OT and OP are drawn). Use the diagram above to prove the theorem which states that the angle subtended by a chord (or arc) at the centre of the circle is equal to twice the angle subtended by the same chord (or arc) at the circumference, that is prove that TÔP = 2 TK̂P.

## Method

central angle theorem proof

## Memo working

Construction: draw KO and produce it beyond O; this splits both the centre angle and the circumference angle into two parts, labelled Ô1, Ô2 and K̂1, K̂2 on either side of the line. In triangle KOT: Ô1 = K̂1 + T̂, because the exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. But OK and OT are radii, so triangle KOT is isosceles and K̂1 = T̂ (angles opposite equal sides). Therefore Ô1 = 2K̂1. By the same argument in triangle KOP: Ô2 = K̂2 + P̂ (exterior angle of triangle) and K̂2 = P̂ (angles opposite equal radii), so Ô2 = 2K̂2. Adding the two results: Ô1 + Ô2 = 2K̂1 + 2K̂2 = 2(K̂1 + K̂2); therefore TÔP = 2 TK̂P. (Alternative memo proof for the reflex case: draw KO; use the isosceles triangles and angle sums, then TÔP = 360° - (KÔT + KÔP) = 2K̂1 + 2K̂2, angles around a point.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

TÔP = 2 TK̂P

## Question (2 marks)

In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle. POF is the diameter of the circle and MF is a tangent to the circle at F. OM cuts the circle at L. P̂ = 32°. (In the figure, P is at the top and F at the bottom of the diameter; chord PL runs to lower-left point L; OM passes through L to the external point M at bottom-left; the angles at O are labelled 1 above OM and 2 below OM.) Calculate, with reasons, the size of: Ô2

## Method

central angle twice inscribed

## Memo working

The centre angle Ô2 and the circumference angle P̂ both stand on the same arc LF. By the theorem that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference: Ô2 = 2 × 32° = 64°. (Alternative memo method: PL̂O = P̂ = 32°, angles opposite equal radii in triangle OPL; then Ô2 = 32° + 32° = 64° as the exterior angle of the triangle.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Ô2 = 64°

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.4b

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q3.2.4b.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

The time spent (in minutes) by 32 customers in a store is given in rank order: 6 8 9 10 12 15 15 15 15 15 17 / 18 19 22 23 23 23 24 25 25 25 26 / 27 28 29 33 37 40 43 43 67 127. The value 127 is an outlier. (b) Vuyo stated that if the outlier value was removed from the data set, the new interquartile range (IQR) value would be 13. Verify Vuyo's statement, showing ALL calculations.

## Method

interquartile range verification

## Memo working

Remove the outlier 127, leaving 31 ordered values. The median is now the 16th value, the lower quartile is the middle of the bottom 15 values (the 8th value) and the upper quartile is the middle of the top 15 values (the 24th value). Counting along the list: New Quartile 1 = 15 (1RT); New Quartile 3 = 28 (1RT). Then apply the formula IQR = Q3 - Q1 (1A correct formula): IQR = 28 - 15 (1MCA subtracting values) = 13. This matches Vuyo's value, so he is CORRECT (1O conclusion).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

New Q1 = 15, new Q3 = 28, IQR = 28 - 15 = 13. He is CORRECT.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q4.2.3.

## Question (5 marks)

TABLE 6 shows the actual number of guests per function at a hotel during a specific month — 2023: 180, 350, 400, 200, 215, 90, 150, 230, 160; 2022: 360, 160, 300, 70, 160, 200, 240. The manager stated that the range of the number of guests per function during 2022 is the same as the range of the number of guests per function during 2023. Verify, showing ALL calculations, whether his statement is valid.

## Method

range comparison verification

## Memo working

The range is the highest value minus the lowest value. For 2022 the highest is 360 and the lowest is 70: Range 2022 = 360 - 70 (1RT both correct values, 1MCA concept of range) = 290 (1CA). For 2023 the highest is 400 and the lowest is 90: Range 2023 = 400 - 90 = 310 (1A range). Since 290 is not equal to 310, the two ranges differ, so the manager's statement is NOT VALID (1O conclusion).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Range 2022 = 360 - 70 = 290; Range 2023 = 400 - 90 = 310. His statement is NOT VALID.

## Question (2 marks)

TABLE 3 shows the population data for South Africa by population group and gender for 2022, with a total of 60 604 992 people. State whether the total number of people in the table represents discrete data or continuous data.

## Method

classify data type

## Memo working

A number of people is a count: it can only take whole-number values — you cannot have a fraction of a person. Counted whole-number data is discrete; continuous data comes from measurement and can take any value in a range (like height or mass). So the total number of people is discrete data. (Memo: 2A correct classification.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Discrete

words to numerals

median of data

difference verification

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P1, November 2025, question Q4.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Comment on how the 'rights issue' improved the solvency of the company to a favourable position. Refer to the effect of the rights issue on the assets, equities and liabilities of the company, assuming that the company's bank balance was favourable.

(The context: Piranna Ltd, declared insolvent in March 2025, implemented a rights issue — new shares issued to existing shareholders only. It offered five million shares at a 30% discounted price of R27 per share while the shares were trading at approximately R39 per share; shareholders responded positively and the company raised sufficient cash to move out of insolvency.)

## Method

rights issue solvency effect

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

The reasoning: trace the rights issue through the accounting equation. The cash received increases assets; the new shares issued increase equity by the same amount; and no debt is created, so liabilities stay the same. With assets rising while liabilities are unchanged, assets move back above liabilities and the solvency position becomes favourable.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Assets will increase as more cash is received (1 mark).
- Equity will increase as more shares have been issued (1 mark).
- Liabilities will remain unchanged (1 mark).

## Question (8 marks)

How can the macroeconomic objective of price stability positively influence the South African economy? (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Price stability ensures that prices remain relatively stable which encourages consumer spending and stimulates economic growth.
- Stable prices promote job creation and reduce unemployment rate in the economy through more foreign direct investments.
- Savings may be encouraged which ensures availability of loanable funds for private investments.
- Interest rates may remain stable and encourage spending on durable goods, such as taking mortgage bonds to purchase houses.
- Price stability maintains the purchasing power of money, since the real incomes of households are better preserved.
- Stable prices help to maintain demand for South African exports on global markets, thereby ensuring exchange rate stability.
- Extreme fluctuations on business cycles may be avoided which promotes more sustainable economic growth.
- Price stability helps to keep inflation expectations low which reduces wage demands by workers and maintain industrial peace.
- Price stability helps consumers and businesses to plan and make informed decisions concerning saving, spending and investments.
- The credit rating of South Africa may improve which could lead to increased investments in the country.

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

## Question (2 marks)

How can the government exclude free riders from the consumption of public goods? (1 x 2)

## Method

explanation

Start from the free-rider problem: because public goods are non-excludable, people can benefit without paying. The government breaks this by making users pay — either directly, through user charges such as toll fees and stadium entrance fees, or indirectly, by financing the goods through taxes so that everyone is forced to contribute. Give one such measure, explained, for the two marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- The government may impose user charges/fees/levies for using collective goods such as stadiums and national roads.
- The government may use taxes to prevent free-riders from consuming public goods by forcing everyone to contribute financially.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2025, question Q2.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Briefly discuss full employment and economic equity as macroeconomic objectives of the government. (2 x 4)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: structure the discussion under two headings, four marks each. For full employment, define it first (everyone who is looking for work is employed), then explain how the government pursues it over the short term (direct employment schemes and youth employment subsidies), the medium term (supporting labour-intensive sectors such as agriculture and offering investment incentives in industries that employ many people) and the long term (supporting knowledge- and capital-intensive sectors and improving education and training). For economic equity, define it (the economy's resources equally distributed amongst the population), anchor it in the Gini coefficient (below 0,5 signals a more equal distribution; South Africa's is above 0,6), then explain the redistribution tools — progressive taxation, where higher earners pay higher rates, and social spending such as free basic education, health care, grants and subsidies.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

**Full employment**

- Full employment is when all people who are looking for jobs get employed.
- The aim of the government is to create decent and sustainable jobs.
- Employment rate is measured as the percentage of the economically active population (EAP) that is employed.
- In the short-term, employment can be increased by using direct employment schemes and subsidies such as youth employment subsidies.
- In the medium term, government can support labour intensive activities especially in agricultural sector and provide investment incentives to businesses in industries that employ many people such as the manufacturing industry.
- In the long term, the government can support knowledge intensive and capital-intensive sectors in order to remain competitive or improve the quality of education and training to increase the employability of the future labour force.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

**Economic equity**

- Economic equity refers to a situation whereby the resources of the economy are equally distributed amongst the population.
- Income is more equally distributed when the Gini-coefficient is less than 0,5.
- The distribution of income in the economy is not fair, as some people earn a large amount of money while others earn less.
- In SA the income gap is still high as evidenced by the Gini-coefficient of above 0,6.
- Through the progressive tax system, the government can redistribute income.
- Progressive taxation means that higher income earners pay higher tax rates.
- The government can help the poor with free basic education, free basic health-care, social grants, free services and subsidies.

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

**Note on a source anomaly:** the official memo's marking note prints 'A maximum of 4 marks my be allocated' — a verbatim misprint of 'may'. The marking note is given above with the standard spelling.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2025, question Q4.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Analyse the fiscal policy measures that can be used to dampen the economy. (4 x 2)

## Method

analysis

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: dampening the economy calls for restrictive (contractionary) fiscal policy, applied during the prosperity phase of the business cycle. Analyse four measures, two marks each: cut government expenditure on infrastructure or the public-sector wage bill to reduce aggregate demand; raise direct taxes (higher personal income tax reduces disposable income and consumer spending; higher business taxes reduce profit prospects and activity); raise indirect taxes such as VAT and excise duties so that higher prices curb expenditure; and trim social spending or subsidies and incentives, alongside encouraging saving rather than spending through vehicles such as tax-free savings accounts.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Restrictive or contractionary fiscal policy is used during the prosperity phase of the business cycle to dampen the economy.
- Decreasing government expenditure on infrastructural projects reduce demand for goods and services.
- Cutting down on public sector wages (compensation of employees), may help to reduce aggregate demand for goods and services and discourage production.
- Raising taxes on businesses will decrease profit prospects in the economy leading to an overall decline in the economic activity.
- Increasing personal income tax may reduce disposable income, leading to a decline in consumer spending.
- Increasing indirect taxes such as VAT, excise duties, etc. will increase the price of goods and services which reduces expenditure.
- Reduction in social spending, such as welfare grants, may reduce the households' income level which leads to lower consumption expenditure.
- A decrease in subsidies and incentives offered to businesses may lead to lower production output as the actual production cost incurred by producers increases.
- The government can provide incentives for savings, such as tax-free savings accounts, to encourage people to save rather than to spend.

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

## Method

## Question (4 marks)

Given: (sin(540° + x).cos(90° + x))/sin(-x). Simplify the expression above fully to a single trigonometric ratio.

## Method

reduction formulae

## Memo working

Reduce each factor one at a time. For the first factor, 540° is a full revolution plus 180°, so sin(540° + x) = sin(180° + x) = -sin x. For the second factor, the co-function shift gives cos(90° + x) = -sin x. In the denominator, sine is an odd function, so sin(-x) = -sin x. The expression becomes (-sin x)(-sin x)/(-sin x): the numerator is sin^2 x, and dividing by -sin x cancels one factor of sin x and flips the sign, leaving -sin x.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

-sin x

## Question (2 marks)

Hence, determine the values of x in the interval x ∈ [0° ; 360°] for which sqrt( (sin(540° + x).cos(90° + x))/sin(-x) ) will be real. (From QUESTION 5.2.1: the expression inside the square root simplifies to -sin x.)

## Method

non negative condition

## Memo working

A square root is real only when the quantity under it is not negative. From QUESTION 5.2.1 the expression equals -sin x, so we need -sin x ≥ 0, that is sin x ≤ 0. On [0° ; 360°], sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants. The endpoints where sin x = 0 (0°, 180°, 360°) must be excluded, because there the original denominator sin(-x) is zero and the expression is undefined. That leaves 180° < x < 360°.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x ∈ (180° ; 360°)  OR  180° < x < 360°

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q6.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Prove that: [tan(180° - x)](1 - cos^2 x) + cos^2 x = ((sin x - cos x)(1 + sin x.cos x))/(-cos x)

## Method

identity proof difference of cubes

## Memo working

Work from the left-hand side. Reduce tan(180° - x) to -tan x, and replace 1 - cos^2 x with sin^2 x (square identity): LHS = (-tan x)(sin^2 x) + cos^2 x. Write tan x as sin x/cos x: LHS = -(sin x/cos x)(sin^2 x) + cos^2 x = -sin^3 x/cos x + cos^2 x. Put both terms over the common denominator -cos x: multiplying cos^2 x by (-cos x)/(-cos x) gives -cos^3 x on top, so LHS = (sin^3 x - cos^3 x)/(-cos x). The numerator is a difference of cubes: sin^3 x - cos^3 x = (sin x - cos x)(sin^2 x + sin x.cos x + cos^2 x). Since sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1, the second bracket is 1 + sin x.cos x. Therefore LHS = (sin x - cos x)(1 + sin x.cos x)/(-cos x) = RHS. (Alternative memo method: start from the right-hand side, expand (sin x - cos x)(cos^2 x + sin^2 x + sin x.cos x), simplify to (sin^3 x - cos^3 x)/(-cos x), split the fraction and use the quotient and square identities to reach the left-hand side.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

LHS = RHS (identity proved)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q6.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (7 marks)

It is given that sin^2 x ; cos^2 x and (1/2) sin 2x are the first three terms of an arithmetic sequence. The constant difference of the arithmetic sequence is NOT zero. Determine the general solution for x.

## Method

arithmetic condition trig equation

## Memo working

In an arithmetic sequence consecutive differences are equal, so cos^2 x - sin^2 x = (1/2)sin 2x - cos^2 x. Expand the double angle: (1/2)sin 2x = (1/2)(2 sin x cos x) = sin x cos x. Bring everything to one side: 2cos^2 x - sin x cos x - sin^2 x = 0. This factorises as (2cos x + sin x)(cos x - sin x) = 0. The first bracket gives sin x = -2cos x, so tan x = -2; the second gives tan x = 1. The reference angles are 63,43° and 45°, so x = 116,57° + k.180° or x = 45° + k.180°, k ∈ Z. But at x = 45° + k.180° all three terms equal 1/2, making the constant difference zero — the question says the difference is NOT zero, so this solution is rejected. (Alternative memo factorisation: group as (cos x - sin x)(cos x + sin x) + cos x(cos x - sin x) = 0.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = 116,57° + k.180°, k ∈ Z (x = 45° + k.180° gives constant difference zero, excluded)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q7.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q7.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Determine the values of x for which (1 - tan 2x)(cos 2x) ≥ 0 in the interval x ∈ [0° ; 135°]. (From QUESTION 7: f(x) = cos 2x and g(x) = tan 2x - 1 are drawn for x ∈ [-135° ; 135°].)

## Method

sign analysis using graphs

## Memo working

Rewrite the inequality in terms of the drawn graphs: 1 - tan 2x = -(tan 2x - 1) = -g(x), so (1 - tan 2x)(cos 2x) ≥ 0 is the same as (tan 2x - 1)(cos 2x) ≤ 0 — we need g and f to have opposite signs (or a zero). The key x-values in [0° ; 135°] are x = 22,5° where tan 2x - 1 = 0, x = 45° where both graphs break (cos 2x = 0 and tan 2x undefined), and x = 112,5° where tan 2x - 1 = 0 again. Reading the signs from the graphs: from 0° to 22,5°, g is negative while f is positive, so the product g·f is negative — included. From 22,5° up to the asymptote region and on through to 112,5°, g and f carry the same sign, so the product is positive — excluded. From 112,5° towards 135°, g is zero and then positive while f is negative, giving g·f ≤ 0 as required — included up to, but excluding, x = 135°, where tan 2x is undefined.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x ∈ [0° ; 22,5°] ∪ [112,5° ; 135°)  OR  0° ≤ x ≤ 22,5° or 112,5° ≤ x < 135°

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q2.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

(Context: a crate of mass 8,5 kg on a rough horizontal table is connected by a light inextensible string over a frictionless pulley to a hanging mass; the system now accelerates.) Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration represented by Y on the graph if the coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the table is 0,40. [Y is the acceleration at a hanging mass of 7,4 kg.]

## Method

connected bodies newton second law

## Memo working

Treat each body separately and apply Newton's second law to each, remembering the string gives both the same acceleration a and the same tension T. For the crate on the table: Fnet = ma, so T – fk = ma, where kinetic friction fk = µkN = 0,4(8,5)(9,8) = 33,32 N. That gives T – 0,4(8,5)(9,8) = 8,5a — equation one. For the hanging mass: Fnet = ma downwards, so mg – T = ma, giving 7,4(9,8) – T = 7,4a — equation two. Add the two equations so T cancels: 7,4(9,8) – 33,32 = (8,5 + 7,4)a, that is 39,2 = 15,9a, so a = 2,47 m·s⁻². (Memo note: T can be calculated first, 54,32 N.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Y = a = 2,47 m·s⁻²

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q4.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Two trolleys, A and B, of masses of 1,5 kg and 2 kg respectively, are held in a stationary position on a straight, horizontal, frictionless track, with a compressed spring between them. The trolleys are released and the spring takes t seconds to return to its natural length. The spring then falls to the ground. Trolley A moves to the left, while trolley B moves to the right and then up a frictionless inclined plane, rising to a maximum vertical height of 1,5 m. [Diagram: before release, trolleys A (1,5 kg) and B (2 kg) with compressed spring between them; after release, A moves left, B moves right and rises 1,5 m up an incline.] Ignore the rotational effects of the wheels. 4.1 Write down the principle of conservation of mechanical energy in words.

## Method

state conservation of mechanical energy

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) This is a definition recall. The key ideas that must appear are: total mechanical energy — the sum of gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy; in an isolated system (no external or non-conservative forces doing work); remains constant / is conserved. (Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The total mechanical energy / sum of gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, in an isolated system remains constant / is conserved.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q4.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

(Context: trolley B, of mass 2 kg, leaves a spring launch on a frictionless horizontal track, then moves up a frictionless inclined plane, rising to a maximum vertical height of 1,5 m.) Calculate the speed of trolley B at the bottom of the inclined plane.

## Method

conservation of mechanical energy

## Memo working

The incline is frictionless, so mechanical energy is conserved between the bottom and the top of the incline. Option 1: (Ep + Ek)top = (Ep + Ek)bottom. At the top the trolley is momentarily at rest at height 1,5 m, so all the energy is potential: (2)(9,8)(1,5) + 0. At the bottom all of it is kinetic: 0 + ½(2)v². Setting them equal: (2)(9,8)(1,5) = ½(2)v², so v² = 2(9,8)(1,5) = 29,4 and v = 5,42 m·s⁻¹. Option 2: Wnc = ΔEk + ΔEp with zero non-conservative work: 0 = [0 – ½vi²] + [(9,8)(1,5 – 0)], giving the same vi = 5,42 m·s⁻¹. (Memo also gives Wnet = ΔEk with FgΔycos180°, ΔEk = –ΔEp, and vf² = vi² + 2aΔx options.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

v = 5,42 m·s⁻¹

Use the information above. QUESTION: Convert 220 mm to metres.

## Method

mm to m conversion

## Memo working

There are 1 000 millimetres in one metre, so to go from millimetres to metres you divide by 1 000. Take the width of the brick, 220 mm, and divide: 220 ÷ 1 000 = 0,22. So the width is 0,22 of a metre. (Memo: 1MA dividing by 1 000; 1A conversion.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

0,22 m

## Question (2 marks)

Hexagonal paving bricks are made up of 6 equal triangles (brick dimensions: equal side lengths L = 90 mm, height H = 50 mm, width W = 220 mm). Choose, from the options (A, B or C) below, the correct one that could be used to calculate the volume of the hexagonal paving brick. A: Volume = 6 x area of triangle x height. B: Volume = side length + height + width. C: Volume = 6 x perimeter x height.

## Method

volume formula multiple choice

## Memo working

Volume of any prism is the area of its base multiplied by its height. The base here is a hexagon made of 6 equal triangles, so the base area is 6 times the area of one triangle, and the volume is 6 x area of triangle x height — option A. Option B just adds three lengths together, which gives a length, not a volume; option C uses the perimeter, which measures the distance around the edge, so multiplying it by height cannot give a volume either. (Memo: 2A correct option.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A

length division

## Question (2 marks)

Mrs Kgomo is a Grade 2 teacher at Happy Valley Primary School. She has a reading corner at the back of her classroom where learners who wait for their transport after school usually sit and read a book. The school day ends at 12:55. Tendani's father was late and only came to fetch him at 14:13. Determine how long Tendani sat in the reading corner.

## Method

elapsed time calculation

## Memo working

Work out the elapsed time from 12:55 to 14:13. A reliable way is to break it at the hour: from 12:55 to 13:00 is 5 minutes, and from 13:00 to 14:13 is 1 hour 13 minutes; together that is 1 hour 18 minutes. Equivalently, subtract the times directly: 14:13 - 12:55 = 1 hour 18 minutes, which is 78 minutes or 1,3 hours. (Memo: 1MA subtracting time; 1A simplification; answer only full marks.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1 hour 18 minutes (OR 78 minutes OR 1,3 hours)

## Question (5 marks)

Mrs Kgomo stores classroom pillows in zip-up storage bags decorated with piping — thin cord covered in fabric used to decorate the bag and reinforce the seams (each bag is 46 cm long, 30 cm wide and 48 cm high). The piping around the bottom edge of some of the bags for the pillows needs to be replaced. The store sells the piping in half-metre lengths. Calculate the total length of piping she will have to purchase to replace the piping around the bottom edges of FOUR bags. You may use the following formula: Perimeter = 2 (length + width)

## Method

perimeter scaling and rounding

## Memo working

The piping runs around the bottom edge of the bag, so work out the perimeter of the base: Perimeter = 2(46 cm + 30 cm) = 2(76 cm) = 152 cm. Four bags need 152 x 4 = 608 cm, which is 6,08 m. Because the store only sells half-metre lengths, she cannot buy exactly 6,08 m — she must round up to the next half metre and buy 6,5 m. (Memo alternatives: convert to metres first, 2(0,46 + 0,3) = 1,52 m, x 4 = 6,08 m, buy 6,5 m; or count half-metre pieces, 608 cm ÷ 50 cm = 12,16, rounded up to 13 half-metre lengths.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

6,5 m (i.e. 13 half-metre lengths; 4 bags need 6,08 m)
