# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q3.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (9 marks)

Mrs Kgomo paints the front surface area of her circular wooden birthday tags every year (each tag is a circle 8 cm high and 8 cm wide with a small circular hole at the top for hanging; the area of the circular hole is 0,3142 cm^2; the spread rate of the paint is 6 m^2/l). The hardware store sells paint in 50 ml, 1 litre, 5 litre and 20 litre containers. Mrs Kgomo claims that a 50 ml can of paint will be sufficient to paint ONE side of 36 circular wooden tags. Verify her statement. Show ALL calculations. Use the following formula: Area of a circle = 3,142 x radius^2

## Method

area paint spread rate verification

## Memo working

The radius of a tag is half of 8 cm, so 4 cm. Area of a circle = 3,142 x (4 cm)^2 = 3,142 x 16 cm^2 = 50,272 cm^2. The hole is not painted, so the painted area per tag is 50,272 - 0,3142 = 49,9578 cm^2. For 36 tags the total area is 36 x 49,9578 cm^2 = 1 798,4808 cm^2. Convert to square metres by dividing by 100^2 (that is, by 10 000): 1 798,4808 ÷ 10 000 = 0,17984808 m^2. The spread rate says 1 litre (1 000 ml) covers 6 m^2, so 50 ml covers 0,3 m^2. Since 0,3 m^2 is more than the 0,17984808 m^2 needed, 50 ml is more than sufficient. (Memo alternative: paint needed = 0,17984808 ÷ 6 = 0,02997466 l, which is about 30 ml — less than 50 ml.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Area per tag = 3,142 x 4^2 = 50,272 cm^2; minus hole = 49,9578 cm^2; 36 tags = 1 798,4808 cm^2 = 0,17984808 m^2; paint needed = 0,17984808/6 l ≈ 30 ml, which is less than 50 ml. Her statement is VALID (50 ml is more than sufficient).

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.1.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q5.1.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

On the map of Australia's A1 motorway (ANNEXURE C), the leg between Cairns and Brisbane is marked as 1 705 km with a driving time of 20 h 40 min. Calculate the average speed, in km/h, from Brisbane to Cairns. You may use the following formula: Distance = speed x time

## Method

average speed from distance and time

## Memo working

Substitute the leg's values into the formula: 1 705 km = speed x 20 h 40 min. The time must be in hours only: 40 minutes is 40/60 of an hour, so 20 h 40 min = 20,67 h. Change the subject of the formula: Speed = 1 705 ÷ 20,67 = 82,5 km/h.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

82,5 km/h

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q5.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Chris and Boipelo plan to visit Uluru. This oval-shaped big rock rises 1 142 feet above the surrounding desert plain. A diagram compares the height of Uluru with other tourist attractions (Sydney Harbour Bridge 134 m; ULURU 348 m; The Eiffel Tower 324 m; The Great Pyramid of Giza 139 m; Big Ben 96 m). Determine, rounded to THREE decimal places, the conversion factor from feet to metres used in this diagram, in the form 1 foot = ... m.

## Method

derive conversion factor

## Memo working

The same height is given in both units: 1 142 feet (in the text) equals 348 m (in the diagram). To find what 1 foot is worth in metres, divide the metres by the feet: 1 foot = 348 ÷ 1 142 = 0,304728546..., which rounds to three decimal places as 0,305 m.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1 foot ≈ 0,305 m

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q5.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

A diagram compares the heights of tourist attractions around the world: Sydney Harbour Bridge 134 m; ULURU 348 m; The Eiffel Tower 324 m; The Great Pyramid of Giza 139 m; Big Ben 96 m. Write, as a simplified ratio, the heights of Uluru : Eiffel Tower : Big Ben.

## Method

simplify three part ratio

## Memo working

Read the three heights from the diagram in the order asked: 348 : 324 : 96. All three numbers divide by 12 (their highest common factor): 348 ÷ 12 = 29, 324 ÷ 12 = 27, 96 ÷ 12 = 8. So the simplified ratio is 29 : 27 : 8.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

29 : 27 : 8

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q1.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

One way to save money during winter is to wrap the geyser and waterpipes with a geyser blanket made of aerolite, an insulating material that can easily be cut (pictures show the steps of wrapping a cylindrical geyser in aerolite). Choose ONE of the following formulae that can be used to calculate how much aerolite is needed for the total surface area of the geyser only. Write only the letter (A-D). A: pi x radius^2 x height + 2 x pi x radius. B: pi x radius x height + length x width. C: 2 x pi x radius x height + 2 x pi x radius^2. D: 1/2 base x height.

## Method

select surface area formula

## Memo working

A geyser is a closed cylinder, so its total surface area has two parts: the curved (lateral) surface, which unrolls into a rectangle of area 2 x pi x radius x height, plus the two circular ends, each with area pi x radius^2, giving 2 x pi x radius^2. Total surface area = 2 x pi x radius x height + 2 x pi x radius^2 — option C. Option A mixes up the pieces (pi r^2 h is a volume, and 2 pi r is a circumference, not an area), option B mixes cylinder and rectangle formulas, and option D is the area of a triangle. (Memo: 2A correct formula.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

C

## Question (2 marks)

One way to save money during winter is to wrap the geyser and waterpipes with a geyser blanket made of aerolite (insulating material). The length of the geyser is 1,2 m. Convert this measurement to mm.

## Method

metric length conversion

## Question (4 marks)

(Context: Mrs Xulu's tree decoration is pasted onto a cardboard template of three sections. Part A is the top triangular section, with a vertical height of 240 mm and a triangle base of 28 cm.) Calculate, in cm², the area of Part A. You may use the following formula: Area of triangle = 1/2 base x height

## Method

triangle area with conversion

## Memo working

The height and the base are in different units, so first convert the height: 240 mm = 24 cm. Then Area = 1/2 x (28 cm x 24 cm) = 336 cm². (Memo option 2: work in millimetres — 1/2 x 280 mm x 240 mm = 33 600 mm², then convert: 33 600 mm² = 336 cm².)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

336 cm²

## Question (5 marks)

(Context: Mrs Xulu's cardboard tree template is made up of three sections — Part A, Part B and Part C. From the previous part, the area of Part A is 336 cm².) The area of Part B is 30 240 mm². The area of Part C is 1,6 times the area of Part B. Calculate, in mm², the total area of the cardboard template.

## Method

scaled area and total

## Memo working

Area of Part C = 30 240 mm² x 1,6 = 48 384 mm². The answer must be in mm², so convert Part A: 336 cm² = 33 600 mm² (multiply by 100, since 1 cm² = 100 mm²). Total area = 48 384 mm² + 30 240 mm² + 33 600 mm² = 112 224 mm². (Consistent accuracy carried from Q3.1.3.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

112 224 mm²

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q3.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (9 marks)

Amanda decides to make 48 pairs of earrings using flower-patterned synthetic leather for the large circles. Both sides of the large circle are covered using synthetic leather, while the small circle is painted black. The radius of one large circle is 1,4 cm. The synthetic leather is sold in rolls with a width of 1,37 m. Amanda buys 30 cm of the synthetic leather. She states that after cutting the leather for ALL the large circles, the remaining synthetic leather will have an area of less than 3 000 cm². Verify her statement, showing ALL calculations. You may use the following formulae: Area of rectangle = length x width; Area of circle = 3,142 x radius²

## Method

remaining area after cutting verification

## Memo working

Work entirely in centimetres: the roll width 1,37 m = 137 cm. Area of the piece of material = 30 cm x 137 cm = 4 110 cm². Count the circle faces needed: 48 pairs = 96 earrings, and each large circle is covered on both sides, so 96 x 2 = 192 circle faces. Total area of all circles = 3,142 x (1,4 cm)² x 48 x 2 x 2 = 1 182,40 cm². Area of the off-cuts = 4 110 - 1 182,40 = 2 927,60 cm², which is less than 3 000 cm². Her statement is CORRECT.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Area of material = 30 cm x 137 cm = 4 110 cm²; total area of all circles = 3,142 x (1,4)² x 48 x 2 x 2 = 1 182,40 cm²; area of off-cuts = 4 110 - 1 182,40 = 2 927,60 cm². Her statement is CORRECT.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q5.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

The wooden pieces for two identical bookcases are cut from ONE complete rectangular piece of wood which is 2 cm thick, 42 cm wide and 430 cm long. (Each bookcase needs six pieces: two side pieces of 90 cm x 20 cm, a top and a bottom piece of 60 cm x 20 cm each, and two shelves of 56 cm x 20 cm — dimensions as printed in the marking guidelines from ANNEXURE D.) Determine the area of the remaining part of the wood after cutting the required material. You may use the following formula: Area of rectangle = length x breadth

## Method

remaining area after cutting

## Memo working

Area of the complete piece = 42 cm x 430 cm = 18 060 cm². For ONE bookcase, pair the pieces: one side (90 cm) plus one top/bottom (60 cm) plus one shelf (56 cm) laid along the length gives 90 + 60 + 56 = 206 cm, and two such strips of 20 cm width give 20 + 20 = 40 cm, so area per bookcase = 206 x 40 = 8 240 cm². Two bookcases use 2 x 8 240 = 16 480 cm². Area of unused wood = 18 060 - 16 480 = 1 580 cm². (Memo option 2, piece by piece per bookcase: E and D 60 x 20 x 2 = 2 400; F and G 56 x 20 x 2 = 2 240; A and B 90 x 20 x 2 = 3 600; total 8 240 cm², x 2 = 16 480 cm²; 18 060 - 16 480 = 1 580 cm². The piece dimensions come from ANNEXURE D but are printed in the memo working; the arithmetic is verified.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Area of complete piece = 42 x 430 = 18 060 cm²; area of pieces of one bookcase = (90 + 60 + 56) x (20 + 20) = 8 240 cm²; area of unused wood = 18 060 - 2(8 240) = 1 580 cm²

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q5.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

The density of the wood is 0,75 g/cm³. A volume of approximately 0,4 m³ unused wood is accumulated each month. Simon states that it will take more than three months to accumulate one ton of unused wood. Verify his statement, showing ALL calculations. You may use the following formula: Density = mass/volume

## Method

density mass volume verification

## Memo working

Convert the monthly volume to cm³ so it matches the density unit: 0,4 m³ x 100³ = 400 000 cm³. Mass per month = density x volume = 0,75 g/cm³ x 400 000 cm³ = 300 000 g = 300 kg. One ton = 1 000 kg. Number of months = 1 000 kg ÷ 300 kg = 3,33 months, which is more than three months, so the statement is VALID. (Memo option 2: in 3 months he accumulates 0,3 ton x 3 = 0,9 ton, which is less than 1 ton, so it must take more than three months — VALID.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Volume per month = 0,4 m³ = 400 000 cm³; mass per month = 0,75 x 400 000 = 300 000 g = 300 kg; number of months for 1 ton (1 000 kg) = 1 000 ÷ 300 = 3,33 months. VALID.

column matching

Recall what an IDZ is designed for: a purpose-built industrial estate located next to a port or international airport, offering incentives to attract investment in manufacturing aimed at foreign markets. ## Answer (per marking guidelines)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.4.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2024, question Q2.4.3.

## Question (4 marks)

(Refer to a sketch map of major roads that link the main industrial areas in the Gauteng (PWV) core industrial region: boxed nodes PRETORIA, WITWATERSRAND and VEREENIGING are linked vertically by major-road arrows, with further major roads radiating outwards to surrounding centres such as Rustenburg, Brits, Emalahleni (Witbank), Middelburg, Bronkhorstspruit, Potchefstroom, Klerksdorp, Delmas, Secunda/Evander, Mabopane and Polokwane.) Refer to the sketch and explain the role of the major roads in supporting industrial development in the Gauteng (PWV) core industrial region. (2 x 2)

## Method

sketch interpretation

Read the sketch as a network: the three industrial nodes are tied together and connected to a ring of surrounding towns. Then explain what a dense road network does for industry — it moves raw materials, finished goods and workers efficiently, gives factories access to major markets, offers the shortest, most cost-effective routes between centres, spreads traffic to reduce congestion and speed up deliveries, and makes the region attractive to investors. Explain any two roles for two marks each.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Allows for effective transportation of goods/raw materials/labour (accept examples) (2)
- Creates accessibility to major markets (2)
- The dense network of roads creates greater accessibility (2)
- The shortest possible distance to the towns/cities is available, making it cost effective (2)
- Effective road network will attract investors (2)
- Decreases traffic congestion/rapid delivery of products (2)

[ANY TWO]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.4.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2024, question Q2.4.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Explain TWO challenges faced by the Gauteng (PWV) core industrial region. (2 x 2)

## Method

explain challenges

Organise the possibilities into a few families and pick the two you can explain best. Location: Gauteng is inland, far from harbours, so transport costs are high and it depends heavily on road transport while rail deteriorates. Services: load-shedding cuts production and water shortages threaten industry. Space and costs: limited land for expansion, high petrol prices, rising operating costs. People and politics: labour strikes, crime, lack of skills, and political issues that dent business confidence. Environment: rising pollution. # Past-Paper Worked Example — Q7.3.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q7.3.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

P is a +2 nC point charge and S, a −2 nC point charge, is 4 cm to the right of P. A third point charge T, placed 2 cm to the right of S, experiences a net electrostatic force of 2,5 x 10⁻⁴ N to the left. Calculate the magnitude of charge T.

## Method

coulombs law net force

## Memo working

POSITIVE MARKING FROM Q7.1 IN TERMS OF CONVERSIONS. OPTION 1: Write Coulomb's law F = kQ1Q2/r² for each force on T. S is 2 cm (0,02 m) from T, so FST = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,02)²; P is 6 cm (0,06 m) from T, so FPT = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,06)². The forces oppose each other, so Fnet = FST – FPT: 2,5 x 10⁻⁴ = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,02)² − (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,06)², giving QT = 6,25 x 10⁻⁹ C. (Memo option 2: work with fields at T — ES = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)/0,02² = 45 000 N·C⁻¹; Enet = EP – ES = 5 x 10³ − 45 000 = –4 x 10⁴ N·C⁻¹; then F = Eq: –2,5 x 10⁻⁴ = (–4 x 10⁴)QT, giving QT = 6,25 x 10⁻⁹ C.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

QT = 6,25 x 10⁻⁹ C

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q7.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2025, question Q7.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Sphere X, carrying a charge of +3 x 10⁻⁷ C, is at point A on a horizontal surface. Sphere Y, carrying a charge of −5 x 10⁻⁷ C, is fixed at point P, which is 0,05 m to the left of X, and sphere Z, carrying a charge of −4 x 10⁻⁷ C, is fixed 0,04 m to the right of sphere X. The NET FORCE acting on sphere X is 0,0427 N at point A. Is the surface frictionless? Choose from YES or NO. Explain the answer by means of a calculation.

## Method

coulombs law net force

## Memo working

Force of Y on X, using Coulomb's law: FXY = kQXQY/r² = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁷)(5 x 10⁻⁷)/(0,05)² = 0,54 N, directed towards Y on the left (opposite charges attract).

Force of Z on X: FXZ = kQXQZ/r² = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁷)(4 x 10⁻⁷)/(0,04)² = 0,68 N, directed towards Z on the right.

These two forces act in opposite directions, so the net electrostatic force on X is 0,68 − 0,54 = 0,14 N. Since 0,14 N is not equal to the given net force of 0,0427 N, another horizontal force must act on X: friction. From 0,0427 = 0,14 − f, the friction is f = 0,0923 N. (Memo note: ignore if negative charges are substituted.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

No. The net electrostatic force is FXZ − FXY = 0,68 − 0,54 = 0,14 N, which is greater than / not equal to the given net force of 0,0427 N (so friction of 0,0923 N acts).

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q10.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

In the diagram, PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral. T is a point on the circle such that QT is perpendicular to SR at V. PT and ST are drawn. Q̂2 = 35° and R̂ = Ŝ1. (In the figure the circle passes through P upper left, Q at the top, R on the right and S on the left; QT crosses SR at right angles at V; T is at the bottom of the circle; the angles at each vertex are numbered, with Q̂2 = 35° marked.) Calculate, with reasons, the size of QT̂S.

## Method

triangle sum same segment

## Memo working

Start in triangle QVR: the angle at V is 90° (QT ⊥ SR) and Q̂2 = 35°, so by the angle sum of a triangle R̂ = 180° - 90° - 35° = 55°. Now QT̂S and R̂ (that is, QR̂S) are angles in the same segment — both subtend chord QS from the same side — so QT̂S = R̂ = 55°. (Alternative memo method: Ŝ2 = 35°, angles in the same segment, then QT̂S = 55° by the angle sum in triangle SVT.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

QT̂S = 55°

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q10.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Prove that PQ || SR. (From QUESTION 10: PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral, QT ⊥ SR at V, Q̂2 = 35°, R̂ = Ŝ1, and from QUESTION 10.1: R̂ = 55°.)

## Method

co interior angles supplementary

## Memo working

PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral, so its opposite angles are supplementary: SP̂Q = 180° - R̂ = 180° - 55° = 125°. It is given that Ŝ1 = R̂ = 55°. Now SP̂Q and Ŝ1 lie between the lines PQ and SR on the same side of the transversal PS, and SP̂Q + Ŝ1 = 125° + 55° = 180°. Since the co-interior angles are supplementary, PQ || SR. (Alternative memo method: Ŝ1 = R̂ = 55° given; PQ̂R = 125°, opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral; Q̂1 = 125° - 35° = 90°; then Q̂1 + V̂1 = 180°, so PQ || SR by co-interior angles.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

PQ || SR

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q10.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Prove that PT is a diameter of the circle. (From QUESTIONS 10.1 and 10.2: PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral, QT ⊥ SR at V, and PQ || SR.)

## Method

converse angle in semicircle

## Memo working

Because PQ || SR and QT is a transversal meeting SR at 90°, the co-interior angles give Q̂1 = 180° - 90° = 90° — that is, PQ̂T = 90°. So the chord PT subtends a right angle at Q, a point on the circle. By the converse of the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem, a chord that subtends 90° at the circumference must be a diameter; therefore PT is a diameter. (Alternative memo method: Ŝ2 = 35° by the exterior angle of triangle SVT or the angle sum; then PŜT = 55° + 35° = 90°, so PT is a diameter by the converse angle in semi-circle.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

PT is a diameter

Differentiate term by term with the power rule: the derivative of 3x is 3, and the derivative of -5x^2 is -10x. d/dx[3x - 5x^2] = 3 - 10x.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

3 - 10x

## Question (4 marks)

Determine g'(x) if g(x) = 2/x^2 - cuberoot(x^7)

## Method

power rule negative fractional exponents

## Memo working

First rewrite each term as a power of x: 2/x^2 = 2x^(-2) and cuberoot(x^7) = x^(7/3), so g(x) = 2x^(-2) - x^(7/3). Apply the power rule to each term: the derivative of 2x^(-2) is -4x^(-3), and the derivative of -x^(7/3) is -(7/3)x^(4/3). g'(x) = -4x^(-3) - (7/3)x^(4/3).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

g'(x) = -4x^(-3) - (7/3)x^(4/3)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q8.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q8.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Determine the equation of the tangent to f(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + 2x + 3 at x = 2.

## Method

tangent line at point

## Memo working

The gradient of the tangent is the derivative at x = 2: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 8x + 2, so m = f'(2) = 3(4) - 8(2) + 2 = -2. The point of contact: y = f(2) = 8 - 16 + 4 + 3 = -1, so the tangent touches at (2 ; -1). Substitute into y - y1 = m(x - x1): y + 1 = -2(x - 2), giving y = -2x + 3.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

y = -2x + 3

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q9.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q9.1.

## Question (2 marks)

A(1 ; 9) and B(5/2 ; 8) are the turning points of the graph of a cubic function f. C(0 ; 7) is the y-intercept of f (the cubic curve rises steeply from below the x-axis on the left, passes through C(0 ; 7), reaches a local maximum at A(1 ; 9), dips to a local minimum at B(5/2 ; 8), then increases). For which values of x is f decreasing?

## Method

decreasing between turning points

## Memo working

A cubic with a positive leading coefficient rises, turns down at its local maximum, falls to its local minimum, and rises again. So f decreases exactly between the two turning points: from the local maximum at x = 1 to the local minimum at x = 5/2.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1 < x < 5/2

## Question (2 marks)

A(1 ; 9) and B(5/2 ; 8) are the turning points of the graph of a cubic function f. C(0 ; 7) is the y-intercept of f (the cubic curve rises steeply from below the x-axis on the left, passes through C(0 ; 7), reaches a local maximum at A(1 ; 9), dips to a local minimum at B(5/2 ; 8), then increases). Write down the x-intercepts of f', the derivative of f.

## Method

derivative zero at turning points

## Memo working

At a turning point the gradient of f is zero, so f'(x) = 0 exactly at the turning points. The turning points are at x = 1 and x = 5/2, so the graph of f' cuts the x-axis at these two values.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

(1 ; 0) and (5/2 ; 0)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q9.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q9.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

A(1 ; 9) and B(5/2 ; 8) are the turning points of the graph of a cubic function f. C(0 ; 7) is the y-intercept of f (the cubic curve rises steeply from below the x-axis on the left, passes through C(0 ; 7), reaches a local maximum at A(1 ; 9), dips to a local minimum at B(5/2 ; 8), then increases). For which values of x will f be concave up?

## Method

concavity from inflection point

## Memo working

For a cubic, the point of inflection lies midway between the two turning points: x = (1 + 5/2)/2 = 7/4. To the left of the inflection point the curve bends downwards (it holds the local maximum); to the right it bends upwards (it holds the local minimum). So f is concave up for x > 7/4.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Concave up for x > 7/4

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q9.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q9.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

A(1 ; 9) and B(5/2 ; 8) are the turning points of the graph of a cubic function f. C(0 ; 7) is the y-intercept of f (the cubic curve rises steeply from below the x-axis on the left, passes through C(0 ; 7), reaches a local maximum at A(1 ; 9), dips to a local minimum at B(5/2 ; 8), then increases). Determine the value of k for which y = f(x) + k will have THREE positive x-intercepts.

## Method

vertical shift root analysis

## Memo working

Adding k slides the whole graph vertically. For three x-intercepts, the x-axis must cut the curve three times, which happens when the axis lies strictly between the shifted local minimum value (8 + k) and the shifted local maximum value (9 + k): 8 + k < 0 < 9 + k. This gives -9 < k < -8. For such k the y-intercept 7 + k is negative, so all three x-intercepts lie to the right of the y-axis — all three are positive.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

-9 < k < -8

tangent line via derivative

## Question (4 marks)

Determine:  dy/dx if y = (2x^4 + 1)/x^2

## Method

simplify then power rule

## Memo working

First rewrite the quotient as a sum of powers of x by dividing each term in the numerator by x^2: y = 2x^4/x^2 + 1/x^2 = 2x^2 + x^(-2). Now apply the power rule term by term: the derivative of 2x^2 is 4x, and the derivative of x^(-2) is -2x^(-3). So dy/dx = 4x - 2x^(-3).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

dy/dx = 4x - 2x^(-3)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q9.1

## Question (4 marks)

Sketched below is the graph of f(x) = x^3 - 8x^2 + 5x + 14. A, B and C are the x-intercepts of f. D and E are the turning points of f. (Figure: cubic curve with x-intercepts A (negative), B and C (positive); local maximum D near the y-axis and local minimum E between B and C, below the x-axis.) Calculate the coordinates of E.

## Method

turning points via derivative

## Memo working

Turning points occur where the derivative is zero. Differentiate: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 16x + 5. Set it equal to zero and factorise: (3x - 1)(x - 5) = 0, so x = 1/3 or x = 5. E is the local minimum, at the larger value x = 5. Substitute back: f(5) = 125 - 200 + 25 + 14 = -36. So E(5 ; -36).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

E(5 ; -36)

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Given f(x) = x^3 - 8x^2 + 5x + 14. For which values of x is f concave down?

## Method

second derivative concavity

## Memo working

Concavity is decided by the second derivative. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 16x + 5, so f''(x) = 6x - 16. The graph is concave down where f''(x) < 0: 6x - 16 < 0, so x < 8/3. (Alternative memo method: the point of inflection lies midway between the turning points, x = (1/3 + 5)/2 = 8/3, and the cubic with positive leading coefficient is concave down to the left of it.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x < 8/3

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q9.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q9.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Given f(x) = x^3 - 8x^2 + 5x + 14 with x-intercepts A, B and C. The coordinates of B are (2 ; 0). Use the graph to determine the values of x for which f(x) . f''(x) < 0

## Method

sign analysis product

## Memo working

With B(2 ; 0) known, divide out the factor (x - 2): f(x) = (x - 2)(x^2 - 6x - 7) = (x - 2)(x - 7)(x + 1), so the x-intercepts are x = -1, x = 2 and x = 7. From Q9.2, f''(x) < 0 for x < 8/3 and f''(x) > 0 for x > 8/3. The product f(x) . f''(x) is negative where the two factors have opposite signs. Reading the graph: f is positive with f'' negative on -1 < x < 2, and f is negative with f'' positive on 8/3 < x < 7. So the product is negative for -1 < x < 2 or 8/3 < x < 7.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

-1 < x < 2 or 8/3 < x < 7

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q9.4.

## Question (6 marks)

Given f(x) = x^3 - 8x^2 + 5x + 14. For which values of t will y = -11x + t intersect f at 3 distinct points?

## Method

tangency bounds for three roots

## Memo working

A line of fixed gradient -11 cuts the cubic in three distinct points exactly when it lies strictly between the two positions where it is tangent to the curve. Find the tangency points from f'(x) = -11: 3x^2 - 16x + 5 = -11 gives 3x^2 - 16x + 16 = 0, which factorises as (x - 4)(3x - 4) = 0, so x = 4 or x = 4/3. At x = 4: f(4) = -30, and the tangent line -11x + t through (4 ; -30) gives t = -30 + 44 = 14. At x = 4/3: f(4/3) = 238/27, giving t = 238/27 + 44/3 = 634/27 = 23 13/27 = 23,48. Three distinct intersection points occur for t strictly between these bounds.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

14 < t < 634/27

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.5.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2025, question Q2.5.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Explain the negative impact of poor river management on the health of rivers. (2 x 2)

## Method

impact explanation

## Memo working

Think of the river as a living system and trace what neglect does to it. Poorly managed rivers receive pollution and waste, so water quality drops. That degraded water damages the habitat of aquatic life and can destroy the organisms themselves, which in turn breaks food chains and food webs and disrupts whole ecosystems, causing a loss of biodiversity. Nutrient-rich pollution triggers eutrophication (algal blooms that starve the water of oxygen), and unmanaged catchments deliver increased sedimentation that chokes the channel. Any two of these impacts, fully explained, earn the four marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Reduced water quality (accept examples) (2); Damages habitat for aquatic life (2); Destroys aquatic life (accept examples) (2); Destroys food chains/food webs (2); Causes eutrophication (accept examples) (2); Disrupt ecosystems (2); Loss of biodiversity (2); Increased sedimentation (accept examples) (2) [ANY TWO]

suggest strategies

Strategies must be realistic actions a municipality can take, and they group naturally. # Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q6.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (9 marks)

Carbon monoxide gas, CO(g), reacts with water vapour, H2O(g), at T °C. The reaction reaches chemical equilibrium according to the balanced equation: CO(g) + H2O(g) ⇌ CO2(g) + H2(g). Initially, 0,6 moles of CO(g), 0,6 moles of H2O(g), 0,1 moles of carbon dioxide gas, CO2(g), and 0,1 moles of hydrogen gas, H2(g), were mixed and sealed in a 2 dm³ flask. If the equilibrium constant, Kc, for this reaction at T °C is 4, calculate the mass of CO(g) present in the flask at equilibrium.

**Note: the official memo works this question by two routes that round differently — a mole-based ICE table (x = 0,37 mol, giving m = 6,44 g) and a concentration-based ICE table (x = 0,18 mol·dm⁻³, giving m = 6,72 g). Any final answer in the accepted range 6,44 – 6,72 g earns the marks.**

## Method

kc ice table calculation

## Memo working

ICE table (moles): initial CO 0,6; H2O 0,6; CO2 0,1; H2 0,1. Change: –x, –x, +x, +x (mole ratio 1:1:1:1). Equilibrium: 0,6–x; 0,6–x; 0,1+x; 0,1+x; divide each by the 2 dm³ volume for concentrations. Substitute into Kc = [CO2][H2]/[CO][H2O]: 4 = ((0,1+x)/2)²/((0,6–x)/2)², so x = 0,37. Then n(CO)eq = 0,6 – 0,37 = 0,23 mol, and from n = m/M: 0,23 = m/28, so m(CO)eq = 6,44 g. (Memo also gives full concentration-based variants: initial concentrations 0,3/0,3/0,05/0,05 mol·dm⁻³ give x = 0,18, [CO]eq = 0,12 mol·dm⁻³, n(CO)eq = 0,24 mol, m = 6,72 g; the range 6,44 – 6,72 g covers rounding.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

m(CO)eq = 6,44 g (accepted range 6,44 – 6,72 g)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q1.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: The following reaction reaches equilibrium in a closed container: H2(g) + S(s) ⇌ H2S(g), ΔH < 0. The reaction rate versus time graph for the reaction is given below. [Graph: two reaction-rate curves at equilibrium (equal, constant); at time t1 both rates jump vertically to higher values, then converge to a new common constant rate.] What change was made to the system at time t1? A The pressure was increased at a constant temperature. B The volume of the container was increased. C The temperature was increased. D More hydrogen was added to the system.

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) At t1 BOTH the forward and the reverse rate jump upward instantaneously. Increasing the pressure at constant temperature (by decreasing the volume) raises the concentrations of both gases, H2 and H2S, at the same instant, so both rates jump — and because there is one mole of gas on each side (the sulfur is a solid), the equilibrium position is unaffected and the rates settle at a new, higher common constant value. Test the distractors: increasing the volume (B) would make both rates drop, not jump; increasing the temperature (C) changes the rates through the rate constants, not through a sudden concentration jump, and for this exothermic reaction would shift the equilibrium; adding hydrogen (D) would make only the forward rate jump at t1.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q6.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Calculate the mass of NH4HS(s) that will be present at equilibrium at 250 °C. (Context: initially 70 g of NH4HS(s) is placed in a sealed 3 dm³ container at 250 °C and the reaction NH4HS(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + H2S(g) reaches equilibrium; Kc = 18 x 10⁻² at 250 °C.)

## Method

kc equilibrium calculation

## Memo working

**Note: the official memo's two solution routes give different final values — the mole-based route (Option 1) obtains 5,1 g while the concentration-based route obtains up to 5,74 g — so the marking guidelines accept the RANGE 4,96 - 5,74 g. The memo's stated answer is 5,61 g.**

Step 1 — initial moles of solid: n(NH4HS) = m/M = 70/51 = 1,37 mol.

Step 2 — Kc expression: NH4HS is a solid, so it is omitted from Kc: Kc = [NH3][H2S].

Step 3 — let x mol of NH4HS decompose (mole ratio NH4HS : NH3 : H2S = 1 : 1 : 1); the container is 3 dm³, so the equilibrium concentrations are [NH3] = [H2S] = x/3.

Step 4 — substitute into Kc: 18 x 10⁻² = (x/3)²; x = 1,27 mol.

Step 5 — moles of solid remaining: n(NH4HS) at equilibrium = 1,37 − 1,27 = 0,1 mol.

Step 6 — mass: m = nM = 0,1 x 51 = 5,1 g.

(Memo option 2, working in concentrations: x = 0,42 mol·dm⁻³ so n(change) = 1,26 mol, m(eq) = 0,11 x 51 = 5,61 g or 70 − 64,26 = 5,74 g; the concentration route gives 4,998 - 5,128 g. Hence the accepted range 4,96 - 5,74 g.)

Marking criteria: (a) n(NH4HS) = 70/51; (b) ratio 1:1:1; (c) equilibrium concentrations (divide equilibrium moles by 3); (d) correct Kc expression; (e) substitute Kc = 18 x 10⁻²; (f) n(NH4HS)eq = n(in) − n(change); (g) substitute 51 in n = m/M; (h) correct final answer. No Kc expression with correct substitution: max 7/8; wrong Kc expression: max 6/8.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

m(NH4HS) at equilibrium ≈ 5,61 g [memo's stated answer; accepted RANGE: 4,96 - 5,74 g; Option 1 of the memo itself obtains 5,1 g]

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: The set-up for electroplating an iron medal with silver is shown in the simplified diagram below. [Diagram: power source connected to an iron medal (left electrode) and a silver rod (right electrode), both immersed in an electrolyte.] Which ONE of the following combinations for the ANODE and REACTION AT THE CATHODE is CORRECT? A Anode: Iron medal, Reaction at the cathode: Ag+(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s) B Anode: Silver rod, Reaction at the cathode: Fe2+(aq) + 2e⁻ → Fe(s) C Anode: Iron medal, Reaction at the cathode: Ag(s) → Ag+(aq) + e⁻ D Anode: Silver rod, Reaction at the cathode: Ag+(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s)

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) In electroplating, the object to be plated is always the CATHODE, and the plating metal is the ANODE. Here the iron medal must receive the silver coating, so the medal is the cathode and the silver rod is the anode — that immediately eliminates A and C. At the cathode, reduction occurs: silver ions from the electrolyte gain electrons and deposit as silver metal, Ag+(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s). Option B wrongly deposits iron; option C writes an oxidation at the cathode. The correct combination is silver rod as anode with Ag+(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s) at the cathode.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q9.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q9.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Calculate the change in mass of electrode R after T hours. (Context: in the copper-refining cell, electrode R is the unrefined copper anode with zinc as the only impurity; after T hours the amount of Cu2+(aq) ions in the electrolyte changed by 0,05 moles and 0,15 moles of Cu(s) were deposited on electrode Q.)

## Method

electrolysis mass change calculation

## Memo working

Electrode R is the impure copper anode, so it loses mass in two ways: zinc impurity is oxidised into the electrolyte, and copper is oxidised to replace the Cu2+ being deposited.

Step 1 — zinc lost: n(Zn2+) formed = n(Cu2+) decrease = 0,05 mol; m(Zn) = nM = (0,05)(65) = 3,25 g Zn lost from R.

Step 2 — copper lost: the cathode gained 0,15 mol Cu but the electrolyte only lost 0,05 mol Cu2+, so the anode supplied the difference: Cu oxidised at R = 0,15 − 0,05 = 0,1 mol; m(Cu) = nM = 0,1(63,5) = 6,35 g Cu lost from R.

Step 3 — total change in mass = 6,35 + 3,25 = 9,6 g (decrease).

Marking criteria: (a) use ratio n(Cu2+) : n(Zn2+) = 1 : 1; (b) formula n = m/M; (c) substitute 65 and n(Zn2+); (d) subtraction of moles; (e) substitute 63,5 and n(Cu); (f) final correct answer 9,6 g.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Change in mass of electrode R = 9,6 g (decrease in mass). (NO RANGE)

## Question (4 marks)

(In the diagram, A lies above the x-axis in the second quadrant, C(-9 ; 0) is on the x-axis, D(3 ; -9) is below the x-axis, and B(-1 ; k) is marked on line DC between C and D.) If M is a point on AD such that AC || MB, calculate the ratio of Area triangle MBD / Area triangle ACD. (DB/DC = 1/3.)

## Method

area ratio with proportionality

## Memo working

Because MB || AC, the proportionality theorem in triangle ACD gives DM/DA = DB/DC = 1/3. Both triangles share the angle at D, so using the area rule: Area ΔMBD / Area ΔACD = [1/2 (DM)(DB) sin D] / [1/2 (DA)(DC) sin D] = (DM/DA)(DB/DC) = (1/3)(1/3) = 1/9.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Area ΔMBD / Area ΔACD = 1/9

## Question (6 marks)

Triangle ACD has vertices A, D(3 ; -9) and C(-9 ; 0), where A is a point in the second quadrant. B(-1 ; k) lies on side DC. (In the diagram, A lies above the x-axis in the second quadrant, C(-9 ; 0) is on the x-axis, D(3 ; -9) is below the x-axis, and B(-1 ; k) is marked on line DC between C and D.) If it is further given that the gradient of AD is -4 and the length of AD is sqrt(612) units, calculate the coordinates of A.

## Method

line and distance equations

## Memo working

Equation of AD through D(3 ; -9) with gradient -4: -9 = -4(3) + c gives c = 3, so y = -4x + 3. A lies on this line at distance sqrt(612) from D: (x - 3)^2 + (y + 9)^2 = 612. Substitute y + 9 = -4x + 12: (x - 3)^2 + (-4x + 12)^2 = 612, which expands to 17x^2 - 102x - 459 = 0, i.e. x^2 - 6x - 27 = 0, so (x - 9)(x + 3) = 0 and x = -3 (x = 9 is not applicable since A is in the second quadrant). Then y = -4(-3) + 3 = 15, so A(-3 ; 15). (Alternative memo method: the y-intercept N(0 ; 3) of AD satisfies ND = 3√17 = ½AD, so N is the midpoint of AD, giving A(-3 ; 15).)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A(-3 ; 15)

inclination angles

(Alternative memo methods: use the right angle at R, the angle in a semi-circle, with PR = 4√5, PL = 4√10 and RL = 4√5 and a trig ratio; or the cosine rule, giving cos L = √2/2.)

With R(7 ; 1), TR is a tangent to the circle at R. Prove that PT ⊥ RT.

## Method

perpendicular gradients

## Memo working

Gradient of the radius MR: m_RM = (1 - 3)/(7 - 1) = -1/3. The tangent at R is perpendicular to this radius, so m_RT = 3. The tangent at P has gradient m_PT = -1/3 (from the equation of ST). Then m_RT × m_PT = 3 × (-1/3) = -1, therefore PT ⊥ RT. (Alternative memo methods: PT || MR with angle MRT = 90° and co-interior angles; or the tan-chord theorem with TP = TR, giving angle PTR = 90°.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

m_RT × m_PT = -1, therefore PT ⊥ RT

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2

## Question (4 marks)

Show that q = 4. (From QUESTION 4: M(-6 ; q) is the centre of a circle cutting the x-axis at A and B; the vertical line MC meets the x-axis at D and the circle at E(-6 ; -1); AD = (q - 1) units.)

## Method

pythagoras with radius

## Memo working

MD̂B = 90° because MC is parallel to the y-axis, so ΔADM is right-angled at D. AM = ME = q + 1 (radii — M is at height q and E is at height -1 on the same vertical line); MD = q (the vertical distance from M down to the x-axis). Pythagoras in ΔADM: AM^2 = AD^2 + MD^2 -> (q + 1)^2 = (q - 1)^2 + q^2 -> q^2 + 2q + 1 = q^2 - 2q + 1 + q^2 -> q^2 - 4q = 0 -> q(q - 4) = 0; q ≠ 0, so q = 4.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

q = 4

## Method

asymptote of exponential

## Memo working

The inverse f^(-1)(x) = (1/3)^x is an exponential function. An exponential of this form gets closer and closer to the x-axis but never reaches it, so its horizontal asymptote is y = 0.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

y = 0

## Method

sketch exponential graph

## Memo working

Memo sketch awards: decreasing exponential shape with asymptote y = 0; y-intercept (0 ; 1); any other point (e.g. (-1 ; 3)). Reasoning: f^(-1)(x) = (1/3)^x has base between 0 and 1, so it decreases from left to right, lying entirely above the x-axis. At x = 0 it gives (1/3)^0 = 1, the y-intercept (0 ; 1); there is no x-intercept because the curve never reaches y = 0. A convenient second point is (-1 ; 3), since (1/3)^(-1) = 3.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Decreasing exponential through (0 ; 1) and (-1 ; 3) with horizontal asymptote y = 0

The graph of h is obtained when f^(-1) is translated 5 units to the right. Determine the y-values of h where x > 4.  (f^(-1)(x) = (1/3)^x)

translate exponential evaluate range

Translating 5 units right gives h(x) = (1/3)^(x-5). At x = 4: h(4) = (1/3)^(-1) = 3, so (4 ; 3) lies on h. The curve is a decreasing exponential with asymptote y = 0, so for x > 4 the y-values drop from 3 towards 0 without reaching either: 0 < y < 3.

0 < y < 3  OR  y ∈ (0 ; 3)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2024, question Q2.4.

## Question (8 marks)

Discuss the exogenous (monetarists) explanations of a business cycle. (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Monetarists believed that markets are inherently stable.
- Any fluctuations in economic activity are caused by external factors.
- The growth path of the economy is determined by supply of factors of production.
- The market forces of demand and supply will always bring the market back to equilibrium when imbalances develop.
- Monetarists suggest that the government should not intervene in market operations because its intervention leads to deviation from the potential growth path.
- Structural changes that affect production, employment, investments, government expenditure, taxes, imports and exports may lead to the expansion of business cycles.
- Random socio-economic shocks, such as sudden increase in fuel prices may affect business confidence and consumers' confidence.
- Natural disasters, such as droughts and floods may negatively affect agriculture, forestry and tourism, reducing the level of economic activity.

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of examples of exogenous factors, or a maximum of 4 marks for the explanation of the examples.)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P1, November 2025, question Q1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Refer to Information B. Calculate the correct value of the closing stock of men's informal shirts.

(The information was taken from the accounting records of Violet Limited. The financial year ended on 28 February 2025. The company trades with women's and men's clothing.)

Information B — Trading stock: It was discovered that the closing stock of one specific brand of men's informal shirts was valued according to the first-in-first-out stock valuation method instead of the weighted-average stock valuation method. This must be corrected. The records applicable to this brand are: stock on 1 March 2024 was 300 units with a total cost of R97 500; purchases during the year were 4 800 units with a total cost of R1 605 000; returns were 100 units with a total cost of R42 500; closing stock on 28 February 2025 was 820 units, shown at a total cost of R285 500 (the incorrect first-in-first-out value).

## Method

weighted average closing stock

## Memo working

Step 1 — total cost of stock available on the weighted-average basis: 97 500 + 1 605 000 - 42 500 = 1 660 000 (one mark plus one method mark).

Step 2 — total number of units available: 300 + 4 800 - 100 = 5 000 units (one mark plus one method mark).

Step 3 — weighted-average cost per unit: 1 660 000 divided by 5 000 = R332 (four marks up to this point).

Step 4 — correct value of the closing stock: 332 x 820 units = 272 240.

(Memo: numerator and denominator must be marked as such; do not award marks for any stand-alone figures, e.g. no ticks if only 97 500/300 is written.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

272 240 (one part correct if x by 820)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q2.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

SUNGLASS CITY: Nosisa is the owner of Sunglass City, selling one type of popular branded sunglasses. The financial year ended on 29 February 2024. (NOTE: Where comments or explanations are required, you should quote calculations, figures and/or trends and give a reason or an explanation in EACH case.) Calculate the weighted average cost of ONE pair of sunglasses.

INFORMATION:

A. Stock records (one 'unit' refers to one pair of sunglasses) (columns: UNITS | TOTAL (R)): Opening stock (1 March 2023) 620 units, R1 719 000; Closing stock (29 February 2024) 840 units, total unknown.

B. Purchases and returns during the financial year (columns: UNITS | UNIT PRICE (R) | TOTAL (R)): May 2023: 855 at 3 200 = 2 736 000; August 2023: 800 at 3 750 = 3 000 000; November 2023: 745 at 4 200 = 3 129 000; December 2023: (20) at 4 200 = (84 000) — a return; TOTALS: 2 380 units, R8 781 000.

C. Sales: 2 050 pairs of sunglasses were sold during the year at R5 600 per pair.

## Method

weighted average unit cost

## Memo working

Weighted average cost per unit is the total cost of all stock available for the year divided by the total units available. Total cost: opening stock plus net purchases: [1 719 000 + 8 781 000] = 10 500 000 (two marks). Total units: opening units plus net purchased units: [620 + 2 380] = 3 000 (two marks). Weighted average cost: 10 500 000 / 3 000 = R3 500.

(Memo: numerator and denominator must be marked as such / all amounts are stand-alone. Do not award marks for any operation done on 10 500 000 and 3 000. Workings in square brackets constitute one part, cannot be separated.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R3 500 (one part correct)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q2.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Calculate the value of closing stock using the first-in-first-out (FIFO) method.

(Sunglass City — same information as Q2.1.1. Closing stock is 840 units. Purchases and returns during the year: May 2023: 855 units at R3 200; August 2023: 800 units at R3 750; November 2023: 745 units at R4 200; December 2023: return of 20 units at R4 200.)

## Method

fifo closing stock

## Memo working

Under FIFO the oldest stock is sold first, so the 840 units on hand at year-end are valued at the most recent purchase prices, working backwards from November.

November purchase net of the December return: [745 - 20] = 725 units x 4 200 = 3 045 000 (two marks).

The remaining (840 - 725) = 115 units come from the August purchase: 115 x 3 750 = 431 250 (one method mark + one mark).

Closing stock: 3 045 000 + 431 250 = R3 476 250. (Memo: for the method mark, both unit figures must add up to 840.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R3 476 250 (one part correct; both figures must be added)

disciplinary action

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.1a

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q2.2.1a.

## Question (3 marks)

PROBLEM-SOLVING: The information is related to Slim-Line Boutique, owned by Mike Ndlela, for the year ended 29 February 2024. The business sold trousers and casual shirts throughout the year and introduced and sold formal shirts only from 1 November 2023. Trousers: Calculate the mark-up percentage achieved for trousers.

INFORMATION (columns: Trousers (units) | Shirts Casual (units) | Shirts Formal (units)):

Opening stock in units: 140 | 200 | 0. Purchases during the year: 720 | 1 300 | 980. Closing stock: 285 | 100 | 125. Returns: 15 | 120 | 0. Total units sold: 560 | 1 280 | 855 (on-site 344 | 560 | 855; online 216 | 720 | 0). Stock holding period: 186 days | 29 days | ?. Mark-up percentage per item: ? | 55% | 25%. Cost price per item: R500 | R400 | R680. Cost of sales: R280 000 | R512 000 | R581 400. Selling price per item: R920 | R620 | R850. Total cash sales banked: R515 200 | R793 600 | R726 750.

## Method

markup percentage

## Memo working

Mark-up percentage is gross profit expressed as a percentage of cost. Per unit: the trousers cost R500 and sell for R920, so [920 - 500] = 420 / 500 x 100 = 84%. OR using totals: [515 200 - 280 000] = 235 200 (one mark) / 280 000 (one mark) x 100 = 84%.

(Memo: numerator and denominator must be marked as such / all amounts are stand-alone. Do not mix rands with units.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

84% (one part correct; 'x 100' does not count as one part correct)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.1b

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q2.2.1b.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Comment on whether the mark-up percentage would benefit the business or not.

(Slim-Line Boutique — follows on from Q2.2.1a: the trousers carry an 84% mark-up, against 55% on casual shirts and 25% on formal shirts, and their stock holding period is 186 days.)

## Method

markup evaluation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Any valid explanation (part marks for partial or unclear responses):

- Customers will not buy / pay higher price for the product.
- Price-sensitive customers may choose competitors offering similar trousers for less, leading to lower sales.
- Regular customers may be discouraged from making repeated purchases.

## Question (4 marks)

Formal shirts: Calculate how long (in days) it will take Mike to sell the closing stock of the formal shirts.

(Slim-Line Boutique — same information as Q2.2.1a: formal shirts were introduced and sold only from 1 November 2023; closing stock 125 units; total units sold 855; cost price R680 per shirt; cost of sales R581 400.)

## Method

stockholding period closing stock

## Memo working

The stock holding period on closing stock is closing stock divided by cost of sales, multiplied by the length of the trading period. Because the formal shirts only traded from 1 November 2023 to 29 February 2024, that period is 120 days (or 121 days), not 365.

In units: 125 / 855 x 120 days (two marks; OR 121 days) = 17,5 days (17,7 with 121 days).

OR in rands: [R680 x 125] = 85 000 (one mark) / 581 400 x 120 days (two marks; OR 121 days).

(Memo: numerator and denominator must be marked as such / all amounts are stand-alone. Do not mix rands with units.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

17,5 / 17,7 days (one part correct; accept 18 days)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q2.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (7 marks)

SUPERSAVERS SUPERMARKET: The information relates to flavoured juices (2-litre bottles) that Supersavers Supermarket trades with. The first-in-first-out (FIFO) stock valuation method is applicable. The business is managed by Bryan Mills. The financial year ended on 28 February 2025. Calculate the value of the closing stock on 28 February 2025, using the FIFO method.

INFORMATION:

A. Balances (columns: DATE | NUMBER OF UNITS | TOTAL (R)): 1 March 2024, 630 units; 28 February 2025, 980 units, total unknown.

B. Purchases and returns during the year (columns: NUMBER OF UNITS | UNIT PRICE (R) | TOTAL (R)): Purchases 10 500 units, R358 250 in total — March-November 2024: 6 900 at 32 = 220 800; December 2024: 2 600 at 37 = 96 200; January 2025: 150 at 37 = 5 550; February 2025: 850 at 42 = 35 700. Returns: 32 units, R1 344.

C. Sales: 10 118 units were sold at R47 per bottle: R475 546.

## Method

fifo closing stock

## Memo working

Under FIFO the oldest stock is sold first, so the 980 units on hand at year-end are made up of the most recent purchases. The returns of 32 units were at R42 each (1 344 / 32), so they come off the February 2025 batch.

Start with February 2025: 850 - 32 returns = 818 units at R42 = (818 x 42) = 34 356 (three marks). The remaining 162 units [980 - 818, or the January 150 plus 12 from December] are valued at R37: (162 x 37) = 5 994 (two method marks + one mark). Closing stock: 34 356 + 5 994 = 40 350.

(Memo: for the two method marks both quantities must add up to 980. OR (35 700 - 1 344) (one mark + two marks) + (5 550 + 444) (one mark + two method marks). Ensure that only one option is marked consistently.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R40 350 (one part correct; both amounts added)

stock management advice

Clear View model: Although the Clear View model had units returned, Moses is very pleased with his decision to introduce it as a new model. Provide TWO points (with figures) to explain why Moses is pleased.

(BANDURA PRINTERS — same information as Q2.2.1: Clear View was introduced in February 2025; 90 units purchased at R35 000, 15 returned, 65 sold at R49 000 for R3 185 000; closing stock 10 units, R350 000. Rotrim sold 79 units for R1 714 300 over 12 months; Punchies sold 100 units for R3 108 000 over 12 months.)

## Method

new model performance comment

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

To reason it out: compare Clear View against the other two models on profitability and speed of sales. Profit per unit: 49 000 - 35 000 = R14 000, giving total gross profit of 65 x 14 000 = R910 000. Pace: 65 units in only 5 months (February to June) is 13 per month, against roughly 7 per month for Rotrim (79 over 12 months) and 8 for Punchies (100 over 12 months). Sell-through: 65 of the 75 available units (90 - 15 returns) is 86,7%. Its sales of R3 185 000 are the highest of the three models, only 10 units (R350 000) are left, and its stockholding period is only 23,1 days over the 5 months since introduction.

**Note: the official memo contains documented slips in this item. Its stockholding bullet quotes a Rotrim stockholding period of 124,7 days, which cannot be reproduced from the given figures (closing-stock basis 635 500 / 1 224 500 x 365 = 189,4 days; average-stock basis 164,0 days), and it attaches 41 units/R780 500 to Rotrim and 35 units/R635 500 to Punchies — the reverse of the values computed in Q2.2.1 and Q2.2.2a (Rotrim is 41 units/R635 500; Punchies is 35 units/R780 500). The memo answer below is transcribed verbatim; the other comparison points recompute correctly (Punchies 127,8 days; Clear View 23,1 days).**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Compare the Clear View printer with the other printers (2 marks); figures (2 marks). Any TWO of:

- Each printer is sold at a profit of R14 000 (total gross profit R910 000), higher than that of the other two printers.
- Sold an average of 13 printers per month, surpassing Rotrim (7) and Punchies (8).
- Sold 86,7% of available printers, compared to (65,8%) of Rotrim or (74,1%) of Punchies / sold 65 units in 5 months, compared to Rotrim (79 units) and Punchies (100 units) over 12 months.
- Achieved the highest sales of R3 185 000, exceeding Rotrim (R1 714 300) and Punchies (R3 108 000).
- Only 10 (R350 000) units left, compared to (41 units) (R780 500) for Rotrim and (35 units) (R635 500) for Punchies.
- Stockholding period is only 23,1 days compared to (127,8 days) of Punchies and (124,7 days) of Rotrim.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1.3a

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2025, question Q4.1.3a.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Monwabisi operates a trailer rental business with these costs: R1 000 refundable deposit per trailer if there is no damage to the trailer; R350 per day per small trailer; R500 per day per large trailer (so a one-day rental including deposit costs R1 350 for a small trailer and R1 500 for a large trailer). On 12 December 2024, Monwabisi rented out TWO small trailers and SIX large trailers to different customers for a day. One of the trailers was returned with a damaged rear light. (a) Monwabisi stated that his total income, after refunding the deposits, amounted to R4 550. Verify, showing ALL calculations, whether his statement is VALID. (Seven of the eight R1 000 deposits are refunded; the deposit of the damaged trailer is retained.)

## Method

income after refund verification

## Memo working

Income = (R1 350 x 2) + (R1 500 x 6) (1MA multiplying values) = R2 700 + R9 000 (1A) = R11 700 (1CA). Total income after refund = R11 700 - R7 000 (1MCA subtracting R7 000) = R4 700 (1CA). Statement NOT VALID (1O conclusion). OR rental income only = (R350 x 2) + (R500 x 6) = R700 + R3 000; plus retained deposit R1 000 = R4 700; NOT VALID

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Income for both trailer types = (R1 350 x 2) + (R1 500 x 6) = R11 700; total income after refunding 7 deposits = R11 700 - R7 000 = R4 700. Statement NOT VALID.

## Question (4 marks)

One of Monwabisi's rental trailers was returned with a damaged rear light; the refundable deposit he holds per trailer is R1 000. (b) The following quotation for the repair and replacement of the rear light was received: New rear light R242; Labour at R480 per hour or part thereof; Time required to complete the repair and replacement is 1 hour 30 minutes. Verify, showing ALL calculations, whether the deposit amount will be sufficient to cover the total cost of the entire repair and replacement. (Because labour is charged per hour or part thereof, 1 hour 30 minutes is charged as 2 hours.)

## Method

cost vs deposit verification

## Memo working

Labour cost = R480 x 2 (1MA multiplying by 2) = R960 (1CA simplification). Total cost = R960 + R242 = R1 202 (1CA simplification). The deposit of R1 000 will not be sufficient (1O conclusion). OR R1 000 - R480 - R480 - R242 = -R202 (1A R480, 1MCA, 1CA); not sufficient (1O)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Labour cost = R480 x 2 = R960; total cost = R960 + R242 = R1 202. The deposit of R1 000 will not be sufficient.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P1, November 2024, question Q1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (39 marks)

Complete the Statement of Comprehensive Income of Ivory Park Ltd for the year ended 29 February 2024. NOTE: Some amounts are provided in the ANSWER BOOK.

(Given balances at 29 February 2024, in rand: Cost of sales 4 780 900; Trading stock 654 500; Debtors' control 516 600; Provision for bad debts 29 520 on 28 February 2023; Audit fees 79 000; Service fee income 1 757 700; Sundry operating expenses 119 900; Bad debts 24 780; Packing material 66 550; Salaries and wages including contributions 1 425 600; Insurance 100 800; Rent income 158 100; Interest on loan 149 400. Adjustments: (ii) mark-up is 60% on cost, but goods costing R115 000, included in cost of sales, were sold to internal employees at a mark-up of only 40% on cost; (iii) physical stocktaking showed trading stock R647 100 and packing material used during the year R58 700; (iv) provision for bad debts must be adjusted to 5% of outstanding debtors; (v) monthly insurance premiums were fixed for the past three years and were paid up to 31 May 2024; (vi) rent for an office has been received up until 30 April 2024, and the rent was decreased by 8% on 1 December 2023; (vii) one employee was omitted from the February 2024 Salaries Journal — his net monthly salary was R19 340 after 35% deductions for pension and personal tax and R2 500 deducted for medical aid, and the employer contributes 10% of gross salary towards pension; (viii) two directors received a combined annual fee of R1 065 200 after their monthly fees were increased by R5 800 each on 1 August 2023, and a third director joined on 1 November 2023 at the same monthly fee as the others excluding the R5 800 increase; (ix) net profit after tax was R992 160 after all adjustments, with income tax at 28% of net profit. From Q1.1: depreciation on equipment 127 800, depreciation on vehicles 181 360, profit on vehicle traded in 3 900.)

## Method

income statement with adjustments

## Memo working

Sales: normally sales would be cost of sales times 1,6 because of the 60% mark-up: [4 780 900 x 1,6] = 7 649 440. But goods costing R115 000 earned only a 40% mark-up instead of 60%, so sales are lower by 20% of that cost: [115 000 x 0,2] = 23 000. Sales = 7 649 440 - 23 000 = 7 626 440 (one part correct; both figures must be added/subtracted). (Memo alternative: [4 665 900 x 1,6] = 7 465 440 (two marks) + [115 000 x 1,4] = 161 000 (two marks).)

Cost of sales: (4 780 900). Gross profit = Sales - Cost of sales = 2 845 540 (6 marks to here).

Other income (operation) 1 902 000, made up of: Service fee income 1 757 700. Profit on sale of asset 3 900 (see 1.1.4; if calculated as a loss in 1.1.4, award method mark under operating expenses). Rent income: R158 100 includes two months (March and April 2024) received in advance at the reduced rate. Working: nine months at the old rent plus five months at 92% of the old rent equals 158 100, so the old monthly rent is 11 625 and the reduced rent is 10 695; deduct the two prepaid months: 158 100 - 21 390 [10 695 x 2] = 136 710 (one part correct) (Memo alternative: 104 625 + 32 085). Provision for bad debts adjustment: the new provision is 5% of 516 600 = 25 830, which is 3 690 lower than 29 520, so 3 690 (should be shown as an income).

Gross operating income = Gross profit + Other income = 4 747 540 (9 marks in this block).

Operating expenses (operation) (3 371 340), made up of: Audit fees 79 000. Sundry operating expenses 119 900. Bad debts 24 780. Packing material used 58 700. Trading stock deficit: 654 500 - 647 100 = 7 400 (should be shown as an expense). Insurance: R100 800 covers 15 months (up to 31 May 2024) at a fixed premium of 6 720 per month, so three months are prepaid: 100 800 - 20 160 [100 800 x 3/15 OR 6 720 x 3] = 80 640 (one part correct; OR 100 800 x 12/15). Salaries and wages: the omitted employee's gross salary is found from his net pay — 65% of gross minus the R2 500 medical aid equals 19 340, so gross = [21 840 + 11 760] = 33 600; add the employer's 10% pension contribution of 3 360: 1 425 600 + 33 600 + 3 360 = 1 462 560 (one part correct). Directors' fees: the combined fee of 1 065 200 equals 24 base monthly fees plus 14 months of the R5 800 increase, so the base monthly fee is 41 000; the third director worked four months (November to February): 1 065 200 + 164 000 [41 000 x 4] = 1 229 200 (one part correct). Depreciation [127 800 + 181 360, see 1.1.1 and 1.1.3; both figures should be added to award method mark] = 309 160 (18 marks in this block).

Operating profit = Gross operating income - Operating expenses = 1 376 200.

Interest income: 151 200 (balancing figure, accept a negative figure). Profit before interest expense = Net profit before tax + interest expense = 1 527 400. Interest expense (149 400). Net profit before tax = Net profit after tax + income tax = 1 378 000 (also 992 160 / 0,72). Income tax = Net profit after tax x 28/72 = (385 840). Net profit after tax 992 160 (given).

(Penalties: -1 foreign items, max -2, i.e. Statement of Financial Position items; -1 presentation, max -1.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Sales 7 626 440; Cost of sales (4 780 900); Gross profit 2 845 540; Other income 1 902 000; Gross operating income 4 747 540; Operating expenses (3 371 340); Operating profit 1 376 200; Interest income 151 200; Profit before interest expense 1 527 400; Interest expense (149 400); Net profit before tax 1 378 000; Income tax (385 840); Net profit after tax 992 160

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P1, November 2024, question Q2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

**Note: the official memo prints TWO accepted versions of this note. The primary version derives net profit after tax from the 40% dividend pay-out rate (1 862 150). The alternative version shows 1 458 167 x 1,175 = 1 713 346 with closing balance 1 477 606, and the memo gives no derivation for the figure 1 458 167. The worked solution below follows the primary version.**

## Question (8 marks)

Prepare the Retained Income Note for the year ended 29 February 2024. (The information relates to Eybers Ltd for the financial year ended 29 February 2024. Given: Retained income on 28 February 2023 was R573 720. On 30 November 2023, 34 000 shares were repurchased at R1,90 per share above the average share price. Dividends: an interim dividend of R416 000 was paid on 1 September 2023; total dividends paid and declared for the year were R744 860; the dividend pay-out rate for the year was 40% after all transactions were correctly recorded.)

## Method

retained income note

## Memo working

Step 1 — Net profit after tax: the pay-out rate says total dividends are 40% of net profit after tax, so work backwards: 744 860 / 40% (dividend pay-out rate) = 1 862 150 (one part correct) OR 744 860 x 100/40.

Step 2 — Repurchase of shares: only the premium above the average share price comes out of retained income: 34 000 x R1,90 = (64 600) (ignore brackets).

Step 3 — Ordinary share dividends (744 860): Interim 416 000 (given, paid); Final = total dividends minus interim = 744 860 - 416 000 = 328 860 (declared).

Step 4 — Balance at the end of the year: 573 720 + 1 862 150 - 64 600 - 744 860 = 1 626 410 (one part correct; check operation; shares repurchased and ordinary share dividends must be subtracted). (-1P if no details, max -1. Memo alternative version: Net profit after tax (1 458 167 x 1,175) = 1 713 346 with closing balance 1 477 606, all other lines identical.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Balance at the beginning of the year 573 720; Net profit after tax 1 862 150; Repurchase of shares (64 600); Ordinary share dividends (744 860): Interim dividend 416 000, Final dividend 328 860; Balance at the end of the year 1 626 410

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P1, November 2024, question Q2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (17 marks)

Complete the Cash Flow Statement of Eybers Ltd for the year ended 29 February 2024. (Given: SARS: Income tax was 44 675 Cr on 28 February 2023 and 66 650 Dr on 29 February 2024; income tax for the year was R462 000. Bank overdraft was R142 680 and cash R36 000 on 28 February 2023. On 1 March 2023 there were 1 200 000 shares in issue; 400 000 shares were issued at R10 per share on 30 June 2023; on 30 November 2023, 34 000 shares were repurchased at R1,90 above the average share price; ordinary share capital was R8 160 000 on 28 February 2023. Dividends: final dividend for 2023 of 17 cents per share was paid during this year; the interim dividend of R416 000 was paid; the final dividend of R328 860 was declared on 29 February 2024. Loan: monthly instalments of R97 120, including interest, were paid; interest capitalised amounted to R685 440. Net change in cash and cash equivalents was R296 460 inflow.)

## Method

cash flow statement

## Memo working

Operating activities. Taxation paid: last year's amount still owing to SARS, plus this year's income tax expense, plus the amount overpaid by year end (the closing debit balance means SARS was paid too much): 44 675 + 462 000 + 66 650 = (573 325) (one part correct; OR -44 675 - 462 000 - 66 650). Dividends paid: cash actually paid this year is last year's final dividend plus this year's interim dividend — the final dividend declared this year is only paid next year: (1 200 000 x 17/100) = 204 000 + [744 860 - 328 860] = 416 000, giving (620 000) (one part correct). [Operating-activities block: 8 marks.]

Financing activities. New shares issued: 400 000 x R10 = 4 000 000. Shares repurchased: the average share price is (8 160 000 + 4 000 000) / 1 600 000 = R7,60, so the buy-back price is 7,60 + 1,90: (34 000 x 7,60) = 258 400 + (34 000 x 1,90) = 64 600 (see 2.1), giving (323 000) (one part correct; both figures added). Loan repaid: total instalments 97 120 x 12 = 1 165 440, of which 685 440 was interest, so the capital portion is (480 000) (if no bracket, award one mark). [Financing-activities block: 6 marks.]

Cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of the year: 36 000 - 142 680 = (106 680) (if no bracket, award one mark). Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year: -106 680 + 296 460 = 189 780 (operation) [3 marks].

(Memo notes: one part correct, reflected as an outflow (brackets); -1 poor presentation (max -1); be alert to alternative workings such as ledger account or use of brackets or signs reversed; for use of reversed signs, ensure that only one option is marked consistently; if no brackets, assume answer is an inflow of cash — award marks for workings only; if a workings amount is shown as a final figure, award the mark/s allocated, ignore the brackets; if correct figure is shown without brackets or workings, award all working marks only, not final mark. The memo's printed layout leaves the Cash generated from operations, Interest paid and investing-activities lines blank — pre-printed/not examined here.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Operating activities: Taxation paid (573 325); Dividends paid (620 000). Financing activities: New shares issued 4 000 000; Shares repurchased (323 000); Loan repaid (480 000). Net change in cash and cash equivalents 296 460; Cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of the year (106 680); Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year 189 780

audit evidence fixed assets
