# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2025, question Q6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (40 marks)

QUESTION 6: ECONOMIC PURSUITS.

- Discuss in detail South African initiatives (endeavours) in regional development. (26 marks)
- How can the government use incentives to promote industrial development? (10 marks)

(Section C essay: answer ONE of two essay questions. Rubric: Introduction max 2 — define the main concept, do not include any part of the question or announce what will be discussed; Body main part max 26 — a maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples; Body additional part max 10 — a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; Conclusion max 2 — a higher-order summary, opinion or recommendation without repeating facts. Total 40.)

## Method

essay

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: open by defining regional development. In the main body, discuss each South African initiative under its own heading. Spatial Development Initiatives: linking economic hubs to underdeveloped areas, attracting private and foreign investment through incentives and public-private partnerships, led by the DTIC and Department of Transport, with examples such as the Wild Coast, Fish River and Lubombo SDIs. Industrial Development Zones: purpose-built, enclosed industrial estates linked to international air or sea ports, offering duty-free imported inputs, dedicated customs services and world-class infrastructure, with examples such as Coega, East London and Richards Bay. Special Economic Zones: geographically demarcated areas with tax relief and support systems, serving both domestic and export markets. Corridors: tracts of land forming passageways with infrastructure and specialisation advantages, such as the Maputo development corridor. For the additional part, explain how incentives — lower corporate taxes and tax holidays, capital-investment subsidies, cash grants and low-interest loans, infrastructure investment, simplified registration, export and duty-free incentives, and funding for skills and small-business support — promote industrial development. Close with a brief higher-order conclusion.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

**INTRODUCTION (Max 2):**

Regional development focuses on policies which are aimed at improving areas or regions of a country that are less developed. OR Regional development is the implementation of policies aimed at increasing the economic livelihood of specific areas or geographical regions. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

**BODY MAIN PART (Max 26) — SOUTH AFRICAN INITIATIVES IN REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT.**

**Spatial Development Initiatives (SDIs)**

- Spatial Development Initiatives can be defined as a link between important economic hubs and regions in a country.
- SDI is a policy to promote sustainable industrial development in areas where poverty and unemployment are at their highest.
- SDIs stimulate economic activities in the underdeveloped areas to create employment and stimulate economic growth.
- The state aimed to enhance private sector and foreign direct investments through the granting of incentives.
- Spatial Development Initiatives promote the establishment of private-public partnerships (PPP) to improve the economic potential of underdeveloped areas.
- In a PPP, private businesses may provide the capital to build the factories, buy raw materials and employ labour.
- The government provides capital for the infrastructure such as roads and water supply networks.
- The SDIs involve an interdepartmental investment strategy that the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC) and the Department of Transport (DoT) lead.
- DTIC is the driving force behind industrial and spatial development as it supports the establishment and growth of businesses.
- SDIs focus on high-level support in areas where socio-economic conditions require concentrated government assistance and inherent economic potential exists.
- SDIs fast-track investments and maximise synergies between various types of investments.
- Examples of SDIs in South Africa include KwaZulu-Natal SDI, Wild Coast SDI, Fish River SDI, West Coast Investment initiative, Platinum SDI, Phalaborwa SDI, Gauteng Special Economic Zone, Lubombo SDI and Richards Bay initiative. (A maximum of 1 mark may be allocated for the examples of SDIs)

**Industrial Development Zones (IDZs)**

- IDZs are geographically designed, purpose-built and physically enclosed industrial estates that are linked to international air or sea ports.
- The focus of IDZs is to attract private investments and foreign direct investments in export-driven industries.
- Industrial Development Zones allow duty-free importation of production-related raw-materials and inputs.
- Businesses in IDZs have access to dedicated customs services to make inspection and clearing more efficient.
- The strategy was aimed at enhancing international competitiveness of local industries in export markets.
- IDZs focus on creating employment by promoting exports of value-added products.
- Businesses that are located in IDZs enjoy world-class infrastructure, a zero rate of VAT on supplies from South African sources and reduced taxation on some products.
- IDZs were established to benefit investing companies through financial support provided by the government.
- Businesses in IDZs have access to transport for exporting purposes and latest technology for global communication.
- IDZs are designed to promote and develop links between domestic and zone-based industries.
- Examples of IDZs in South Africa include Coega IDZ, OR Tambo International Airport, East London IDZ, Richards Bay IDZ and Saldanha Bay IDZ. (A maximum of 1 mark may be allocated for the examples of IDZs)

**Special Economic Zones (SEZ)**

- Special Economic Zones are geographically demarcated areas where specific economic activities have been identified to be developed.
- Businesses located in SEZs may enjoy incentives such as tax relief and support systems to promote industrial development.
- SEZs create a basis for a broader range of industrial parks and provide economic infrastructure to enable the clustering of manufacturers.
- The aim of creating SEZs is to attract new businesses which develop new product lines and create employment.
- The DTIC indicated that the existing IDZs where special tax incentives do not apply, would be graduated to SEZs.
- SEZs are not necessarily linked to international air or sea port and the purpose of manufacturing is to cater for both domestic and export markets.

**Corridors**

- A corridor is a track of land that forms a passageway allowing access from one area to another and is developed as part of regional development.
- Corridors in South Africa are spatial areas that offer advantages to mining, manufacturing and other businesses.
- The advantages include the presence of proper infrastructure and the specialisation of products or services.
- Corridors are development areas within South Africa and are the priorities of all development agencies.
- The DTIC provides help in support of the development corridors such as the Maputo development corridor, that starts in Gauteng and extends through Mpumalanga to the Maputo port, offers opportunity to the transport industry.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a max of 8 marks for headings/subheadings/examples)

**ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10):**

- Reduce corporate taxes and offer tax holidays or exemptions to increase the profit prospects of businesses, which will attract investments in existing industries.
- Provide subsidies on capital investment to reduce the development cost for potential investors in specific industries.
- Government can provide cash grants or low-interest loans to businesses looking to expand and adopt new technologies.
- The government can create a supportive environment for industries to thrive by investing in infrastructure development projects, such as roads, utilities, and industrial parks.
- Simplify business registration procedure, reducing bureaucratic hurdles and providing easier access to licences can help industries grow efficiently.
- Offer export incentives such as information on export markets and concessions on transport charges, to encourage production of goods and services for exporting.
- Provide duty-free incentives to reduce the cost of production for businesses that import production inputs.
- The government can provide direct financial support for skills development which helps to increase skills base and productivity of businesses.
- Provide business support programmes to help improve the delivery of small business support to small business and entrepreneurs.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples)

**CONCLUSION (Max 2):**

Regional development policies solve the long-term problems of unemployment and poverty, although certain constraints such as skills shortages and high costs still need to be addressed. (Accept any other relevant higher order conclusion.)

Teachable steps: monetary policy — and specifically the repo rate — is the tool used against inflation, and monetary policy in South Africa is run by the central bank, not the government. The central bank is the South African Reserve Bank.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

South African Reserve Bank / SARB

definition

## Question (2 marks)

Explain the impact of inflation on taxpayers. (Refers to a cartoon titled IMPACT OF INFLATION ON THE CONSUMER, showing a man dragging a ball and chain labelled INFLATION.)

## Method

explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: the key idea is bracket creep. Inflation pushes up nominal wages even when real income stands still, and because income tax brackets are set in nominal terms, the taxpayer slides into a higher bracket and pays a higher rate — while being no better off in real terms.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Inflation increases the taxpayers' nominal income even when their real income remains unchanged or decrease
- Taxpayers pay higher tax rates as their nominal income increases even if they are not better off than before (bracket creep)

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

How can natural disasters contribute to inflation in the economy? (2 x 2) (Refers to a cartoon titled IMPACT OF INFLATION ON THE CONSUMER, showing a man dragging a ball and chain labelled INFLATION.)

## Method

explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: natural disasters work on the supply side. Trace each disaster to either higher production costs (cost-push: rebuilding costs, damaged inputs get recovered through prices) or reduced supply of goods while demand stays the same, which pushes the general price level up. ## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Unfavourable weather conditions such as droughts, floods and global warming may increase the cost of production, resulting in an increase in prices for goods and services.
- Natural disasters may lead to unplanned expenditure such rebuilding cost by businesses which may be recovered by increasing the prices of goods and services.
- Natural disasters may reduce the supply of goods and services which may increase the general price level if demand remains the same.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q3.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Briefly discuss export earnings and government expenditure as causes of demand-pull inflation. (2 x 4)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: demand-pull inflation happens when aggregate demand grows faster than aggregate supply. Handle the two causes under separate headings, up to 4 marks each. For export earnings, trace the chain: foreign demand rises, export income flows into South Africa, that income adds to aggregate demand, and without extra supply, prices rise. For government expenditure, the chain is: more spending on infrastructure, consumption and social grants raises aggregate demand — especially when financed by borrowing from the banking system, which adds money to circulation — and without a matching rise in supply, prices rise. **Marking note: a maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Export earnings (Max 4):

- Growth in economies of trading partner countries may create demand for a variety of local products
- Increase in world demand for commodities may lead to greater volumes of South African exports such as gold
- The income earned from exports may add to aggregate demand in South Africa, resulting in higher prices
- Increase in demand for exports without corresponding increase in supply of goods and services may result in price increases

Government expenditure (Max 4):

- An increase in government expenditure on infrastructure development, consumption spending and social spending may lead to an increase in aggregate demand
- An increase in government spending without a corresponding rise in aggregate supply may lead to price increases
- Increases in government spending that are financed by borrowing from the banking system add money into circulation which increases demand for goods and services

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

## Question (2 marks)

How can the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) use open-market transactions to reduce money supply in the economy? (1 x 2)

## Method

explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: in an open-market transaction the SARB trades government securities with banks. To REDUCE the money supply it must pull money out of circulation, so it SELLS securities — the banks pay for them, and that payment drains money from the banking system. (Buying securities would do the opposite and inject money.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) can sell government securities or bonds to commercial banks which will reduce the amount of money in circulation

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q4.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Analyse the measures that can be used to combat cost-push inflation. (4 x 2)

## Method

analysis

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: cost-push inflation comes from rising production costs, so every valid measure must lower costs or restrain the cost-price spiral. Group them: raise productivity (education, training, technology), lower input and operating costs (subsidies, cheaper imported inputs, efficient energy and transport infrastructure, lower business taxes), restrain the spiral (wage policy, price controls) and sharpen competition (domestic and foreign competition, small business development). Give FOUR measures, each linked to how it reduces costs, for 2 marks each. **Marking note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Improvement of education and training to increase productivity which helps to reduce the average cost of production and increase aggregate supply
- Investing in technology to improve productivity which will reduce the cost of production
- Promoting competition domestically and from abroad which helps to control high profit margins by businesses
- Imposing price controls, such as maximum prices, on certain goods and services to ensure that they remain affordable
- Implementing a wage policy to break the inflationary spiral of increased wages and prices
- Reducing import controls to make imported production inputs, such agricultural chemical, cheaper and reduce cost of production
- Improve the efficiency of infrastructural services, such energy and transport, to reduce the cost of doing business in the economy
- Providing subsidies to producers of certain goods and services to reduce their cost of production
- Promoting small business development to increase competition and increase the supply of goods and services
- Reducing taxes paid by business to reduce their cost of production which allows them to produce output

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

## Question (2 marks)

When the general price level increases, the real value of savings will …

A rise.
B decline.
C remain the same.
D increase.

**Note: the question paper prints options A ('rise') and D ('increase') as synonymous alternatives — a documented anomaly in the source paper, transcribed verbatim. The memo's accepted answer, B, is unaffected.**

## Method

multiple choice recall

Reason with real value: inflation erodes what a fixed sum of money can buy. If the general price level rises, the same amount of saved money buys fewer goods and services, so the purchasing power — the real value — of those savings declines.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B - decline

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (40 marks)

QUESTION 6: CONTEMPORARY ECONOMIC ISSUES.

- Discuss, in detail, the measures to combat inflation. (26 marks)
- How can South Africa's trading partners, such as the USA and China, influence the domestic inflation rate? (10 marks)

(Section C essay: answer ONE of two essay questions. Rubric: Introduction max 2 — define the main concept, do not include any part of the question or announce what will be discussed; Body main part max 26 — a maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples; Body additional part max 10 — a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; Conclusion max 2 — a higher-order summary, opinion or recommendation without repeating facts. Total 40.)

## Method

essay

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: structure the essay in four parts. Open by defining inflation — a considerable and sustained increase in the general price level over time. Organise the main body under three headings. Monetary policy (the SARB, within the 3% - 6% inflation-targeting framework): raising the repo rate to make borrowing expensive and cool spending, open market transactions selling securities to drain money supply, higher cash reserve requirements to limit credit creation, and moral suasion. Fiscal policy (the Minister of Finance): cutting government expenditure, financing deficits from the non-banking sector, and raising direct and indirect taxes, surcharges and loan levies to reduce disposable income and demand. Other measures: raising productivity, promoting competition, price controls, a wage policy, stricter consumer-credit conditions, relaxing import controls, a floating exchange rate, cutting the cost of doing business, and indexation. In the additional part, trace how trading partners transmit inflation into South Africa: their growth raising demand for local goods, imported inflation through higher prices of goods and inputs like oil and gas, tariff changes shifting export demand, and political tensions disrupting supply — as well as channels that lower inflation, such as import competition and cheaper imported inputs. Close with a brief higher-order conclusion.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):

Inflation is a considerable and sustainable increase in the general price level of goods and services over a period of time. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

BODY MAIN PART (Max 26) — MEASURES TO COMBAT INFLATION:

MONETARY POLICY MEASURES — Monetary policy in South Africa is formulated and implemented by the SARB within an inflation targeting framework of 3% - 6%. Monetary policy measures that can be taken include:

- Interest rates: The SARB curbs inflation by increasing the repo rate, which makes it more expensive to borrow money. Banks pass on the increased cost of borrowing (repo rate) to their households and businesses by increasing the interest rate. High interest rate discourages consumers from taking unnecessary credit, which helps to reduce consumer spending. A decrease in credit creation results to a reduction of money supply thereby reducing demand-pull inflation. The increase in interest rates stabilises the value of the currency, which helps to reduce cost-push inflation through lower import cost.
- Open market transactions / Open market operations: The SARB can directly decrease the supply of money by selling government securities in the open market. When banks buy securities money flows from banks to the SARB which, reduces money supply. Reduction in money supply will reduce aggregate demand controlling demand-pull inflation.
- Cash Reserve Requirements: Commercial banks are required to hold a certain minimum cash reserve with the central bank. An increase in the cash reserve requirement limits the amount of money that banks can give out as credit and helps to curb inflation.
- Moral suasion / Persuasion: The SARB can persuade commercial banks to act in a responsible manner when granting credit under inflationary conditions. Moral suasion helps to reduce inflation because credit will be granted to fewer consumers.

FISCAL POLICY MEASURES — Fiscal policy refers to the measures taken by the Minister of Finance regarding taxation and expenditure. The following are actions that can be taken:

- Government expenditure: The state can reduce expenditure by postponing some government projects such as road, hospital and school construction. Aggregate demand will decrease thereby reducing demand-pull inflation. The government may finance a budget deficit from the non-banking sector to limit inflation.
- Taxation: Government can increase direct taxation, such as personal income tax to decrease demand. An increase in indirect taxation (VAT) causes spending to decrease because goods become more expensive. The state can impose surcharges on imported goods, which will increase their prices thus discouraging consumer spending. A loan levy can be used to reduce disposable income of consumers. The government may reduce taxes on savings or introduce tax-free savings accounts to encourage saving and reduce spending.

OTHER MEASURES — Additional measures that can be used to combat inflation include:

- Increase productivity: Improving education and training to increase productivity which helps to reduce the average cost of production and increase aggregate supply. Investing in technology to improve productivity which will reduce the cost of production.
- Promote competition: Promoting competition domestically and from abroad which helps to control high profit margins by businesses. Promoting small business development to increase competition and increase the supply of goods and services.
- Price Control: The government ensures that certain essential goods remain affordable by imposing price controls, such as maximum prices.
- Wage Policy: Implementing a wage policy to break the inflationary spiral of increased wages and prices.
- Stricter conditions for consumer credit: The National Credit Regulator may impose strict requirement on consumer credit which will reduce aggregate demand.
- Import controls relaxation: More imports may help to supplement local supply of goods and services, reducing inflation caused by product shortages. Reduction of import controls helps to reduce the cost imported production inputs, such as agricultural chemical and reduce cost of production.
- Floating exchange rate: Prices are automatically adjusted to international conditions, which allow free operation of the price mechanism (real prices).
- Decrease in the cost of doing business: Improve the efficiency of infrastructural services, such energy and transport, to reduce the cost of doing business in the economy. Providing subsidies to producers of certain goods and services to reduce their cost of production. Reducing taxes paid by business to reduce their cost of production which allows them to produce output.
- Indexation: Linking prices of items such as wages, pensions and mortgage bond interest rates to price indices to eliminate the effects of inflation.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for headings/subheadings/examples)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10):

- Growth of the economies of South Africa's trading partner may increase demand for a variety of locally produced goods without a corresponding increase in supply, which increases demand-pull inflation.
- Price increases in trading partner countries may lead to imported inflation as South Africa import goods and services at higher prices.
- The removal of tariffs on South African exports in trading partner countries, such as China, may increase demand for local product contributing to higher inflation.
- Increase in prices of commodity imports may lead to higher cost of importing production inputs, such as oil and gas contributing to cost push inflation.
- Increase in demand for commodity exports, such as gold and coal by trading partner countries may increase export earnings leading to demand pull inflation.
- Political tensions between South Africa and its trading partner countries, such as USA may disrupt the supply of production inputs which leads to a decrease in production output and higher prices for goods and services.
- Increase in import tariffs especially on imported production inputs may increase the cost of production resulting in cost push inflation.
- Imports from South Africa's trading partners may increase competition on local markets which helps to control prices increases.
- Import tariffs imposed by South Africa's trading partners may reduce demand for South African exports which helps to control demand-pull inflation.
- Decrease in prices of imported production inputs may reduce the cost of production in South Africa which reduces the domestic inflation rate.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):

Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money which means consumers can buy fewer goods resulting in a decrease in the standard of living. (Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q1.3.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

TABLE 2 gives definitions of terminology used in Mathematical Literacy (A: an increase in the price of a basket of goods or services over time that is representative of the economy as a whole; B: sum of all the values divided by the number of values; C: the income received from the item sold and the cost price of the item is the same; D: value or values appearing most often in a data set; E: the difference between the highest and lowest values in a data set; F: an amount paid regularly at a particular rate for the use/loan of money; G: amounts that must be paid every month and which stay the same, like rent, school fees and transport costs; H: middle value in an ordered data set; I: expenses that change over time or from one week/month to the next, e.g. telephone and electricity costs; J: the point where the income exceeds the expenses). Match the definition with the term: Variable expenses. Write only the letter (A-J).

match definition

## Memo working

Variable expenses are costs whose amounts differ from one week or month to the next — like a telephone or electricity bill. ## Answer (per marking guidelines)

I

## Question (6 marks)

A house in Chennai, India, is valued at 5 000 000 rupees at the end of 2024. TABLE 7 shows the inflation rates in India for house prices: 2024: 8%; 2023: 7,5%; 2022: 7%; 2021: 6,5%; 2020: 6%. Calculate how much the house was worth at the end of 2022.

## Method

reverse inflation calculation

## Memo working

Work backwards one year at a time, dividing by each year's growth factor instead of multiplying. The 2024 value grew by 8% from the end-of-2023 value, so undo it: Price at end of 2023 = 5 000 000 / 1,08 (1A 1,08 or 108%, 1MA dividing) = 4 629 629,63 rupees (1CA). That value grew by 7,5% during 2023 from the end-of-2022 value, so undo it too: Price at end of 2022 = 4 629 629,63 / 1,075 (1MCA 1,075 or 107,5%, 1MA dividing) = 4 306 632,214 rupees (1CA simplification). (Memo alternative in one line: 5 000 000 x 100/108 x 100/107,5 = 4 306 632,214 rupees. NPU, NPR)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

4 306 632,214 rupees

## Memo working

In L1's branch: VR1 + VL1 = V(parallel), so VR1 + 20 = 32, giving VR1 = 12 V. Then V = IR with the branch current: 12 = 1,8R1, giving R1 = 6,67 Ω. (Memo option 2: 32 = 1,8R gives the whole branch resistance R = 17,77 Ω; RL1 = 20²/36 = 11,11 Ω; then R1 = 17,77 – 11,11 = 6,67 Ω.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

emf internal resistance

## Memo working

POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 8.2.2 and 8.2.3. OPTION 1: The series resistor's potential difference is V2 = ITOT·R2 = 3,3(4) = 13,2 V. The external voltage is V2 plus the 32 V across the parallel section, so ε = Vext + Ir = (13,2 + 32) + 3,3(0,6) = 47,18 V. (Memo options 2/3: combine resistances first — Rp = (21,33)(11,11 + 6,67)/(21,33 + 11,11 + 6,67) = 9,69 Ω; Rext = 9,69 + 4 = 13,69 Ω; then ε = I(R + r) = 3,3(13,69) + 3,3(0,6) = 47,18 V.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

ε = 47,18 V (accepted range 47,16 – 47,19 V)

ohms law

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q8.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2025, question Q8.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

A car battery of unknown emf (Ɛ) and internal resistance (r) is connected to two identical parallel headlights (12 Ω each, switched by S1) and a starter motor (0,1 Ω, switched by S2). With S1 open and S2 closed, the motor current is 120 A. With S1 closed and S2 open, the total headlight current is 2,24 A. Calculate the emf of the battery.

## Method

emf internal resistance simultaneous

## Memo working

First combine the two parallel headlights: 1/Rp = 1/12 + 1/12, so Rp = 6 Ω.

With S1 closed and S2 open, the emf equation is Ɛ = I(R + r) = 2,24(6 + r). With S1 open and S2 closed, the same battery gives Ɛ = 120(0,1 + r). The emf is the same in both cases, so equate: 2,24(6 + r) = 120(0,1 + r), which gives r = 0,012 Ω.

Substitute back: Ɛ = 2,24(6 + 0,012) = 13,46 V (or Ɛ = 120(0,1 + 0,012) = 13,47 V). (Memo option 2 uses Ɛ = 12 + 120r and Ɛ = 13,42 + 2,24r, from V = 13,42 V across the headlights, giving 13,45 - 13,47 V. POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 8.2 AND 8.3.2.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Ɛ = 13,46 V [accepted RANGE: 13,42 V - 13,47 V]

Indicate whether the following statements are TRUE or FALSE. Write only 'true' or 'false' next to the question numbers (1.1.1 to 1.1.3) in the ANSWER BOOK.

## Method

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

To reason each one out: an EFT receipt from a debtor only becomes reliable once the business has proof that the money actually arrived, so it is recorded in the Cash Receipts Journal only after proof of payment or a bank statement entry confirms it — true. Output VAT is VAT the business collects from customers on behalf of SARS; it is owed to SARS, so it is a liability, not an asset — false. When a debt is written off as bad, the output VAT originally charged on that credit sale may be claimed back, which reduces the amount payable to SARS — true.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1.1.1 True; 1.1.2 False; 1.1.3 True

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q1.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

MATSAMO TRADERS: The information relates to Matsamo Traders for August 2024. The business sells goods for cash and on credit. Calculate the correct balance of the Debtors' Control account on 31 August 2024. Provide figures and a plus (+) or minus (-) sign for each correction. If there is no change to the balance, indicate with (0).

INFORMATION:

A. Balances on 31 August 2024 before taking the errors and omissions below into account:

(i) Debtors' Control Account balance in the General Ledger, R359 100

(ii) List of debtors' balances as per Debtors' Ledger (columns: Debtors | Amount (R)): N Naidoo 63 000; S Sibiya 69 000; V Esterhuizen 114 000; J Nyoka 95 700; W du Plessis 11 500; Total 353 200.

B. Errors and omissions:

(i) No entry was made for the credit sale invoice issued to N Naidoo, R4 500.

(ii) Merchandise sold on credit to S Sibiya for R18 000 was incorrectly posted to the account of V Esterhuizen.

(iii) The debtors' allowances column in the DAJ was undercast by R11 000.

(iv) An EFT payment of R5 700 was made by W du Plessis. This was correctly recorded in the relevant journal, but was posted as R7 500 to his account in the Debtors' Ledger.

(v) Credit sales to V Esterhuizen, R5 200, were incorrectly recorded as R2 500 in the Debtors' Journal and posted as such to the Debtors' Control Account and Esterhuizen's account in the Debtors' Ledger.

(vi) Goods returned by J Nyoka, R3 450, were posted to the wrong side of his account in the Debtors' Ledger.

## Method

debtors control corrections

## Memo working

Start with the Debtors' Control balance before errors and omissions: R359 100. For each error, ask whether it affects the Debtors' Control account in the General Ledger (an error in a journal entry or a journal column total), or only an individual debtor's personal account in the Debtors' Ledger (a posting error).

(i) The credit sale invoice was never entered anywhere, so the control account must increase: +4 500.

(ii) The sale was posted to the wrong debtor's personal account — this moves the amount between accounts inside the Debtors' Ledger only, so no change to control: 0.

(iii) The debtors' allowances column total of the DAJ posts to the control account; an undercast of R11 000 means allowances were understated, so the balance decreases: -11 000.

(iv) The EFT was correctly recorded in the journal; only the posting to the personal account was wrong, so no change to control: 0.

(v) Credit sales of R5 200 were recorded as R2 500 in the journal, so the control account is understated: +2 700 ([+5 200 - 2 500], two marks for both figures; R2 700 must be positive).

(vi) Wrong side of the personal account in the Debtors' Ledger only, so no change to control: 0.

Correct balance: 359 100 + 4 500 - 11 000 + 2 700 = 355 300. (Memo: a superfluous entry loses the method mark on the total.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Correct balance of Debtors' Control Account: 355 300 (one part correct; should include R359 100)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q1.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (14 marks)

Complete the correct Debtors' List on 31 August 2024. The pre-adjustment figures have been entered.

(MATSAMO TRADERS — same information as Q1.2.1. Pre-adjustment debtors' balances: N Naidoo 63 000; S Sibiya 69 000; V Esterhuizen 114 000; J Nyoka 95 700; W du Plessis 11 500; Total 353 200. Errors and omissions: (i) credit sale invoice to N Naidoo, R4 500, not entered; (ii) credit sale to S Sibiya, R18 000, posted to V Esterhuizen's account; (iii) debtors' allowances column in the DAJ undercast by R11 000; (iv) EFT of R5 700 by W du Plessis correctly journalised but posted as R7 500 to his account; (v) credit sales to V Esterhuizen, R5 200, recorded as R2 500 in the Debtors' Journal and posted as such; (vi) goods returned by J Nyoka, R3 450, posted to the wrong side of his account in the Debtors' Ledger.)

## Method

debtors list corrections

## Memo working

Correct each debtor's personal account for the errors that touch the Debtors' Ledger. Note that error (iii), the DAJ column undercast, affects only the control account total, not any individual debtor.

N Naidoo: the omitted invoice must be added: 63 000 + 4 500 = 67 500.

S Sibiya: his R18 000 sale was posted to the wrong account, so add it back: 69 000 + 18 000 = 87 000.

V Esterhuizen: remove the R18 000 that belongs to Sibiya, then add the understated sale: 114 000 - 18 000 + 2 700 (see 1.2.1(v)) = 98 700 (one part correct).

J Nyoka: the returns of R3 450 were debited instead of credited, so the correction is double the amount: 95 700 - 3 450 - 3 450 (i.e. -6 900, two marks) = 88 800 (one part correct).

W du Plessis: reverse the wrong posting of R7 500 and post the correct R5 700: 11 500 + 7 500 - 5 700 (i.e. +1 800, two marks) = 13 300 (one part correct).

Total: 67 500 + 87 000 + 98 700 + 88 800 + 13 300 = 355 300 (one part correct) — this agrees with the corrected Debtors' Control balance of R355 300 from Q1.2.1, which is the whole point of the reconciliation.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

N Naidoo 67 500; S Sibiya 87 000; V Esterhuizen 98 700; J Nyoka 88 800; W du Plessis 13 300; Correct total of Debtors' List 355 300 (one part correct)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q1.3.1.

## Question (4 marks)

DEBTORS' AGE ANALYSIS: The information relates to Timo Traders. Their credit terms are 60 days and it is expected at least 90% of debtors will adhere to these terms. Provide a calculation or figures to show why Timo Traders should not be satisfied with the figures in the Debtors' Age Analysis.

INFORMATION:

Debtors' Age Analysis on 31 August 2024 (columns: Total | Current month | 30 days | 60 days | 90 days | 90+): R240 000 | R118 000 | R36 000 | R38 000 | R29 200 | R18 800

## Method

age analysis percentage within terms

## Memo working

With 60-day credit terms, debts in the current month, 30-day and 60-day columns are within terms; the 90-day and 90+ columns are overdue. Compare the within-terms percentage to the 90% target.

Within terms: [240 000 - 48 000] OR [118 000 + 36 000 + 38 000] = 192 000 (two marks) / 240 000 (one mark) x 100 = 80% OR 49,2% + 15% + 15,8%. This is below the expected 90%.

OR overdue: [29 200 + 18 800] = 48 000 (two marks) / 240 000 (one mark) x 100 = 20% OR 12,2% + 7,8% — more than the 10% that would be acceptable.

('x 100' does not count as one part correct.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

80% within credit terms (one part correct; accept 10% below target; do not accept 'R') OR 20% overdue (one part correct; do not accept 'R')

Explain TWO points of advice that you will offer to the owner. NOTE: Maximum discount is granted to debtors who settle their accounts timeously. Interest at the accepted rate is being charged.

debtors control advice

(see marking guidelines)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q1.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (10 marks)

BANK RECONCILIATION: The information relates to Duma Stores on 31 July 2025. The business is owned by Duma Mathupha. They use the official Bank Statement, received on the 28th of each month, to reconcile their Cash Journals. Complete the table provided in the ANSWER BOOK by showing the entries that must be recorded in the Cash Journals on 31 July 2025. (The ANSWER BOOK pre-prints a two-column table headed Cash Receipts Journal R162 000 and Cash Payments Journal R55 200.)

INFORMATION:

A. Extract from the Bank Reconciliation Statement on 30 June 2025: outstanding deposits dated 29 June 2025, R132 000, and 30 June 2025, R18 600; outstanding EFTs: EFT 124 (Typek Stationers) R5 310 and EFT 125 (Cola Stores) R9 990.

B. Provisional totals in the Cash Journals on 31 July 2025 before receiving the Bank Statement: Cash Receipts Journal R162 000; Cash Payments Journal R55 200.

C. Items on the Bank Statement that do not agree with the July 2025 Cash Journals (columns: Date | Details | Debit (R) | Credit (R)): 29 June deposit, credit 132 000; 30 June deposit, credit 8 600; 3 July EFT 124 (Typek Stationers), debit 3 150; 5 July EFT 125 (Cola Stores), debit 9 990; 10 July direct deposit (Q Ngcobo), credit 16 500; 15 July debit order (Prime Insurers), debit 2 700; 15 July debit order (Prime Insurers), debit 2 700; 25 July interest, debit 975; July service fees, debit 605; 28 July A-Z Suppliers, debit 12 000. Notes: (i) the internal auditor discovered that the supporting cash slips for the deposit on 30 June 2025 amounted to R18 600 — the shortfall is irrecoverable because the cashier at that time has resigned; (ii) EFT 124 on 3 July 2025 (Typek Stationers) is correct on the Bank Statement; (iii) the direct deposit on 10 July 2025 by Q Ngcobo (a tenant) was recorded incorrectly in the Cash Payments Journal; (iv) the debit order on 15 July 2025 to Prime Insurers for the business insurance was processed twice due to insufficient funds in June — the amounts covered payments for both June and July 2025 to bring the account up to date; (v) a bank transfer on 28 July 2025 in favour of A-Z Suppliers was overstated by R11 000 by the bank clerk — the bank was notified and will correct the error in August 2025.

D. Entries in the Cash Journals for July 2025 that were not reflected on the July 2025 Bank Statement: deposit on 30 July 2025 R41 850; EFT 207 R7 650; EFT 208 R10 800.

E. Duma, the owner, used a business debit card on 29 July 2025 for the payment of R13 000 to Star Motors for repairs to the company vehicle, but he neglected to submit the transaction slip to the bookkeeper.

F. The Bank Statement on 28 July 2025 showed a favourable balance of R119 080.

## Method

cash journal supplementary entries

## Memo working

Work through each difference and decide whether it belongs in the Cash Receipts Journal or the Cash Payments Journal.

Cash Receipts Journal (on the provisional R162 000): 2 160 (two marks) corrects EFT 124 — it was recorded at R5 310 in June but the Bank Statement shows the correct amount of R3 150, so the overstatement of 5 310 - 3 150 = 2 160 comes back in. Then 16 500 (one mark) + 16 500 (one mark) = 33 000 corrects the tenant Q Ngcobo's direct deposit that was recorded in the CPJ: one 16 500 cancels the wrong CPJ entry and the other records the receipt itself.

Cash Payments Journal (on the provisional R55 200): 10 000 (two marks) is the missing cash on the 30 June deposit (cash slips R18 600 versus only R8 600 banked; irrecoverable, so it is written off); 2 700 (one mark) + 2 700 (one mark) = 5 400 for the Prime Insurers debit orders covering June and July; 13 000 (one mark) for the owner's debit card payment to Star Motors; 975 (one mark) interest charged by the bank; 605 (one mark) service fees.

(Memo: -1 foreign items, max -1, only if marks are scored elsewhere for the same figure; -1 superfluous items, max -1; ensure that the candidate does not get full marks for including any incorrect figure/s. Note that the A-Z Suppliers bank error of R11 000 is the bank's mistake — it belongs in the Bank Reconciliation Statement, not in the journals.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Cash Receipts Journal (on R162 000): 2 160; 33 000 [16 500 + 16 500]. Cash Payments Journal (on R55 200): 10 000; 5 400 [2 700 + 2 700]; 13 000; 975; 605

Prepare the Bank Reconciliation Statement on 31 July 2025. (The ANSWER BOOK offers a choice of two templates: a two-column method with Debit and Credit columns, OR a one-column method. Choose only ONE.)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q1.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (11 marks)

CREDITORS' RECONCILIATION: PG Stores is owned by Portia Gina and she buys goods on credit from Matsulu Suppliers. The statement of account received from Matsulu Suppliers reflected a balance of R287 600 for June 2025. Use the table in the ANSWER BOOK to indicate how the relevant balances will change when preparing the Creditors' Reconciliation. Indicate the amount, as well as a (+) for increase and a (-) for decrease. (The ANSWER BOOK pre-prints a table with rows (i) to (vi) and the incorrect balances: Creditors' Ledger Account of Matsulu Suppliers 270 140 | Statement of Account 287 600.)

INFORMATION:

A. Creditors' Ledger of PG Stores — Matsulu Suppliers (columns: Date | Details | Debit (R) | Credit (R) | Balance (R)): 1 June balance b/d 135 000; 12 June Invoice 320, credit 162 000; 14 June EFT, debit 67 500; 19 June Debit Note 785, debit 13 680; 20 June Invoice 412, credit 50 000; 23 June Invoice 471, credit 100 500; 24 June Debit Note 1106, credit 16 200; 28 June Invoice 681, credit 42 000; 29 June EFT and discount, debit 154 380; closing balance 270 140.

B. When comparing the Creditors' Ledger to the statement of account received from Matsulu Suppliers, the following differences were noted: (i) Debit Note 785 was incorrectly recorded in the Creditors' Ledger — the statement shows the correct amount of R17 280; (ii) Invoice 471 was incorrectly recorded on the statement from Matsulu Suppliers as R40 500; (iii) the transaction on 24 June 2025 in the Creditors' Ledger is for merchandise returned to Matsulu Suppliers; (iv) the statement showed interest charged at R1 080 — the correct amount of interest is R1 410, and no entry was made into the Creditors' Ledger; (v) the statement reflects transactions up to 25 June 2025; (vi) all other transactions recorded in the Creditors' Ledger appeared correctly in the statement of account received from Matsulu Suppliers.

## Method

creditors reconciliation table

## Memo working

Correct each side for the errors that belong to it, then show that both corrected balances agree.

Creditors' Ledger Account of Matsulu Suppliers (start at 270 140): (i) Debit Note 785 was under-recorded at 13 680 instead of 17 280, so a further [-17 280 + 13 680] = -3 600 (two marks). (iii) the 24 June return of R16 200 was entered in the credit column instead of the debit column, so the correction is double the amount: -16 200 (one mark) - 16 200 (one mark) = -32 400. (iv) the interest of R1 410 was never recorded in the ledger: +1 410 (one mark). Corrected balance: 270 140 - 3 600 - 32 400 + 1 410 = 235 550.

Statement of Account (start at 287 600): (ii) Invoice 471 appears at 40 500 instead of 100 500, so [100 500 - 40 500] = +60 000 (two marks). (iv) interest of 1 080 must be corrected to 1 410: +330 (one mark). (v) the statement runs only to 25 June, so Invoice 681 of 28 June must be added: +42 000 (one mark). (vi) the EFT and discount of 29 June must be deducted: -154 380 (one mark). Corrected balance: 287 600 + 60 000 + 330 + 42 000 - 154 380 = 235 550.

Totals 235 550 in both columns (one part correct for both totals; must include opening balances; could be different amounts).

(Memo: accept brackets for a negative sign; if no sign, assume positive; accept correct identifiable amounts presented in wrong line/s; foreign entries -1 per line if a mark has been scored on that line.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Creditors' Ledger Account of Matsulu Suppliers: balance 270 140; (i) -3 600; (iii) -32 400; (iv) +1 410; total 235 550. Statement of Account: balance 287 600; (ii) +60 000; (iv) +330; (v) +42 000; (vi) -154 380; total 235 550

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q8.3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q8.3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Given: f(x) = -6x^2. Determine f'(x) from first principles.

## Method

first principles

## Memo working

Start from the definition f'(x) = lim_{h->0} [f(x + h) - f(x)]/h. f(x + h) = -6(x + h)^2 = -6x^2 - 12xh - 6h^2. So f(x + h) - f(x) = -6x^2 - 12xh - 6h^2 + 6x^2 = -12xh - 6h^2. Divide by h: (-12xh - 6h^2)/h = -12x - 6h. Let h tend to zero: f'(x) = lim_{h->0} (-12x - 6h) = -12x.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

f'(x) = -12x

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q8.1

## Question (4 marks)

Determine f'(x) from first principles if it is given that f(x) = -2x + 3.

## Method

first principles

## Memo working

Apply the definition of the derivative: f'(x) = lim_{h->0} [f(x + h) - f(x)]/h. Compute f(x + h) = -2(x + h) + 3 = -2x - 2h + 3. Then f(x + h) - f(x) = (-2x - 2h + 3) - (-2x + 3) = -2h. So f'(x) = lim_{h->0} (-2h)/h = lim_{h->0} (-2) = -2.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

f'(x) = -2

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1

In the diagram, P(-1 ; 8), Q(-4 ; -6) and R(12 ; 2) are the vertices of ΔPQR. The angle of inclination of QR is θ. distance formula

QR = √320 = 8√5 units

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q3.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

T is a point on QR such that PT ⊥ QR. Calculate the coordinates of T. (From QUESTION 3: P(-1 ; 8), Q(-4 ; -6) and R(12 ; 2); from QUESTION 3.4 the equation of QR is y = (1/2)x - 4.)

## Method

foot of perpendicular intersection

## Memo working

PT ⊥ QR, so m_PT = -2 (negative reciprocal of 1/2). Equation of PT through P(-1 ; 8): 8 = -2(-1) + c -> c = 6, so y = -2x + 6. Intersect with QR's equation y = (1/2)x - 4: -2x + 6 = (1/2)x - 4 -> 10 = (5/2)x -> 5x = 20 -> x = 4; then y = (1/2)(4) - 4 = -2. So T(4 ; -2). (Memo alternative: PQ = PR = √205, so ΔPQR is isosceles and the perpendicular height bisects the base QR; T is the midpoint of QR = (4 ; -2).)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

T(4 ; -2)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.7

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q3.7.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Calculate the area of parallelogram PQRS. (From QUESTION 3: P(-1 ; 8), Q(-4 ; -6), R(12 ; 2), S(15 ; 16); from QUESTION 3.1 QR = 8√5; from QUESTION 3.6 T(4 ; -2) is the foot of the perpendicular from P to QR.)

## Method

base times height

## Memo working

The height of the parallelogram on base QR is PT: PT = sqrt((4 - (-1))^2 + (-2 - 8)^2) = sqrt(25 + 100) = √125 = 5√5 = 11,18 units. Area of parallelogram = base × height: area PQRS = QR·PT = (8√5)(5√5) = 200 units^2. (Memo alternative: area ΔPQR = (1/2)(8√5)(5√5) = 100 units^2; area PQRS = 2 × 100 = 200 units^2.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

200 units^2

## Question (2 marks)

Miecke plans to install a home solar system unit consisting of solar panels, a battery and an inverter. A newspaper advertisement shows two payment options for the same unit (OPTION 1: RENT-TO-OWN - pay for 7 years at R1 549 p/m, plus additional costs of a R782 initiation fee and a buy-out of R7 820 after the rental period. OPTION 2: CASH PRICE - R78 200 including VAT). Write down the monthly instalment for the rent-to-own option.

## Method

read value from document

## Memo working

The monthly instalment is the amount labelled "p/m" (per month) under the rent-to-own option: R1 549. The initiation fee and buy-out amount are once-off extras, not the monthly instalment. (Memo: 2RT correct amount, NPU.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R1 549

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q2.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

A home solar system unit can be paid for in two ways (OPTION 1: RENT-TO-OWN - pay for 7 years at R1 549 p/m, plus a R782 initiation fee and a buy-out of R7 820 after the rental period. OPTION 2: CASH PRICE - R78 200 including VAT). After seven years, Miecke decides to buy-out the rent-to-own option. Calculate the extra amount she has to pay compared to buying the home solar system unit for cash.

## Method

total cost comparison

## Memo working

First convert the rental period to months: 12 x 7 = 84 months (1A). Then total up everything the rent-to-own route costs: (R1 549 x 84) + R782 + R7 820 = R130 116 + R782 + R7 820 (1MCA adding ALL correct values) = R138 718 (1CA). Finally compare with the cash price: Difference = R138 718 - R78 200 (1MCA subtracting values) = R60 518 (1CA simplification).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R60 518

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q3.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Mapwork on the 1 : 50 000 topographical map 2529CC eMALAHLENI (WITBANK) and the 1 : 10 000 orthophoto map 2529 CC 15 eMALAHLENI (WITBANK). eMalahleni is a coal-mining city on the Highveld of Mpumalanga, with opencast coal mines, power stations and a steel mill nearby. (The physical map sheets are separate; map-read inputs come from the memo's accepted values.)

Refer to the orthophoto map. Calculate the area of the demarcated feature 6 in blocks B4, C3 and C4 in m². Use the following information:

Measured breadth (orthophoto map distance) = 1,8 cm

Formula: Area = Length (L) x Breadth (B)  (4 x 1)

(The length is measured off the map by the candidate; the memo's accepted measurement is 3,5 cm, range 3,4 cm - 3,6 cm.)

## Method

area calculation

## Memo working

On the 1 : 10 000 orthophoto map, 1 cm on the map represents 10 000 cm = 100 m on the ground.

Length: 3,5 (1) cm [measurement range 3,4 cm - 3,6 cm] x 100 = 350 (1) m [range 340 m - 360 m].

Breadth (given): 1,8 cm x 100 = 180 (1) m.

Area = Length x Breadth = 350 m x 180 m = 63 000 m² (1) [range 61 200 m² - 64 800 m²].

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

63 000 m² (1) [accepted range 61 200 m² - 64 800 m²]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q3.1.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Mapwork on the 1 : 50 000 topographical map 2529CC eMALAHLENI (WITBANK) and the 1 : 10 000 orthophoto map 2529 CC 15 eMALAHLENI (WITBANK). eMalahleni is a coal-mining city on the Highveld of Mpumalanga, with opencast coal mines, power stations and a steel mill nearby. (The physical map sheets are separate; map-read inputs come from the memo's accepted values.)

Refer to the topographical map. Calculate the magnetic declination of eMalahleni (Witbank) for 2025. Use the following information:

Difference in years: 11

Mean annual change: 5' W  (3 x 1)

(The mean magnetic declination of 18°19' west of true north is read from the map margin; the 11-year difference implies a base year of 2014.)

## Method

magnetic declination calculation

## Memo working

Total change over the period: 11 years x 5' per year = 55' (1) westwards (a westward change is added).

Magnetic declination for 2025 = mean magnetic declination + total change = 18°19' + (1) 55' = 18°74'.

Convert 74 minutes to 1°14' (60' = 1°): 18°74' = 19°14' west of true north (1).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

19°14' west of true north (1)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2025, question Q3.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Calculate the difference in height between trigonometrical station F in block C3 and trigonometrical station G in block D3. (2 x 1)

(Based on the 1 : 50 000 topographical map 3318DD STELLENBOSCH. The map sheet is a separate physical sheet; heights as read for the memo: trigonometrical station F = 1167,5 m, trigonometrical station G = 928,0 m.)

## Method

height difference calculation

## Memo working

Read the height printed next to each trigonometrical station on the map: station F in block C3 is 1167,5 m above sea level and station G in block D3 is 928,0 m. The difference in height is the higher value minus the lower value: 1167,5 - 928,0 = 239,5 m. One mark is for the correct subtraction of the two map-read heights, one mark for the answer.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1167,5 m - 928,0 m (1) = 239,5 m (1)

Perennial water/Dams (1); Reservoirs (1); Non-perennial rivers (1) [ANY ONE]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2025, question Q3.2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Give evidence from the map to support your answer to QUESTION 3.2.4. (1 x 2)

(QUESTION 3.2.4 asked for the general night-time wind direction around the row of trees labelled J in block E3 on the 1 : 50 000 topographical map; the memo accepts north/NW/NNW/north-east — the wind blowing from that side towards the south.)

## Method

map evidence

## Memo working

Two lines of map evidence support the direction. First, the row of trees is a windbreak, and windbreaks are planted perpendicular to the prevailing wind — on the map the trees stand on the north/north-east side of the orchards and vineyards, so the wind they shield against must come from that side. Second, at night air on the mountain slopes cools, becomes dense and drains downslope as a katabatic (mountain) wind — flowing down from the high ground towards the valley, which fits the same direction. Any one piece of evidence, fully stated, earns the two marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Row of trees (windbreaks) are on the north/north east of the orchards or vineyards (2); Wind blows down the mountain slopes (katabatic wind) (2); Wind breaks are planted perpendicular to the prevailing wind (2) [ANY ONE]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2025, question Q3.2.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Refer to the topographical map. Stellenboschberg is a watershed. Give evidence from the map to support this statement. (1 x 2)

(Based on the 1 : 50 000 topographical map 3318DD STELLENBOSCH.)

## Method

map evidence

## Memo working

A watershed is the high ground that separates one drainage basin from another, so the evidence to look for is rivers rising on the high ground and flowing away from it on opposite sides. On the map, many river systems flow away from Stellenboschberg in opposite directions — towards the north-east on one side and the south-west on the other — which is exactly what a watershed produces.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Many river systems flow in a north easterly and south westerly direction (2); Many river systems are flowing (away) in opposite directions from the Stellenboschberg (2) [ANY ONE]

column matching

## Question (1 mark)

Multiple choice: The slope at X on the inner bank of a meander is also referred to as a/an ... slope. (Sketch of a meandering river: arrow X points to the gently sloping deposition bank on the inside of a meander bend; the outer bank opposite is steep.)  A steep  B undercut  C concave  D slip-off

## Method

fluvial mcq

On the inside of a meander bend the water flows slowest, so the river deposits material there and builds a gentle bank. That gentle depositional bank is called the slip-off slope; the steep, eroded outer bank is the undercut slope. X sits on the inner bank, so it is the slip-off slope.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D (slip-off)

(Sketch of a river on its flood plain with raised banks labelled 'Natural levees' on either side of the channel; flood plain deposits layered beside the channel.)  A increased deposition  B reduced flooding  C reduced fertility  D increased flooding

## Method

fluvial mcq

Natural levees are raised banks of coarse sediment deposited right next to the channel during floods. Because they stand higher than the flood plain behind them, they help contain the river in its channel, so the benefit is reduced flooding on the flood plain.

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B (reduced flooding)

## Question (1 mark)

Multiple choice: Deltas form at the river mouth when the following conditions occur:  (i) Shallow sea bed  (ii) Steep sea bed  (iii) Strong currents  (iv) Small tidal range  A (i) and (ii)  B (ii) and (iii)  C (iii) and (iv)  D (i) and (iv)

## Method

fluvial mcq

A delta needs deposited sediment to accumulate at the mouth. That happens where the sea bed is shallow, so sediment can build up to the surface, and where the tidal range is small, so the sea does not sweep the sediment away. Steep sea beds and strong currents prevent delta formation, so conditions (i) and (iv) apply.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D ((i) shallow sea bed and (iv) small tidal range)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.4.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2025, question Q2.4.2.

## Question (2 marks)

Account for the gentle gradient of the inner bank at C in photograph A. (1 x 2)  (Photograph A - aerial photo of a strongly meandering river on a flat flood plain; a line C-D crosses one meander bend from the inner bank at C to the outer bank at D, and the cross-section shows a gently sloping bank at C rising to a steep undercut bank at D.)

## Method

explain reason

## Memo working

C is the inner bank (slip-off slope) of the meander bend. Water on the inside of the bend moves slowly, so it has too little energy to carry its load and deposition takes place, building a gently sloping bank. Either the deposition point or the slow velocity point earns the 2 marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Due to deposition (2); Slow movement/velocity of water (2) [ANY ONE]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.4.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2025, question Q2.4.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Refer to photograph A. In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, explain how an oxbow lake is formed. (4 x 2)

(Photograph A is an aerial photo of a strongly meandering river on a flat flood plain with farmland; a cross-section drawn across one meander bend shows a gently sloping inner bank at C rising to a steep, undercut outer bank at D.)

## Method

paragraph process

## Memo working

Work through the life of one meander bend. On the outer bank — the undercut slope, where the water flows fastest — continuous lateral erosion keeps eating into the bank. On the inner bank — the slip-off slope, where the water is slow — deposition builds the bank outwards. Erosion on the outside and deposition on the inside make the neck of land between the two limbs of the meander narrower and narrower. During a flood the river takes the shortcut and cuts straight through the narrow meander neck. The abandoned meander loop is then sealed off from the new straight channel by deposition, leaving a horseshoe-shaped body of standing water: an oxbow lake.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Continuous (lateral) erosion takes place on the outer bank/under-cut slope (2); Deposition on the inner bank/slip off slope (2); Meander neck narrows (2); River floods and cuts through meander neck (2); Meander loop is separated from the main stream (by deposition resulting in an ox-bow lake) (2) [ANY FOUR]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q1.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Shown below is the information regarding a South African Airways flight from Cape Town to Johannesburg (flight information card: Wednesday 8 January 2025; distance 1 278 km; aircraft Boeing 737-800; codeshare NZ 3120; flight number SA332; maximum number of passengers 189; departure 12:15 Cape Town; arrival 14:15 Johannesburg). State, in words, the arrival time of the flight using the 12-hour format.

## Method

convert time to words 12 hour

## Memo working

The arrival time on the card is 14:15 in the 24-hour format. Subtract 12 hours to move into the 12-hour format: 14:15 becomes 2:15. Since it is after midday, it is in the afternoon. Fifteen minutes past the hour is "quarter past", so 2:15 in the afternoon is quarter past two in the afternoon. (Memo: 1RT correct time in words; 1A correct time of day.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Quarter past two in the afternoon. OR Fifteen minutes after two in the afternoon.

## Question (2 marks)

Shown below is the information regarding a South African Airways flight from Cape Town to Johannesburg (flight information card: Wednesday 8 January 2025; distance 1 278 km; departure 12:15 Cape Town; arrival 14:15 Johannesburg). Write down which ONE of the methods below is the CORRECT method to calculate the speed in km/h of the aircraft. Write only the letter (A-C). A: 1 278 / 14:15. B: 1 278 / 2. C: 2 / 1 278.

## Method

select correct speed formula

## Memo working

Speed = distance ÷ time. The distance is 1 278 km. The time is NOT the clock reading 14:15 — it is the duration of the flight: from departure 12:15 to arrival 14:15 is 2 hours. So speed = 1 278 km ÷ 2 h, which is option B. Option A wrongly divides by a clock time, and option C divides the wrong way around (time by distance). (Memo: 2A correct letter.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B

## Question (3 marks)

(Context: a GPS-tracked flamingo flew from area A southwards. On 14 June it spent the night at a small pan at area B. On 15 June at 19:00, it flew non-stop for 14 hours and 25 minutes to arrive at area E, the end point.) Determine the bird's date and time of arrival at area E.

add duration to start time

## Memo working

Time of arrival = 19:00 + 14 hours 25 minutes. From 19:00 to midnight is 5 hours, which uses up 5 of the 14 hours 25 minutes; the remaining 9 hours 25 minutes run into the next day, giving 09:25. Since the flight started on 15 June, the arrival is on 16 June at 09:25.

## Question (4 marks)

(Context: a GPS-tracked flamingo flew non-stop from area B to area E in 14 hours and 25 minutes.) The flight from area B to area E is 770 km. Calculate (in km/h) the average speed of the bird as it flew from area B to area E. You may use this formula: Distance = speed x time

## Method

speed from distance and time

## Memo working

Substitute into the formula: 770 km = speed x 14 hours 25 min. Change the subject: speed = 770 km ÷ 14 hours 25 min. Convert the minutes to a decimal of an hour: 25 min = 25/60 hour, so the time is 14,4166... hours. Speed = 770 ÷ 14,4166... = 53,41 km/h.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

53,41 km/h

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q4.2.5.

## Question (5 marks)

(Context: a GPS-tracked flamingo flew 770 km from area B to area E.) The direct distance between area B and area E is 311,72 miles. The person tracking the bird's GPS stated that the bird flew an extra distance of 268,13 km when compared to the direct distance. 1 mile = 1,60934 km. Verify, with calculations, whether this statement is VALID.

## Method

mile conversion and difference verification

## Memo working

Convert the direct distance to kilometres: 311,72 miles x 1,60934 = 501,6634... km. Extra distance actually flown = 770 km - 501,6634... km = 268,336... km, which is not the claimed 268,13 km. The statement is INVALID. (Memo option 2: 501,6634... + 268,13 = 769,7934... km, which is not 770 km, so INVALID.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

311,72 miles = 311,72 x 1,60934 = 501,6634... km; extra distance = 770 - 501,6634... = 268,336... km, not 268,13 km. INVALID.

On the left is a steeply curved front A with a towering cumulonimbus cloud, heavy rain shafts and rapid uplift, with air behind it at 12 °C. On the right is a gently sloping front B with small scattered clouds and light rain, with air below it at 8 °C.) How does front A give rise to the formation of cumulonimbus clouds? (2 x 2)

## Method

process explanation

Front A is the cold front. Follow the sequence verbally: the dense cold air drives in underneath the warm air ahead of it; the steep frontal slope forces that warm air upward rapidly; and the rising air cools to dew point, so condensation builds towering cumulonimbus cloud.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Cold front will undercut the warm air (ahead of it) (2)
- The steeper gradient will cause rapid uplift of the warm air (2)
- Cooling and condensation occurs (2)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2024, question Q1.3.4.

## Question (8 marks)

(Refer to a cross-section of a mid-latitude cyclone. A bold arrow labelled 'DIRECTION OF MOVEMENT' runs from west on the left to east on the right. On the left is a steeply curved front A with a towering cumulonimbus cloud, heavy rain shafts and rapid uplift, with air behind it at 12 °C. On the right is a gently sloping front B with small scattered clouds and light rain, with air below it at 8 °C.) In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, explain strategies that can be put in place to manage the negative environmental impact of the heavy rainfall associated with mid-latitude cyclones. (4 x 2)

## Method

paragraph strategies

Group the strategies so they are easy to recall aloud. First, protect and restore vegetation cover — natural vegetation, afforestation, wetlands and buffer zones — so water infiltrates instead of running off. Second, engineer the flow: drainage systems, dams or weirs, artificial levees, gabions, widened or canalised river channels. Third, shield vulnerable slopes: retaining walls, sandbags, catch nets and canopies where rockfalls threaten, contour ploughing and terracing. Fourth, prepare people: environmental-conservation education and awareness or early-warning systems. Any four well-explained strategies at two marks each earn the eight marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Maintain natural vegetation (2)
- Encourage afforestation (2)
- Buffering of the area (2)
- Create effective drainage systems (2)
- Use of sandbags (2)
- Building of retaining walls (accept examples) (2)
- Use of catch nets (areas prone to rockfalls) (2)
- Use of canopies (areas prone to rockfalls) (2)
- Construction of gabions (2)
- Construct dams (wall)/weir (2)
- Construct artificial levees/barriers (2)
- Conserve wetlands/marshes/swamps (2)
- Implement contour ploughing (2)
- Terracing of slopes (2)
- Widening river channels (water management systems) (2)
- Canalising rivers (2)
- Educate people about environmental conservation (2)
- Awareness/early warning systems (2)

[ANY FOUR]

## Question (1 mark)

## Method

explain reason

The polar front is only a smooth line while the two air flows stay undisturbed. Any disturbance — unstable air, friction with the surface, an upper-air jet stream, a mountain barrier, or differences in temperature or wind speed across the front — lets warm air bulge poleward while cold air pushes equatorward, kinking the boundary into a wave. Any one such reason earns the mark.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Atmospheric instability (1)
- Frictional drag (1)
- Jet streams (1)
- Orographic features (accept examples) (1)
- Temperature differences (1)
- Windspeed differences (1)

[ANY ONE]

process explanation

The flooded street comes from the rain: the cold air behind the cold front undercuts the warm air ahead of it, forcing rapid uplift that builds cumulonimbus clouds and releases heavy rainfall. A full answer must mention both the gale-force or strong winds and the heavy rainfall, each explained by its process, for two marks apiece.

- Strong updraughts/rapid upliftment results in (cumulonimbus clouds) heavy rainfall (2)
- Air behind the cold front undercuts the warm air ahead of it gives rise to (cumulonimbus clouds) and heavy rainfall (2)

[ANY TWO — MUST MENTION GALE FORCE/STRONG WINDS AND HEAVY RAINFALL]

labelled sketch

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P1, November 2025, question Q1.3.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

(Refer to sketch B on the mid-latitude cyclone: a synoptic plan of a wave cyclone with a cold front trailing south-west from the low centre, a warm front to the north-east, warm air flowing in from the north-east and cold air behind the cold front.) Refer to sketch B. Explain how the difference in temperature of the air masses behind the cold front and ahead of the warm front will result in the formation of a cold front occlusion. (2 x 2)

## Method

process explanation

Reason through the temperatures step by step. The air behind the advancing cold front is colder than the cool air ahead of the warm front. Because the cold front moves faster, it catches up with the warm front; being the coldest and densest air present, the air behind the cold front slides under both the warm sector and the cool air ahead of the warm front. The warmer, less dense air is lifted completely off the ground over the colder, denser air — producing a cold front occlusion. Two well-explained statements at two marks each earn the four marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- The air behind the cold front is colder than the air in front of the warm front (2)
- The cold air behind the cold front undercuts the warmer air in front of the warm front (2)
- The warmer (less dense air) is uplifted over the colder (denser) air (2)

[PART MARKING: The air behind the cold front is colder (1); The cold air behind the cold front undercuts (1); The warmer (less dense) air is uplifted (1); MAXIMUM TWO MARKS]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2024, question Q2.3.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

(The answer to QUESTION 2.3.3 was that the smallest number of coal mining employees was recorded between 2021 and 2022.) Give ONE possible reason for the small number of employees (answer to QUESTION 2.3.3). (1 x 2)

## Method

explain reason

Ask what could shrink a mining workforce around 2021/2022 or in the industry generally. Think along several lines: the coal itself running out (depletion of seams), the economy (recession), health shocks (pandemics), labour unrest (strikes), machines replacing people (mechanisation), policy uncertainty (threats of nationalisation), the shift to environmentally friendly energy reducing coal demand, load-shedding disrupting operations, or mine accidents. Any one well-stated reason earns the two marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Depletion of coal (2)
- Economic recession (accept examples) (2)
- Impact of illness/pandemics (accept examples) (2)
- Possible strikes/uprisings (accept examples) (2)
- Increase in mechanisation (2)
- Threats of nationalisation (accept examples) (2)
- Use of environmentally friendly energy sources/reduced demand of coal (accept examples) (2)
- Load-shedding (2)
- Mine accidents (2)

[ANY ONE]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2024, question Q2.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

(Refer to an extract on coal mining in South Africa: 'The high-quality coal reserves in South Africa have been decreasing over the years. Shallow and high-quality resources in the Emalahleni (Witbank) coal field have been depleted. Mining companies are required to find other more cost-effective methods to extract the deeper, low quality coal seams of the basin.') According to the extract, the high-quality coal reserves in South Africa have been decreasing over the years. Explain the negative impact of decreasing high-quality coal reserves for the future supply of power in South Africa. (2 x 2)

## Method

impact explanation

Link the coal supply directly to electricity generation: South Africa's power stations burn coal, so less high-quality coal means less reliable generation. Follow the chain of consequences — demand starts to outstrip supply, load-shedding becomes more frequent, power stations must burn lower-quality coal or shut down for maintenance, and the cost of electricity rises. There is also the expensive fallback of investing in alternative or renewable energy sources. Explain any two of these impacts for two marks each.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- There would be more frequent load-shedding/load reduction (2)
- There would be a greater demand than supply (2)
- The cost of electricity would increase (accept examples) (2)
- Invest in alternate sources of renewable energy (2)
- Lower quality coal will have to be used (2)
- Leads to shut downs/maintenance of power stations (2)
- Expensive to invest in alternative energy sources (accept examples) (2)

[ANY TWO]
