# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.3.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2024, question Q2.3.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Explain why the coal mining industry is important to the economy of South Africa. (3 x 2)

## Method

explain importance

Work through the standard economic-contribution checklist and expand each point. Jobs: coal mining creates employment, which reduces dependency on the state and raises buying power. National income: the industry contributes to GDP, pays taxes, and coal exports earn foreign exchange. Linkages: coal is the country's main source of electricity on which every sector depends, it serves as a raw material for other products, and the multiplier effect stimulates other industries and infrastructure development. A bare fact without expansion earns only one mark, so tie each fact to its economic consequence. Any three expanded points earn the six marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- It creates employment opportunities thus reducing dependency on government/increasing the buying power of people (2)
- Multiplier effect stimulates other industries growing the economy (2)
- Coal mining contributes to the GDP that stimulates the economy (2)
- Coal is our main source of power that all sectors of our economy are dependent on (2)
- Export of coal will earn foreign exchange (2)
- Taxes from coal mining industry contribute to the GDP/GNP (2)
- The use of coal as a raw material to manufacture other products (2)
- Promotes the development/upgrading of infrastructure (accept examples) that benefits other sectors of the economy (2)

[ANY THREE] [PART MARKING: fact without expansion (1) each, MAXIMUM OF THREE MARKS]

## Question (1 mark)

Choose the answer and write only the letter (A–D). (This question is based on gold mining in South Africa.)

The province that produces the most gold in South Africa is …

A Limpopo.  B Mpumalanga.  C KwaZulu-Natal.  D Gauteng.

## Method

mcq

## Memo working

South Africa's gold comes from the Witwatersrand Basin, the gold-bearing reef on which Johannesburg was founded. That reef lies in Gauteng, which remains the country's leading gold-producing province. Limpopo and Mpumalanga are associated with platinum and coal respectively, and KwaZulu-Natal is not a gold province. The answer is D.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D (Gauteng)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q2.1.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Refer to the line graph showing the number of people employed in gold mines in South Africa between 1995 and 2025. (The line starts near 385 000 in 1995, falls steeply to about 250 000 by 2000, continues down to roughly 200 000 in 2005, about 160 000 to 170 000 in 2010, near 120 000 in 2015, then declines gently to below 100 000 by 2025.)

The number of people employed in South African gold mines decreased the most between …

A 1995 and 2000.  B 2000 and 2005.  C 2005 and 2010.  D 2010 and 2015.

## Method

graph mcq

## Memo working

Compare the drop across each five-year interval rather than the overall level. From 1995 to 2000 the line plunges from about 385 000 to about 250 000 — a fall of roughly 135 000, the steepest segment on the whole graph. The later intervals each lose only about 30 000 to 50 000 jobs. The biggest decrease is therefore in the first interval, option A.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A (1995 and 2000)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.7

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q2.1.7.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Choose the answer and write only the letter (A–D). (This question is based on gold mining in South Africa.)

A physical (natural) factor causing employment numbers to decrease in South African gold mines is/are …

A threats of nationalisation.  B depletion of gold in mines.  C unskilled labourers.  D less foreign investment in mines.

## Method

mcq

## Memo working

The qualifier is "physical (natural)". Threats of nationalisation are political, unskilled labourers are a social/human factor, and less foreign investment is economic. The only factor rooted in nature itself is the depletion of gold in the mines — the ore body is finite, and as the gold runs out mines close and jobs disappear. The answer is B.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B (depletion of gold in mines)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.8

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q2.1.8.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Refer to the line graph showing the number of people employed in gold mines in South Africa between 1995 and 2025 (employment declines gently from near 120 000 in 2015 to below 100 000 by 2025).

An economic factor that has caused employment numbers to decrease from 2015 onwards is/are …

A HIV and Aids.  B fluctuating prices of gold.  C environmental degradation.  D strikes and protests.

## Method

mcq

## Memo working

Again filter by the type of factor demanded — economic. HIV and Aids is a social (health) factor, environmental degradation is environmental, and strikes and protests are social/labour factors. The economic factor is the fluctuating price of gold: when the price swings or falls, revenue becomes uncertain, marginal shafts become unprofitable and mines shed workers. The answer is B.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B (fluctuating prices of gold)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q4.3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

(Context: trolleys A, 1,5 kg, and B, 2 kg, are released from rest with a compressed spring between them on a frictionless horizontal track; trolley B moves off to the right at 5,42 m·s⁻¹.) For the t seconds that the spring takes to return to its natural length: Calculate the change in momentum of trolley B.

## Method

change in momentum

## Memo working

POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 4.2 — use the 5,42 m·s⁻¹ found there. Change in momentum is final momentum minus initial momentum: Δp = mvf – mvi. Trolley B starts at rest, so vi = 0, and leaves the spring at 5,42 m·s⁻¹ to the right: Δp = 2(5,42 – 0) = 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ to the right. Momentum is a vector, so the direction must be stated. (Taking right as negative instead gives 2(–5,42 – 0) = –10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹, the same change expressed with the opposite sign convention.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Δp = 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ to the right

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q4.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

(Context: trolleys A, 1,5 kg, and B, 2 kg, are pushed apart from rest by a compressed spring on a frictionless horizontal track; trolley B's change in momentum is 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ to the right.) For the t seconds that the spring takes to return to its natural length: Write down the change in momentum of trolley A.

## Method

newton third law momentum

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) By Newton's third law the spring pushes the two trolleys with equal and opposite forces for the same time t, so the trolleys receive equal and opposite impulses. Equivalently, total momentum is conserved and starts at zero, so trolley A's change in momentum must exactly cancel trolley B's. Trolley A therefore gains momentum of the same magnitude, 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹, but directed to the left. No calculation is needed — write it down.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ left / opposite direction. (POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 4.3.1.)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q4.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

(Context: trolleys A, 1,5 kg, and B, 2 kg, are pushed apart from rest by a compressed spring on a frictionless horizontal track; trolley B moves off to the right at 5,42 m·s⁻¹ and trolley A's change in momentum is 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ to the left.) Calculate the speed of trolley A after t seconds.

## Method

conservation of momentum

## Memo working

POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 4.2 and 4.3.1. Route one, from trolley A's change in momentum: ΔpA = mvf – mvi, so with right positive, –10,84 = 1,5(vf – 0), giving vf = –7,23 m·s⁻¹ — that is, 7,23 m·s⁻¹ to the left, so the speed is 7,23 m·s⁻¹. Route two, conservation of momentum for the system: the total momentum is zero before release, so Σpi = Σpf gives 0 = 1,5vf + (2)(5,42), and again vf = –7,23 m·s⁻¹, speed 7,23 m·s⁻¹. The lighter trolley moves off faster, in the inverse ratio of the masses.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

v = 7,23 m·s⁻¹

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2025, question Q4.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Cricketers at an academy conduct an experiment to determine the relationship between the contact time and the final momentum of a ball for a constant average net force. A cricket ball of mass 150 g is thrown horizontally with a certain initial velocity and is struck by a bat so that the ball moves in the opposite direction. The average net force acting on the ball is horizontal. (Diagram: bat striking a ball; initial velocity vi towards the bat, final velocity vf away from the bat.) The experiment is repeated using the same ball. The average net force and the initial velocity of the ball are kept constant. The contact time between the bat and the ball is changed EACH time. The results are plotted as a straight-line graph of final momentum pf in kg·m·s⁻¹ versus contact time Δt in s, passing through the points (0,01; 0) and (0,03; 4,5). Define the term impulse.

## Method

define impulse

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The product of the resultant/net force acting on an object and the time the (net) force acts on the object. OR: The product of the resultant/net force and the contact time.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2025, question Q4.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Calculate the average net force acting on the ball. (A 150 g cricket ball is struck by a bat with a constant average net force; the graph of final momentum pf in kg·m·s⁻¹ versus contact time Δt in s is a straight line through the points (0,01; 0) and (0,03; 4,5).)

## Method

impulse momentum gradient

## Memo working

Option 1: The gradient of a pf versus Δt graph equals the net force. Gradient = Fnet = Δpf/Δ(Δt) = (4,5 − 0)/(0,03 − 0,01) = 225 N. (Memo options 2/3: apply FnetΔt = Δp at the two graph points — Fnet(0,01) = 0 − pi and Fnet(0,03) = 4,5 − pi — and solve simultaneously, which also gives Fnet = 225 N to the right / opposite to the original direction of the ball.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Fnet = 225 N to the right / opposite to the original direction of the ball

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

vi = 15 m·s⁻¹

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q2.2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Why does a monopolist enjoy greater profits than a monopolistic competitor? (2 x 2) (Refers to an extract on monopolistic competition among restaurants competing on food quality, prices, ingredients, location and services.)

## Method

explanation — compare the two structures point by point: how much competition each faces, how much control each has over price, and how elastic the demand for each one's product is. Each contrast, fully explained, earns two marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Any TWO of:

- A monopolist has no competition whereas the monopolistic competitor has a higher degree of competition which lowers prices, hence less profit
- A monopolist can manipulate prices to higher levels whereas the monopolistic competitor has little control over prices due to many sellers
- A monopolist can charge higher prices and make higher profit because demand is inelastic whereas a monopolistic competitor cannot charge higher due to elastic demand which leads to lower profit

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (40 marks)

QUESTION 5: MICROECONOMICS.

- Examine in detail the oligopoly market structure. (26 marks)
- How has the competition policy helped to reduce anti-competitive behaviour in South Africa? (10 marks)

(Section C essay: answer ONE of two essay questions. Rubric: Introduction max 2 — define the main concept, do not include any part of the question or announce what will be discussed; Body main part max 26 — a maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples; Body additional part max 10 — a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; Conclusion max 2 — a higher-order summary, opinion or recommendation without repeating facts. Total 40.)

## Method

essay

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: structure the essay in four parts. Open by defining market structure — one clean definition, nothing from the question itself. In the main body, examine oligopoly characteristic by characteristic, using each as a heading: few large firms, nature of the product (pure versus differentiated oligopoly), barriers to entry, incomplete information, considerable price control, mutual dependence, the kinked demand curve (drawn and explained — elastic above the kink, inelastic below, so the price sticks at the kink), collusion (overt cartels versus tacit price leadership), non-price competition, economic profit in the long run, and the failure to reach productive and allocative efficiency. In the additional part, link the Competition Policy institutions — Commission, Tribunal, Appeal Court — to specific reductions in anti-competitive behaviour. Close with a brief higher-order conclusion.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):

Market structure describes how buyers and sellers are organised and interact in a market / Refers to the characteristic of a market that influence its performance and the level of competition. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

BODY MAIN PART (Max 26) — CHARACTERISTICS OF OLIGOPOLY:

- Number of businesses: Only few large businesses dominate the oligopoly market, e.g. the mobile network industry. There is limited competition in an oligopoly market structure. A market that is dominated by two businesses only is referred to as a duopoly.
- Nature of the product: When the product is differentiated, the market is known as a differentiated oligopoly. Product differentiation is a strategy used by businesses to make their products different from competitors in terms of colour, size, quality and appearance, e.g. cell-phone industry. When the product is homogeneous, the market is regarded as pure oligopoly, e.g. fuel industry.
- Entrance: Barriers to entry make it difficult for new businesses to enter an oligopoly market. The barriers to entry include economies of scale, high development costs, licenses and huge capital requirements. Barriers to entry allow oligopoly businesses to make economic profit in the long-run.
- Information: Neither the producer nor the consumer has full knowledge about the current market conditions. Even though oligopoly businesses watch each other closely, it is difficult for them to know how their competitors will react to their decisions and actions. It is difficult for Vodacom to know how MTN, Telkom and Cell-C will respond to its promotion strategies such as night shifts.
- Control over the price: Oligopoly businesses generally have considerable control over the price of their product, although it is less than a monopoly. Oligopolies gain control over the price especially when they make joint decisions, through price leaderships and cartels.
- Mutual dependence: There are few businesses selling a particular product, each business depends on other businesses' actions. Decisions by one business can influence decisions by other businesses. An oligopoly's decisions on decreasing or increasing the price are more complex than other markets because of other businesses actions and reaction.
- Demand curve: Oligopoly businesses have a kinked demand curve due to mutual dependence. A kinked demand curve is a demand curve with two segments, one that is elastic and the other one that is inelastic. When one business increases the price, its competitors will not follow the move and customers will shift their purchases to other businesses with lower prices; the business that increased the price will lose a lot of customers and demand will be elastic. When one business decides to decrease the price, other businesses will also decrease their prices; the business that decreased the price will gain very few customers and demand will be inelastic. (KINKED DEMAND CURVE graph: Price against Quantity; demand curve D kinked at point A at price P and quantity Q. Marks: correct labelling of the axes = 1; correct indication of the kink = 1; correct labelling of demand curve = 1; correct labelling on the axes (price and quantity) = 1. 4 marks.) Above price P, demand is elastic and below price P, demand is inelastic. An oligopoly will always maintain the price at the kink because there is no incentive for an oligopoly to increase or decrease the price.
- Collusion: Collusion is an agreement within the same industry to reduce competition amongst themselves, e.g. price fixing. Formal collusion is in the form of cartels such as OPEC which is also referred to as explicit or overt collusion. Informal collusion is in the form of price leadership which is also referred to as implicit or tacit collusion.
- Non-price competition: Oligopolies try to avoid competing on prices because reduction in prices may result in destructive price wars which eliminate their profits. They make use of non-price competition, such as product differentiation, branding, and advertising, to attract customers and increase their market share.
- Economic profit/Loss: Oligopolistic firms can make economic profit in both short run and long-run.
- Productive and allocative efficiency: Oligopoly businesses do not achieve allocative efficiency because they do not produce the optimum output. Oligopolies do not achieve productive efficiency because they do not produce at the lowest possible average cost.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for mere listing of facts/examples)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10):

- The Competition Policy prevented the abuse of economic power by monopolist through the establishment of new businesses in various markets.
- Regulation of mergers and takeovers helped to reduce the growth of market powers.
- The Competition Policy provided for the establishment of the Competition Commission to investigate restrictive practices such as price fixing by oligopolies.
- The establishment of the Competition Tribunal has helped to reduce unfair methods of exercising market powers by imposing fines and penalties on businesses that are found guilty.
- The Competition Appeal Court reviews or amends decisions taken by the Competition Tribunal in a way that ensures that competition is not compromised.
- Consumers are protected from unfair prices and inferior products through the implementation of the Competition Act.
- The Competition Policy has improved the equity in markets by giving all South Africans equal opportunities to participate in economic activity.
- Foreign competition has been allowed which has helped to reduce market dominance by domestic large businesses.
- Healthy competition has been promoted which has helped to improve the efficiency of markets.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):

Oligopoly businesses may enjoy economic profit in both the short-run and long-run due to the market powers they possess / Oligopolies produce goods and services at a higher cost and use resources inefficiently which may lead to higher prices and wastage of resources in the economy. (Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (40 marks)

QUESTION 5: MICROECONOMICS.

- Discuss, in detail, the characteristics of a monopoly market structure, including a graph showing long-run economic profit. (26 marks)
- How can the government prevent the abuse of market power by dominant businesses? (10 marks)

(Section C essay: answer ONE of two essay questions. Rubric: Introduction max 2 — define the main concept, do not include any part of the question or announce what will be discussed; Body main part max 26 — a maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples; Body additional part max 10 — a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; Conclusion max 2 — a higher-order summary, opinion or recommendation without repeating facts. Total 40.)

## Method

essay

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: structure the essay in four parts. Open by defining market structure — one clean definition, nothing from the question itself. In the main body, discuss monopoly characteristic by characteristic, using each as a heading: one firm supplying the whole industry (Eskom), a unique product with no close substitutes (De Beers) and relatively inelastic demand, completely blocked entry — split into natural monopolies (huge development costs, like power stations) and artificial monopolies (patents and licences) — price-maker control limited only by consumers' budgets, market information, a downward-sloping demand curve equal to average revenue with marginal revenue below it, economic profit or loss in the short run but the ability to sustain economic profit in the long run, independent decision-making, the irrelevance of collusion, and the failure to reach productive and allocative efficiency. Draw the long-run economic profit graph: downward-sloping D = AR with MR below it, rising LMC and U-shaped LAC; equilibrium e where MR = LMC at 100 units; price R40 read off the demand curve, average cost R30 read off LAC; the rectangle between R40 and R30 over 100 units is the economic profit. In the additional part, link each government tool — price regulation (NERSA), lowering entry barriers, private-sector incentives, and the Competition Commission, Tribunal and Appeal Court — to how it curbs the abuse of market power. Close with a brief higher-order conclusion.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):

Market structure describes how buyers and sellers are organised and interact in a market / Refers to the characteristic of a market that influence its performance and the level of competition. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

BODY MAIN PART (Max 26) — MONOPOLY MARKET STRUCTURE:

- Number of firms/businesses: The monopolist is the only supplier of a product which implies that there is no competition in this market structure. The monopoly is responsible for the industry's total output, for example Eskom is responsible for the thermal electricity industry.
- Nature of product: The product is unique and it has no close substitutes for example, De Beers selling unique diamonds. Consumers' choice is limited to the product sold by the monopolist. The product has relatively inelasticity demand which means that quantity demanded is less responsive to price changes.
- Market entry: Entry into a monopoly market structure is completely blocked which implies that new businesses cannot enter the market. A monopoly is protected by barriers to entry, which allows it to enjoy favourable market conditions. These barriers to entry divide monopoly into the following two broad types:
- Natural monopolies: High development costs are frequently a reason for the existence of natural monopolies. In South Africa, Eskom is an example of natural monopoly because the provision of electricity requires building power stations and transmission lines costing billions of rand. A single business in the industry can serve the whole market at a lower price than two or more businesses as it is regulated by the government.
- Artificial monopolies: Artificial monopolies exist due to barriers to entry that are not being economic in nature, such a patent. A patent is the legal and exclusive right of a patent holder to manufacture a product using his or her unique invention. Licenses protect monopolies against the entry of competitors and is another way in which an artificial monopoly may exist. In South Africa licenses are required for radio and TV broadcasting and telephone communication networks.
- Control over price: A monopolist can influence the market price and it is regarded as a price maker. A monopolist can decide on a price-quantity combination that suits it the best, on the demand curve. There is always the possibility of consumer exploitation because a monopolist is the only supplier of a product. A monopoly business may restrict output or supply of the product to charge higher price although it is limited by market demand. A monopoly cannot charge excessively high prices because consumers have limited budgets. The monopolist's product has to compete for consumers' favour (and money) with all the other products available in the economy.
- Market information: Both buyer and the seller have full knowledge about the market conditions which shows that there is complete market information. A high degree of transparency exist in the market as there is no incentive for the monopoly to hide information from consumers. In some cases, a monopoly maybe characterised by incomplete information to make informed decisions. The monopolist may withhold information which leads to exploitation of consumers and restriction of new firms from entering the market.
- Demand curve: A monopolist is faced with a normal demand curve which slopes downwards from left to right. The demand curve is relatively inelastic because the product has no close substitutes. The demand curve for a monopoly is equal to its average revenue curve. For every additional unit sold by a monopoly, marginal revenue is less than the price, thus marginal revenue curve lies below the demand curve.
- Economic profit/loss: A monopolist can earn an economic profit or economic loss in the short run. Economic loss in the short-run will force the monopoly to build a new production plant that yields economic profit in the long-run. Economic profit in the short-run allows the monopoly to expand its production scale or capacity in order to make more economic profit in the long-run.
- Decision making: A monopoly business makes decisions independently because there are no competitors. A monopoly's decisions may be influenced by government laws and regulations.
- Collusion: Collusion is irrelevant because there is one business in the market.
- Productive and allocative efficiency: A monopoly does not achieve productive efficiency because output is produced without minimising the average cost. Allocative efficiency is not achieved because the output produced by a monopoly does not correspond with the quantity demanded by consumers. Monopoly produces output level where the price is above the marginal cost.

(Max. 22)

Long-run Economic profit graph (Max 4): (Memo graph: axes Price/Cost/Revenue on the vertical and Quantity on the horizontal. A downward-sloping demand curve labelled D = AR with the MR curve below it; a rising LMC curve and a U-shaped LAC curve. Equilibrium/profit-maximisation point e is where MR = LMC at quantity 100; point a on the demand curve above e gives price R40; point b on the LAC curve above e gives average cost R30; the rectangle between R40 and R30 over 100 units is labelled 'Economic profit'.) Allocation of marks: Correct positioning and labelling of cost curves = 1 Mark; Correct drawing and labelling of revenue curves = 1 Mark; Correct indication of equilibrium / profit maximisation point = 1 Mark; Correct indication of economic profit = 1 Mark.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for headings/subheadings/examples)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10):

- The government may regulate the pricing of goods and services by monopolies to prevent excessively high prices, for example NERSA regulates the pricing of electricity by Eskom.
- Reduce or remove barriers to entry, such as patents and licenses, in oligopoly and monopoly industries to attract new businesses and increase competition.
- Encourage private sector investments through subsidies and incentives to reduce the dominance of state monopolies in industries such as electricity, rail transport.
- Intensify the implementation of the Competition policy which promotes fair competition through the Competition Commission, Competition Tribunal and Competition Appeal Court.
- The Competition Commission may intensify its investigations on oligopolies and monopolies that may abuse their market powers by deploying more officials to monitor business practices.
- The Competition Tribunal should impose penalties on all dominant businesses that are found guilty of abusing market powers at the expense of other businesses and consumers.
- Prevent the market dominance by prohibiting mergers and takeovers that may lead to monopolies that could exploit consumers.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):

Monopolies may result in low economic growth and high inflation which may lead to low standard of living. (Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion)

## Question (7 marks)

Miecke purchased prepaid electricity for R1 300,00, of which R1 130,43 is the electricity amount excluding VAT (per her till slip). A partial residential electricity tariff table (excluding VAT) is shown (TABLE 3: Block 1, consumption 0-350 kWh, tariff R2,19 per kWh; Block 2, consumption more than 350 kWh, tariff R2,91 per kWh). Determine the number of kWh units Miecke purchased.

## Method

block tariff reverse calculation

## Memo working

Work out how far the money stretches, block by block. Amount for Block 1 (the first 350 kWh): 350 kWh x R2,19 = R766,50 (1MA, 1CA). Money left over for Block 2: R1 130,43 - R766,50 = R363,93 (1MCA). Units bought in Block 2 at the higher tariff: R363,93 ÷ R2,91 = 125,0618557 kWh (1MCA, 1CA). Total units = 350 kWh + 125,0618557 kWh = 475,06 kWh (1MCA adding, 1CA simplification). (Memo alternative with VAT-inclusive tariffs: R2,19 x 1,15 = R2,5185 and R2,91 x 1,15 = R3,3465; 350 x R2,5185 = R881,475; R1 300 - R881,475 = R418,525; 418,525 ÷ 3,3465 = 125,06 kWh; total 475,06 kWh. NPR)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

475,06 kWh

construct cost formula

DJ Rain charges R4 000 for 5 hours or less, thereafter an additional tariff of R1 250 per hour. evaluate cost formula

P is the cost for 3 hours: that is still within the first 5 hours, so the flat fee applies and P = 4 000 (1A). Q is the cost for 6 hours: one hour beyond 5, so Q = R4 000 + R1 250 x 1 = 5 250 (2A). R is the cost for 9 hours: four hours beyond 5, so R = R4 000 + R1 250 x 4 = R4 000 + R5 000 = 9 000 (1A). As a check, the printed values follow the same pattern: 7 hours gives 4 000 + 2 x 1 250 = 6 500 and 8 hours gives 4 000 + 3 x 1 250 = 7 750.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

P = 4 000; Q = 5 250; R = 9 000

Join ALL the plotted points on the slanted part of the graph (1A). (CA from Question 4.1.1(b).)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q4.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Lee's 21st birthday party starts at 18:00 at a hotel. The budgeted expenses (TABLE 4) are: cost of the venue — R750 deposit and R6 185 for the day; food and drinks — R18 000; birthday cake — R1 250. Lee's parents decide to hire DJ 5-Star, who charges R1 000 per hour or part thereof and will provide the music entertainment from 18:00 until 01:30. Determine the total budgeted expenses for the party.

## Method

total budget with time based cost

## Memo working

First work out the playing time: from 18:00 to 01:30 is 7 hours 30 minutes. Because DJ 5-Star charges per hour "or part thereof", the extra 30 minutes counts as a full hour, so charge for 8 hours (1A calculating hours). Cost for the DJ = 8 x R1 000 (1MCA) = R8 000 (1CA). Now add every budgeted item: food and drinks, venue deposit, venue day fee, cake and DJ. Total cost = R18 000 + R750 + R6 185 + R1 250 + R8 000 (1MCA adding all values) = R34 185 (1CA simplification).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R34 185

## Question (3 marks)

TABLE 4 shows Metrobus fares in Johannesburg for three passenger categories: for a single daily trip an adult (15-59 years) pays R14,20, a child (3-14 years) pays R10,30 and a pensioner (60+ years) pays R4,20. percentage saving calculation

(Memo option 2: % savings = (R14,20 - R4,20)/R14,20 × 100% (1MA subtracting correct values, 1A correct denominator) = 70,42% (1CA simplification).)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

70,42%

## Question (5 marks)

TABLE 4 shows Metrobus trip packages for adults: a single daily trip costs R14,20, while a monthly package of 44 trips costs R465,60. Muriel travels to work by bus. Determine the amount Muriel will save per trip if she buys the monthly package instead of the daily trip package.

unit cost comparison

(Memo option 2: total cost of 44 daily trips = R14,20 × 44 = R624,80; difference = R624,80 - R465,60 = R159,20; saving per trip = R159,20/44 = R3,62.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R3,62

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2025, question Q2.2.4.

## Question (4 marks)

Johannesburg Metrobus introduced a compulsory card payment system. All passengers must purchase the Metrobus card for R35 to activate it, and then upload trip fares according to the available trip packages (the weekly package of 12 trips costs R127,10). Muriel purchased a Metrobus card together with an uploaded trip package to the total value of R416,30. Calculate the maximum number of weekly trips Muriel can take using this card.

## Method

remaining amount division

## Memo working

First remove the once-off card cost to see how much is left for trip packages: Package amount left = R416,30 - R35,00 (1RT R35) = R381,30 (1A simplification). Then see how many weekly packages fit into that amount: Number of weekly trips = R381,30 ÷ R127,10 (1MCA dividing values) = 3 (1CA simplification). (Memo option 2: R416,30 - R127,10 - R127,10 - R127,10 (1RT R127,10, 1MA subtracting values) = R35 (1A), so 3 (1CA). Note: the memo interprets "weekly trips" as the number of 12-trip weekly packages, at R127,10 each, that fit into the remaining R381,30 — giving 3.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

3

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q4.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (7 marks)

A worker is replacing both of her double garage doors with double-brick walls (bricks are sold per pallet of 525 bricks at R6,45 per brick; 2 pallets are needed). The opening of a garage door has dimensions of 2,13 m x 3 m. Other costs to build the double-brick wall: Material, other than bricks, cost R2 000,00; Labour is R500,00 per square metre. The owner states that the total cost to replace both garage doors with walls would be R15 200,00. Verify her statement by means of calculations. You may use the following formula: Area = length x width

## Method

area based cost verification

## Memo working

Work out each cost separately, then compare the total with the claim. Area of the 2 door openings = 2 x 2,13 x 3 = 12,78 m^2. Labour is charged per square metre: 12,78 x R500 = R6 390. Bricks: 2 pallets x 525 bricks x R6,45 = R6 772,50. Total cost = R2 000 + R6 390 + R6 772,50 = R15 162,50. This is not equal to the claimed R15 200,00, so her statement is NOT VALID. (The number of pallets carries over from Q4.2.1. A third memo alternative rounds the area to 13 m^2, giving labour R6 500 and a total of R15 272,50 — also Not VALID.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Area of 2 doors = 12,78 m^2; labour = R6 390; bricks (2 pallets) = R6 772,50; total = R2 000 + R6 390 + R6 772,50 = R15 162,50. Her statement is NOT VALID.

## Question (2 marks)

(Context: a crate of mass 8,5 kg lies stationary on a rough horizontal table, connected by a light inextensible string over a frictionless pulley to a hanging mass hanger.) Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing ALL the HORIZONTAL forces acting on the crate JUST BEFORE it starts moving.

free body diagram

[Free-body diagram: dot with static friction fs to the left and tension T to the right (directions may be mirrored).] Accepted labels: fs = static friction/f/Ff; T = FT/Fstring/tension. Do not penalise if vertical forces (w, N) are shown; mark awarded for label and arrow; if arrows do not touch the dot max 1/2; any additional force except w and N max 1/2; correct but no arrows max 1/2.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q10.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

A cyclist rode from town P and stopped at town T. The speed (in km/h) at which this cyclist rode, is represented by the equation s'(t) = -3t^2 + 18t. NOTE: Speed is the rate of change in distance with respect to time. Calculate the maximum speed that the cyclist reached on this ride.

## Method

optimisation set derivative zero

## Memo working

The speed s'(t) = -3t^2 + 18t is itself a concave-down parabola in t, so its maximum sits where its derivative is zero: -6t + 18 = 0 -> t = 3. Substitute back into the speed: s'(3) = -3(3)^2 + 18(3) = -27 + 54 = 27.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

27 km/h

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q10.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

A cyclist rode from town P and stopped at town T. The speed (in km/h) at which this cyclist rode, is represented by the equation s'(t) = -3t^2 + 18t, where speed is the rate of change in distance with respect to time. Calculate the distance between town P and town T.

## Method

antiderivative of rate

## Memo working

The ride starts and ends when the speed is zero: -3t^2 + 18t = 0 -> -3t(t - 6) = 0 -> t = 0 or t = 6, so the ride lasts 6 hours. Distance is the function whose derivative is the speed. Try s(t) = at^3 + bt^2, so s'(t) = 3at^2 + 2bt; matching -3t^2 + 18t gives 3a = -3 and 2b = 18, so a = -1 and b = 9. Thus s(t) = -t^3 + 9t^2, and the distance covered is s(6) = -(6)^3 + 9(6)^2 = -216 + 324 = 108.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

108 km

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q10.1.

## Question (3 marks)

A rectangular metal sheet has dimensions x and h units, with x > h, and a perimeter of 50 units. The metal sheet is rolled into a cylinder with two open ends (top and bottom) and height h units. (Figure: rectangle with width x and height h alongside an open cylinder of height h formed by rolling the sheet.) Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by V = 25x^2/(4π) - x^3/(4π)

## Method

build volume function

## Memo working

From the perimeter: 2x + 2h = 50, so h = 25 - x. When the sheet is rolled up, the side of length x becomes the circumference of the circular end: 2πr = x, so r = x/(2π). Substitute into the cylinder volume formula: V = πr^2 h = π(x/(2π))^2 (25 - x) = x^2(25 - x)/(4π) = 25x^2/(4π) - x^3/(4π).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

V = 25x^2/(4π) - x^3/(4π)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q10.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

The volume of the cylinder in Q10.1 is given by V = 25x^2/(4π) - x^3/(4π). Calculate the value of x that will maximise the volume of the cylinder.

## Method

optimisation set derivative zero

## Memo working

At the maximum volume the derivative of V with respect to x is zero. Differentiate: V'(x) = 50x/(4π) - 3x^2/(4π). Set V'(x) = 0 and multiply through by 4π: 50x - 3x^2 = 0, so x(50 - 3x) = 0. Since x ≠ 0 for a real cylinder, 50 - 3x = 0, giving x = 50/3 = 16,67.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = 50/3 = 16,67

## Question (5 marks)

Compounds R and T are positional isomers. The inorganic reagents shown below are available for reactions IV and V: Br2, H2SO4(conc.), NaOH(conc.), HBr, H2. Write down the balanced equation for reaction IV, using STRUCTURAL FORMULAE and the correct inorganic reagent shown above. (From the flow diagram: reaction III, an elimination, converts CH3CH2CH2CH2Br into compound R; reaction IV links compound R and organic compound S.)

## Method

addition reaction equation

## Memo working

Marking criteria: functional group of alkene on first C atom; whole structural formula of alkene correct; HBr; functional group of haloalkane correct; whole structural formula of haloalkane correct (halogen on second/first C atom). If condensed, semi-structural or molecular formula: max 1/5. For extra product or reactant, deduct 1 mark. Working: reaction III eliminates HBr from 1-bromobutane, so R is the alkene but-1-ene, CH2=CH–CH2–CH3. Reaction IV must turn the alkene R into the haloalkane S, which is an addition reaction — the only reagent on the list that adds across a double bond to give a bromoalkane is HBr. Adding HBr across the double bond of but-1-ene gives 2-bromobutane (Br on the second carbon, the major product) or 1-bromobutane (Br on the first carbon); the memo accepts either. Both reactant and product must be drawn in full structural formulae showing every bond.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

[Balanced equation in structural formulae: but-1-ene (CH2=CH–CH2–CH3 drawn in full) + HBr → 2-bromobutane (CH3–CHBr–CH2–CH3 drawn in full) OR 1-bromobutane (CH3CH2CH2CH2Br drawn in full).]

multiple choice

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q2.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Calculate the TOTAL volume of the GASES present in the container at the end of the reaction. (Refers to QUESTION 2.3: C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(g); initially 8 cm³ of C3H8 and 50 cm³ of O2 were injected into a container of adjustable volume.)

## Method

gas volume stoichiometry

## Memo working

V(O2) used = 5V(C3H8) = (5)(8) = 40 cm³. V(CO2) formed = 3V(C3H8) = (3)(8) = 24 cm³. V(H2O) formed = 4V(C3H8) = (4)(8) = 32 cm³. V(O2) unused = 50 − 40 = 10 cm³. Total volume of gas in the container = 10 + 24 + 32 = 66 cm³. Step by step: because all species are gases at the same temperature and pressure, the mole ratio in the balanced equation is also the VOLUME ratio. The 8 cm³ of propane needs five times its volume of oxygen, 40 cm³, so oxygen is in excess and propane is the limiting reagent — all 8 cm³ of propane reacts. The products are three volumes of CO2 (24 cm³) and four volumes of water VAPOUR (32 cm³) per volume of propane. Do not forget the leftover oxygen: 50 − 40 = 10 cm³ remains. Adding the three gases still present gives 10 + 24 + 32 = 66 cm³. Marking criteria: (a) volume O2 and C3H8 used; (b) volume CO2 and H2O produced; (c) volume O2 remaining; (d) addition of the three volumes; (e) correct final answer 66 cm³ or 0,066 dm³. (Mole-based calculations using Vm = 22,4 dm³ also accepted.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Total volume of gases = 66 cm³ (or 0,066 dm³)

reactivity saturation reasoning

## Memo working

So X reacts faster.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

X / C3H6 / propene. X is unsaturated / has a double bond / is an alkene; X undergoes addition (OR alkenes are more reactive than alkanes / unsaturated compounds react faster than saturated compounds / addition reaction is faster than substitution / addition reaction does not need UV/light).

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q5.3.

## Question (2 marks)

Calculate the value of a, given that f(x) = a/(x - 1) - 2 cuts the y-axis at (0 ; 1).

## Method

substitute point solve parameter

## Memo working

Substitute (0 ; 1) into f: 1 = a/(0 - 1) - 2, so 3 = a/(-1), giving a = -3

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

a = -3

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q5.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

For which values of x is f(x) >= 0, where f(x) = -3/(x - 1) - 2?

## Method

hyperbola inequality

## Memo working

Find the x-intercept: -3/(x - 1) - 2 = 0 -> -3 = 2x - 2 -> x = -1/2. On the branch between this intercept and the vertical asymptote x = 1 the graph rises above the x-axis, so f(x) >= 0 from the x-intercept up to (but excluding) the asymptote.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x ∈ [-1/2 ; 1)  OR  -1/2 <= x < 1

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q5.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Graph f, where f(x) = -3/(x - 1) - 2, undergoes a transformation to h where: (a) the domain and range of h are the same as that of f; (b) h'(x), the derivative of h, is negative on its domain. Describe a possible transformation that f could have undergone to result in h.

## Method

describe transformation

## Memo working

The asymptotes (and hence the domain and range) must stay at x = 1 and y = -2, while the branches must swap into the quadrants where the hyperbola decreases. Any one of the following works: reflection in the y-axis then translation 2 units right; reflection in the x-axis then translation 4 units down; reflection about the line x = 1; reflection about the line y = -2.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

f is reflected in the y-axis, then translated 2 units to the right

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q5.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

The graphs of f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c and g(x) = -4/(x - 3) + 8 are drawn below. P is the turning point of f and the point of intersection of the asymptotes of g. The graphs intersect at D(5 ; 6). M and T are x-intercepts of f and g respectively. (Figure: concave-down parabola f with x-intercept M left of the origin and turning point P on the dotted vertical asymptote x = 3; hyperbola g with branches above-left and below-right of the asymptote intersection, dotted horizontal asymptote through P, g cutting the x-axis at T; f and g intersect at D(5 ; 6).) Write down the domain of g.

## Method

domain of hyperbola

## Memo working

The hyperbola g(x) = -4/(x - 3) + 8 is undefined where its denominator is zero, that is at x = 3 (the vertical asymptote). Every other real x is allowed, so the domain is x ∈ R, x ≠ 3.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x ∈ R, x ≠ 3

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q5.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Write down the range of f. (Concave-down parabola f whose turning point P is the intersection of the asymptotes of g(x) = -4/(x - 3) + 8)

## Method

range of parabola

## Memo working

P is the intersection of the asymptotes x = 3 and y = 8 of g, so P is the point (3 ; 8). Since f is concave down, P(3 ; 8) is a maximum turning point: the parabola takes every value up to and including 8, so the range is y ≤ 8.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

y ≤ 8

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q5.3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Determine the values of x for which g(x) ≤ f(x)  (Concave-down parabola f with maximum turning point P(3 ; 8); hyperbola g(x) = -4/(x - 3) + 8; the graphs intersect at D(5 ; 6))

## Method

graph inequality reading

## Memo working

Read the graphs: the lower branch of the hyperbola lies on or below the parabola only between the vertical asymptote x = 3 and the intersection point D(5 ; 6). To the left of the asymptote g sits above its horizontal asymptote y = 8, which is the maximum of f, and to the right of D the hyperbola climbs back above the falling parabola. So g(x) ≤ f(x) for 3 < x ≤ 5 (x = 3 excluded because g is undefined there; x = 5 included because the graphs are equal at D).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

3 < x ≤ 5  OR  x ∈ (3 ; 5]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q5.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Determine the values of x for which f(x) < 6  (Concave-down parabola f with maximum turning point P(3 ; 8), passing through D(5 ; 6))

## Method

graph inequality reading

## Memo working

The parabola reaches the height y = 6 at x = 5 (point D). By symmetry about the axis x = 3, it is also at height 6 at x = 1, since 5 and 1 are equally far from 3. Between these two values the concave-down parabola is above 6 (its maximum is 8 at x = 3), so f(x) < 6 outside them: x < 1 or x > 5.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x < 1 or x > 5  OR  x ∈ (-∞ ; 1) or x ∈ (5 ; ∞)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q5.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

The graphs of f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c and g(x) = -4/(x - 3) + 8 are drawn. P is the turning point of f and also the point of intersection of the asymptotes of g. The graphs intersect at D(5 ; 6). (Figure: concave-down parabola f with turning point P on the vertical asymptote x = 3; hyperbola g whose asymptotes cross at P; f and g intersect at D(5 ; 6).) Show that the equation of the parabola is f(x) = -(1/2)x^2 + 3x + 7/2

## Method

turning point form substitute point

## Memo working

The asymptotes of g are x = 3 and y = 8, so their intersection — which is also the turning point of f — is P(3 ; 8). Write f in turning point form: y = a(x - 3)^2 + 8. Substitute the point D(5 ; 6): 6 = a(5 - 3)^2 + 8, so 4a = -2 and a = -1/2. Then y = -(1/2)(x - 3)^2 + 8 = -(1/2)x^2 + 3x - 9/2 + 8 = -(1/2)x^2 + 3x + 7/2.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

f(x) = -(1/2)x^2 + 3x + 7/2

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q5.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

The graphs of f(x) = -(1/2)x^2 + 3x + 7/2 and g(x) = -4/(x - 3) + 8 are drawn. M and T are x-intercepts of f and g respectively, with M left of the origin. Calculate the length of MT.

## Method

x intercepts distance

## Memo working

Find M from f: -(1/2)x^2 + 3x + 7/2 = 0. Multiply by -2 to clear the fraction: x^2 - 6x - 7 = 0, which factorises as (x - 7)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 7 or x = -1. M is the x-intercept left of the origin, so M(-1 ; 0). Find T from g: 0 = -4/(x - 3) + 8. Multiply through by (x - 3): -8x + 24 = -4, so 8x = 28 and x = 7/2, giving T(7/2 ; 0). Both points lie on the x-axis, so the length MT is the difference of the x-values: MT = 7/2 - (-1) = 7/2 + 1 = 9/2 = 4,5.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

MT = 9/2 = 4,5

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q6.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

The graphs of g(x) = x + c and f(x) = a/(x + p) + q are drawn. Graph g and the vertical asymptote of f intersect at the x-axis. (Figure: increasing line g cutting the x-axis where the vertical asymptote of f meets it; hyperbola f with one branch above its horizontal asymptote to the right of the vertical asymptote and the other branch below it to the left.) Write down the coordinates of the x-intercept of g in terms of p.

## Method

read intercept from asymptote

## Memo working

The vertical asymptote of f(x) = a/(x + p) + q is the line x = -p. The question states that g cuts the x-axis exactly where this asymptote meets it, so the x-intercept of g is the point on the x-axis with x = -p.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

(-p ; 0)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q6.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

The graphs of g(x) = x + c and f(x) = a/(x + p) + q are drawn, and graph g and the vertical asymptote of f intersect at the x-axis. Graph g intersects the horizontal asymptote of graph f at x = 1 and the graph f at x = 3. Graphs f and g also intersect on the y-axis. Determine the equation of f.

## Method

solve hyperbola parameters from conditions

## Memo working

The x-intercept of g is x = -c, and this is where the vertical asymptote of f meets the x-axis, so -p = -c, meaning p = c. Graph g meets the horizontal asymptote y = q at x = 1, so q = g(1) = 1 + c. This gives f(x) = a/(x + c) + 1 + c. The graphs meet on the y-axis at (0 ; c), so c = a/c + 1 + c, which gives a = -c. The point where g cuts f at x = 3 is (3 ; 3 + c), so 3 + c = -c/(3 + c) + 1 + c. Multiplying out: 9 + 6c + c^2 = -c + 3 + 4c + c^2, so 3c = -6 and c = -2. Then a = 2, p = -2 and q = -1, so f(x) = 2/(x - 2) - 1. (Alternative memo method: find a = 6 + 2c from the point (3 ; 3 + c) first, then use the y-axis intersection (0 ; c) to get c = -2, a = 2, q = -1.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

f(x) = 2/(x - 2) - 1

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q6.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

The graphs of g(x) = x - 2 and f(x) = 2/(x - 2) - 1 are drawn. Describe the transformation that g must undergo to become an axis of symmetry of f that cuts f at two points.

## Method

describe transformation

## Memo working

The asymptotes of f cross at (2 ; -1). The axis of symmetry of f with gradient +1 — the one that actually cuts the hyperbola in two points — passes through this centre point: y = x - 3. Graph g is y = x - 2, one unit above this line. Shifting g one unit down gives y = x - 3, and shifting g one unit to the right gives y = (x - 1) - 2 = x - 3 as well, so either translation works.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Translation of 1 unit down OR translation of 1 unit to the right

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q2.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, explain the relationship between total cost (TC), fixed cost (FC) and variable cost (VC). (2 x 4)

## Method

graph drawing explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: draw cost on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. Fixed cost does not change with output, so FC is a horizontal line. Variable cost starts at zero — with no output there is no variable cost — and slopes upwards. Total cost is simply fixed cost plus variable cost, so the TC curve runs parallel to the VC curve but starts higher up, at the FC intercept on the vertical axis; the constant vertical gap between TC and VC is exactly the fixed cost. Marks: labelling of the axes = 1; correct drawing and labelling of the TC curve = 1; of the VC curve = 1; of the FC curve = 1 (max 4 for the graph, max 4 for the explanation).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Graph: Cost on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal axis; a horizontal FC line; a VC curve starting from the origin and sloping upwards; a TC curve parallel to VC starting from the FC intercept on the vertical axis.

Explanation (Max 4):

- Fixed cost (FC) is the difference between the total cost (TC) and the variable cost (VC) / Variable cost is the difference between the total cost and fixed cost / Total cost is the sum of fixed cost and variable cost
- The variable cost curve starts from zero (0) while the total cost curve starts from the fixed cost level on the vertical axis
- Total cost and variable cost curves slope upwards as quantity increases.
- The gap between the total cost curve and the variable cost curve represents the value of fixed cost

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q4.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Identify the curve that represents the supply curve for the individual firm in the graph.

(Two side-by-side graphs of a perfectly competitive market. The INDUSTRY/MARKET graph shows demand curve D1 with supply curves S1 and S2, where S2 lies to the left of S1; equilibrium E1 at price P1 and quantity Q1, and equilibrium E2 at higher price P2 and lower quantity Q2. The INDIVIDUAL FIRM graph shows U-shaped MC and AC curves with horizontal lines D1 = AR1 = MR1 at price P1, sitting below the AC minimum and showing an economic loss, and D2 = AR2 = MR2 at the higher price P2, tangent to AC at its minimum at point E2.)

## Method

data response identification

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: a perfectly competitive firm produces where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, so for every market price the quantity it supplies is read off its marginal cost curve. The rising portion of MC (above average variable cost) therefore IS the firm's supply curve.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Marginal cost / MC

## Question (2 marks)

Briefly describe the term marginal revenue. (Refers to graphs of a perfectly competitive market showing the industry and the individual firm.)

## Method

definition

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: "marginal" in economics always means "from one extra unit". So marginal revenue is the extra income earned when one more unit of the product is sold. In perfect competition it equals the market price, which is why the firm's demand, average revenue and marginal revenue lines coincide.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The additional amount of income gained from selling one extra unit of a product

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q4.2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Use the graphs to explain how economic loss in the short run leads to normal profit in the long run. (2 x 2)

(Two side-by-side graphs of a perfectly competitive market. The INDUSTRY/MARKET graph shows demand curve D1 with supply curves S1 and S2, where S2 lies to the left of S1; equilibrium E1 at price P1 and quantity Q1, and equilibrium E2 at higher price P2 and lower quantity Q2. The INDIVIDUAL FIRM graph shows U-shaped MC and AC curves with horizontal lines D1 = AR1 = MR1 at price P1, sitting below the AC minimum and showing an economic loss, and D2 = AR2 = MR2 at the higher price P2, tangent to AC at its minimum at point E2.)

## Method

graph interpretation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: read the story across both graphs. At price P1 the firm's price line lies below the bottom of its average cost curve, so every firm makes an economic loss. Losses drive some firms out; on the market graph that exit shifts supply left from S1 to S2. Less supply pushes the market price up from P1 to P2. At P2 the price line just touches the AC curve at its minimum — price equals average cost — so the surviving firms earn exactly normal profit, and the exit stops.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Economic loss forces some businesses to exit the market and the market supply curve shifts to the left from S1 to S2
- The decrease in supply will result in an increase in market price from P1 to P2 which leads to a decrease in losses
- In the long-run the remaining businesses will make normal profit when the price, P2 will be equal to the average cost

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q1.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

The costs that will always decrease when production increases, is referred to as … cost.

A average
B average variable
C total
D average fixed

## Method

multiple choice recall

Think about which cost is spread ever thinner as output grows. Fixed costs, like rent, stay the same in total no matter how much is produced, so dividing the same rand amount by more and more units means average fixed cost falls continuously. Average variable cost and average cost eventually rise again as diminishing returns set in, and total cost always rises — only average fixed cost always decreases.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D - average fixed

## Question (2 marks)

The price that is set by the government above the equilibrium price to allow producers to make a fair profit is called ...

A market price.
B selling price.
C maximum price.
D minimum price.

## Method

multiple choice recall

Listen for two clues: the price is set above equilibrium, and it protects producers. A price set above equilibrium is a floor below which the price may not fall — a minimum price. A maximum price would sit below equilibrium and protect consumers instead.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D - minimum price

matching items

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q1.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Match COLUMN A item 'Price-taker' to a description from COLUMN B. (COLUMN B options for Q1.2.1 to Q1.2.8: A - method used to prevent the extinction of non-renewable resources; B - people who enjoy goods and services without paying for them; C - the activities of people travelling to and staying in places outside their usual environment; D - a firm that has no influence over the market price; E - goods that are identical in terms of appearance, packaging and quality; F - monetary policy approach used by the SARB to keep price changes within 3–6%; G - an agreement among firms within the same industry to reduce competition through price fixing; H - a firm that has control over the market price; I - activities of people visiting places to enjoy the natural environment.)

## Method

matching items

A price-taker must accept the market price as given. That is the position of a firm in perfect competition: it supplies too small a share of the market to influence the price — option D. Contrast this with option H, the price-maker, which has control over the market price.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D - a firm that has no influence over the market price

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q2.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Why would a perfectly competitive firm consider shutting down its operations? (1 x 2)

## Method

explanation

Apply the shut-down rule. In the short run a firm keeps producing as long as its revenue at least covers its variable costs, because the fixed costs are lost either way. Once average revenue falls below average variable cost — equivalently, total revenue below total variable cost — every unit produced deepens the loss, so the firm shuts down.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A perfectly competitive firm will shut down because its average revenue cannot cover all the average variable cost or total revenue is not able to cover its variable cost of production.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

data response identification

Name the concept that refers to income earned by a business for each unit sold. (Refers to the COST AND REVENUE SCHEDULE table in Q2.2.1.)

recall

## Question (2 marks)

Briefly describe the term implicit cost. (Refers to the COST AND REVENUE SCHEDULE table in Q2.2.1.)

## Method

definition

Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of the entrepreneur's own resources used in production — inputs the owner already possesses, such as their own building or their own labour, for which no money changes hands but which still carry a value.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The value of inputs owned by the entrepreneur and used in the production process.

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q2.2.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Why is the marginal revenue the same for a perfectly competitive firm when production increases? (Refers to the COST AND REVENUE SCHEDULE table in Q2.2.1.)

## Method

explanation

Link marginal revenue to price-taking. A perfectly competitive firm can sell any quantity at the going market price, so every extra unit sold adds exactly that same price to total revenue. That is why the marginal revenue column stays constant at 20 rand as production increases.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A perfectly competitive firm sells every additional unit of a product at the same prices

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q2.2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Use the information in the table above to calculate the marginal cost (A) if 10 units are produced. Show ALL calculations.

(Refers to a table for Q2.2.1 to Q2.2.5 titled COST AND REVENUE SCHEDULE, with columns Quantity, Total revenue in rands, Marginal revenue in rands, Marginal cost in rands and Total cost in rands. The rows read: at quantity 0 — total revenue 0, no marginal figures, total cost 100; at quantity 2 — total revenue 40, marginal revenue 20, marginal cost 10, total cost 120; at quantity 4 — 80, 20, 8, 136; at quantity 6 — 120, 20, 10, 156; at quantity 8 — 160, 20, 20, 196; at quantity 10 — 200, 20, A, 256.)

## Method

marginal cost calculation

Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in quantity. Read the last two rows of the table: total cost rises from 196 rand at 8 units to 256 rand at 10 units — a change of 60 rand for 2 extra units. Divide 60 by 2 to get 30 rand.

## Memo working

Marginal cost (A) = ΔTC / ΔQ = (R256 - R196) / (10 - 8) = 60 / 2 = 30

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Marginal cost (A) = 30

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Why would a firm in a perfect market always make normal profit in the long run? (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: the driver is free entry and exit. Tell the story from both sides. If existing firms make economic profit in the short run, the absence of entry barriers lets new firms in; market supply rises, price falls, and profits shrink until average revenue equals average cost (AR = AC, or TR = TC) — normal profit. If existing firms make economic loss, some exit; market supply falls, price rises, and losses shrink until the survivors again make normal profit. In long-run equilibrium there is no incentive left to enter or leave, so normal profit persists. Four fully explained links earn the 8 marks. **Marking note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.**

**Note: the official memo's final bullet reads 'Normal profit in the long-run will remain as there is incentive to enter or leave the market' — contextually this appears to be a misprint for 'no incentive to enter or leave the market'. The memo wording is reproduced verbatim in the answer below.**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- The absence of barriers to entry allows new businesses to enter the market when the existing firms make economic profit in the short-run.
- New entrants/businesses may compete for the economic profit until the existing firms earn normal profit in the long-run.
- An increase in the number of businesses in a perfect market may increase the market supply resulting in a decrease in prices.
- Profits will decline up to a point where average revenue is equal to average cost or total revenue is equal to total cost (AR = AC or TR = TC).
- Some existing businesses may be forced to exit/leave the market when they make economic loss in the short-run.
- A decrease in the number of businesses will reduce market supply which results in an increase in price.
- The economic loss will be reduced until all the firms make normal profit in the long-run.
- Normal profit in the long-run will remain as there is incentive to enter or leave the market.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q4.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, explain economic loss for a perfectly competitive firm.

## Method

graph drawing explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: draw price, cost and revenue on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. Sketch a U-shaped average cost (AC) curve and a marginal cost (MC) curve rising through AC from below. Because the firm is a price-taker, its demand line is horizontal: D = AR = MR, drawn at the market price P (R10). The firm minimises loss where MC = MR — point e, at quantity Q (100 units). Now look straight up from e to the AC curve: point a shows the average cost P1 (R12), which sits above the price. Since average revenue (R10) is below average cost (R12), the firm makes an economic loss — the rectangle between the price line and the average cost level over the 100 units. Check the size of the loss: TR - TC = (P x Q) - (AC x Q) = (10 x 100) - (12 x 100) = R1 000 - R1 200 = -R200.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Graph: axes 'Price, Cost, Revenue' (vertical) and 'Quantity' (horizontal); a U-shaped AC curve and a rising MC curve cutting AC from below; a horizontal line at P/R10 labelled D = AR = MR; the loss-minimising point e where MC = MR at quantity Q/100; point a directly above e on the AC curve corresponds to P1/R12 on the price axis; the rectangle between P/R10 and P1/R12 over the quantity Q/100 is labelled 'Economic loss'.

Allocation of marks (Max 4): Correct labelling of the axes = 1 Mark; Correct drawing and labelling of cost curves = 1 Mark; Correct positioning and labelling of revenue curves = 1 Mark; Correct indication of economic loss = 1 Mark.

Explanation (Max 4):

- A firm minimises loss at point e, where MR = MC / At point e, the firm produces 100 units at the price of P/R10.
- The firm will make economic loss because the average revenue of (P/R10) is less than the average cost of (P1/R12).
- The firm makes total economic loss of TR (P x Q) - TC (AC x Q) = (10 x 100) - (12 x 100) = R1 000 - R1 200 = -R200.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q3.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

The vapour pressures of compounds A, B and C are given in random order below: 79 kPa, 146 kPa, 58 kPa. Write down the vapour pressure of compound C. (Refers to the table in QUESTION 3.1: A pentane, B 2-methylbutane, C 2,2-dimethylpropane, all with molar mass 72 g·mol⁻¹.)

## Method

vapour pressure branching

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Compounds A, B and C are chain isomers of C5H12, all with molar mass 72 g·mol⁻¹. Compound C, 2,2-dimethylpropane, is the most branched, so it has the smallest surface area, the weakest London forces between its molecules, and therefore evaporates most easily. It must have the HIGHEST vapour pressure of the three values given: 146 kPa.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

146 (kPa). Accept: 146 000 Pa.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q3.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Fully explain your answer to QUESTION 3.2.1. (In QUESTION 3.2.1 the vapour pressure of compound C, 2,2-dimethylpropane, was identified as 146 kPa — the highest of the three isomers A pentane, B 2-methylbutane and C 2,2-dimethylpropane.)

## Method

intermolecular forces explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The memo awards the three marks for the structure point, the intermolecular-forces point and the energy point listed in the answer below: branching reduces the surface area over which London forces act, weaker forces need less energy to overcome, so more molecules escape to the vapour phase and the vapour pressure is highest for the most branched isomer.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Comparing compound C/2,2-dimethylpropane with compounds A/pentane and B/2-methylbutane: Structure - compound C is more branched than compounds A and B / shorter chain length / most compact / most spherical / smallest surface area (over which intermolecular forces act). Intermolecular forces - compound C has weaker/fewer intermolecular forces/Van der Waals forces/London forces than A and B. Energy - less energy needed to overcome or break intermolecular forces/Van der Waals forces in compound C than A and B.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q3.3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Compounds D and E are compared. Which compound has the lower boiling point? (From the vapour-pressure table at 20 °C: D propanoic acid, molar mass 74 g·mol⁻¹, vapour pressure 0,32 kPa; E butanal, molar mass 72 g·mol⁻¹, vapour pressure 12,2 kPa.)

## Method

boiling point comparison

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The two compounds have almost the same molar mass, so the comparison comes down to the strength of the intermolecular forces. Butanal (E) has the much higher vapour pressure (12,2 kPa versus 0,32 kPa), which tells you its intermolecular forces are weaker — an aldehyde has only dipole-dipole and London forces, while a carboxylic acid also has hydrogen bonding. Weaker forces need less energy to overcome, so butanal boils at the lower temperature.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

E / butanal
