# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q3.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Fully explain the difference in the vapour pressures between compounds D and E. (From the vapour-pressure table at 20 °C: D propanoic acid, molar mass 74 g·mol⁻¹, vapour pressure 0,32 kPa; E butanal, molar mass 72 g·mol⁻¹, vapour pressure 12,2 kPa.)

## Method

intermolecular forces explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The four marks follow the standard structure-forces-energy chain: name the intermolecular forces in each compound, compare their strengths, then link that to the energy needed to escape to the vapour phase. Propanoic acid (D) is a carboxylic acid, so its molecules hydrogen-bond to each other (on top of dipole-dipole and London forces). Butanal (E) is an aldehyde: no O–H bond, so no hydrogen bonding — only dipole-dipole and London forces. Hydrogen bonds are the stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed for a molecule of D to break free into the vapour phase; fewer molecules escape, and D's vapour pressure (0,32 kPa) is far lower than E's (12,2 kPa).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Compound D/propanoic acid has hydrogen bonding (dipole-dipole and London forces) between molecules. Compound E/butanal has dipole-dipole forces (and London forces) between molecules. Intermolecular forces between molecules of compound D are stronger than intermolecular forces between molecules of compound E. More energy is needed to overcome/break intermolecular forces between molecules of compound D than in compound E. (Equivalent formulation comparing E as weaker also accepted.)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q3.3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

The following are the vapour pressures of these compounds at a given temperature: Compound A 0,071 kPa; Compound B 9,7 kPa. Write down the STRUCTURAL FORMULA of compound A. (Refers to QUESTION 3: compounds A and B share the molecular formula C4H8O2, are straight chain molecules, and belong to two different homologous series — the ester and the carboxylic acid.)

## Method

structural formula from properties

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Link vapour pressure to intermolecular forces: the LOWER the vapour pressure, the STRONGER the intermolecular forces holding the molecules in the liquid. Compound A's vapour pressure (0,071 kPa) is far lower than compound B's (9,7 kPa), so A has the stronger intermolecular forces. Between a carboxylic acid and an ester of the same molecular formula, the carboxylic acid has the stronger forces because its O-H bond allows hydrogen bonding between molecules; an ester has no O-H and cannot hydrogen-bond with itself. So A is the straight-chain carboxylic acid with formula C4H8O2: butanoic acid. Draw the full structural formula: a four-carbon chain in which the fourth carbon is the carboxyl carbon, showing the double-bonded O and the O-H. Memo marking criteria: (a) functional group correct; (b) whole structure correct.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Butanoic acid: full structural formula of a four-carbon chain CH3-CH2-CH2-COOH, with the carboxyl carbon showing the double-bonded O and the O-H.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Two bottles contain compounds A and B with the same molecular formula, C4H8O2. These compounds are straight chain organic molecules that belong to two different homologous series; the strongest intermolecular forces are hydrogen bonds between molecules of compound A and dipole-dipole forces between molecules of compound B. Which compound, A or B, has a higher boiling point? Give a reason for the answer by referring to the strength of the intermolecular forces.

## Method

boiling point imf reasoning

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Boiling point rises with the strength of the intermolecular forces: stronger forces need more energy to overcome before molecules can escape into the vapour phase. Hydrogen bonds between the molecules of A are stronger than the dipole-dipole forces between the molecules of B, so A boils at the higher temperature.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A. The hydrogen bond is stronger than the dipole-dipole force. (OR: the dipole-dipole force is weaker than the hydrogen bonds / compound A has stronger intermolecular forces (than B) / compound B has weaker intermolecular forces (than A).)

## Question (1 mark)

Compound A is a straight chain organic compound with molecular formula C4H8O2 whose molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds. The boiling point of compound A is measured again on another day when the atmospheric pressure is much lower. How will the boiling point of this compound now be affected? ## Method

boiling point pressure reasoning

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the surrounding atmospheric pressure. When the atmospheric pressure is much lower, the vapour pressure needed for boiling is reached at a lower temperature, so the boiling point decreases.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Decreases

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Several forces are acting on a moving object. Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT when these forces are in equilibrium? A The velocity of the object is increasing. B The object is moving at a constant velocity. C The kinetic energy of the object is decreasing. D The object has a non-zero acceleration.

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Forces in equilibrium mean the net force is zero. By Newton's first law, a zero net force on a moving object means zero acceleration, so the object keeps moving at a constant velocity. That rules out A (velocity increasing needs a net force), C (decreasing kinetic energy means the speed is changing, which needs a net force) and D (a non-zero acceleration needs a non-zero net force).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.10

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q1.10.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for the photoelectric effect? The photoelectric effect demonstrates that: (i) Light has a wave nature (ii) Light has a particle nature (iii) Light energy is quantised. A (i) only B (ii) only C (i) and (iii) only D (ii) and (iii) only

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The photoelectric effect is the key evidence for the particle model of light: light arrives as photons, each carrying one packet (quantum) of energy E = hf, and a single photon ejects a single electron only if its energy exceeds the work function. So statement (ii) is true — light behaves as particles — and statement (iii) is true — light energy comes in quantised packets. Statement (i) is false here: the wave nature of light is demonstrated by interference and diffraction, not by the photoelectric effect.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: A stone thrown vertically downwards from the top of a building takes t seconds to strike the ground. Consider the acceleration-time graph for the motion of the stone. The effects of air friction are ignored. [Graph: acceleration (m·s⁻²) constant at 9,8 from 0 to t seconds; the area under the graph between 0 and t is shaded.] What does the shaded area between 0 and t seconds, shown in the graph, represent? A The final velocity of the stone B The change in position of the stone C The constant velocity of the stone D The change in velocity of the stone

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The area under an acceleration-time graph equals acceleration multiplied by time, and a·Δt is the change in velocity, Δv. Here the area is 9,8 x t, the amount the stone's velocity changes during the fall. It is not the final velocity, because the stone already had a non-zero starting velocity when it was thrown downwards; the area gives only the change, not the final value. Change in position would come from the area under a velocity-time graph, not an acceleration-time graph.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: A ball moving horizontally has constant momentum p and kinetic energy K. The ball collides with a wall and bounces back horizontally. Immediately after the collision, the ball has momentum ½p. The mass of the ball remains constant. [Diagram: ball moving with momentum p towards a wall; after bouncing it moves away with momentum ½p.] Which ONE of the following is the kinetic energy of the ball immediately after the collision? A ¼K B ½K C 2K D 4K

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Link kinetic energy to momentum: Ek = ½mv² and p = mv, so Ek = p²/(2m). Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the momentum when the mass is constant. Before the collision, K = p²/(2m). After the collision the momentum magnitude is halved to ½p, so the new kinetic energy is (½p)²/(2m) = ¼ · p²/(2m) = ¼K. Halving the momentum quarters the kinetic energy.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q1.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: A force F acts on a box as the box moves from rest down a rough incline at a constant acceleration. The force is parallel to the incline, as shown in the diagram. [Diagram: box on an incline with force F directed up the slope, box moving down the slope.] Choose the option that CORRECTLY completes the following statement: The work done by the gravitational force is ... the work done by the frictional force and the work done by F. A equal to the sum of B less than the sum of C greater than the sum of D equal to the difference between

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Apply the work-energy theorem: Wnet = ΔEk. The box starts from rest and accelerates down the slope, so its kinetic energy increases and the net work is positive. The motion is down the slope, while both friction and F point up the slope, so friction and F each do negative work. Gravity is the only force doing positive work. For the net work to come out positive, the positive work done by gravity must be larger in magnitude than the combined magnitude of the work done by friction and by F — greater than their sum, not equal to it.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

C

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: A ball falling vertically downwards from point A strikes the ground with velocity v and bounces, reaching a maximum height at point B, as shown in the diagram. [Diagram: point A above point B; B is the lower maximum-rebound height above the ground.] Which ONE of the combinations below is CORRECT for the direction of the impulse on the ball upon striking the ground and the magnitude of the velocity with which the ball leaves the ground? A Upward; Greater than v B Downward; Greater than v C Upward; Less than v D Downward; Less than v

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Impulse equals the change in momentum. The ball arrives moving downwards and leaves moving upwards, so its momentum changes from downward to upward — the change in momentum, and therefore the impulse the ground exerts on the ball, points upward. For the speed: the ball rebounds only to point B, which is lower than the drop height A. A lower rebound height means less kinetic energy leaving the ground than arriving, so the ball leaves the ground with a speed less than v.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

C

multiple choice

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.7

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q1.7.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Two small identical spheres, each with mass m and charge +Q, are placed in a vertical cylinder. The spheres remain stationary when their centres are r metres apart, as shown in the diagram. Ignore ALL frictional effects. [Diagram: vertical cylinder with one charged sphere (+Q, mass m) floating a distance r above an identical sphere (+Q, mass m) at the bottom.] Which ONE of the following expressions can be used to CORRECTLY calculate the distance r? A √(kQ²/mg) B √(kmg/Q²) C √(Q²/kmg) D √(mg/kQ²)

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The upper sphere floats in equilibrium, so the upward electrostatic repulsion from the identical charge below balances its weight. Coulomb's law gives the repulsion as kQ·Q/r² = kQ²/r², and the weight is mg. Setting them equal: kQ²/r² = mg. Solve for r: r² = kQ²/(mg), so r = √(kQ²/mg).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: The diagram shows a simplified electric motor. The rotation of the coil is observed from the battery. [Diagram: rectangular coil between magnetic poles N (left) and S (right), connected via a split-ring commutator to a battery.] Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT while the motor is in operation? The coil and the ... A slip rings rotate anti-clockwise. B slip rings rotate clockwise. C commutator rotate clockwise. D commutator rotate anti-clockwise.

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) First eliminate by component: a DC motor uses a split-ring commutator, not slip rings — slip rings belong to AC machines. The diagram shows a split-ring commutator connected to a battery, so options A and B fall away immediately. That leaves the direction. Applying the motor rule (left-hand rule for conventional current) to the current direction and the field from the N pole on the left to the S pole on the right, the forces on the two sides of the coil in this diagram turn the coil anti-clockwise as seen from the battery. The coil and the commutator rotate together, anti-clockwise.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.1.1a

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q5.1.1(a).

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Simon is a carpenter who builds wooden bookcases using wooden pieces for the shelves and the frame, and hardboard for the back. ANNEXURE D shows two diagrams: DIAGRAM 1 shows the wooden pieces for the top, bottom, sides and shelves of a bookcase, with hardboard for the back; DIAGRAM 2 shows the hardboard and SIX pieces of wood, with dimensions, labelled with letters A to G (A and B are the side pieces of 90 cm x 20 cm; E and D are the top and bottom pieces of 60 cm x 20 cm; F and G are the shelves of 56 cm x 20 cm; C is the hardboard back of 60 cm x 90 cm). Choose the letter (A-G) in DIAGRAM 2 that matches the item in DIAGRAM 1 given below: (a) Shelf

**Note: ANNEXURE D is printed in the 2025 Special Answer Book, which is not in the archive; the diagram labelling above is reconstructed from the marking guidelines. The memo answer is definitive.**

## Method

match component on diagram

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The shelves are the two internal horizontal pieces of 56 cm x 20 cm, labelled F and G on DIAGRAM 2 — either letter earns the marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

F OR G

## Question (2 marks)

(Context: Simon the carpenter's bookcase on ANNEXURE D — the frame is 60 cm wide and 90 cm high, and the back is a single piece of hardboard.) The back of the bookcase is made out of hardboard. (a) Explain why the dimensions of the hardboard is 60 cm by 90 cm.

## Method

explain dimensions

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Link the hardboard's dimensions to the bookcase frame it must close off: the back sheet must span the full length and full height of the bookcase.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The length of the bookcase is 60 cm and the height of the bookcase is 90 cm. OR It covers the entire back of the bookcase.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.1.3b

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q5.1.3(b).

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

(Context: the back of Simon's bookcase is a piece of hardboard measuring 60 cm by 90 cm.) (b) Draw a scaled diagram of the hardboard according to scale 1 : 20.

## Method

scale drawing

## Memo working

A scale of 1 : 20 means every real length is divided by 20 on the drawing. Width on the drawing = 60 cm ÷ 20 = 3 cm. Height on the drawing = 90 cm ÷ 20 = 4,5 cm. Draw a rectangle of 3 cm wide by 4,5 cm high — marks are awarded for the correct width, the correct height and the rectangular shape.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Width = 60 cm ÷ 20 = 3 cm; height = 90 cm ÷ 20 = 4,5 cm; a rectangle of 3 cm x 4,5 cm is drawn.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q1.1.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

In an SGB election at School X, the probability of randomly selecting a voter from School X is 0,56 during the 17:30-18:00 time slot. Write 0,56 as a simplified fraction.

## Method

decimal to simplified fraction

## Memo working

0,56 has two decimal places, so write it over 100: 0,56 = 56/100 (1A writing as a fraction). Divide the top and bottom by their highest common factor, 4: 56 ÷ 4 = 14 and 100 ÷ 4 = 25, giving 14/25 (1A simplification).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

14/25

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q3.1.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

ANNEXURE B, GRAPH 1 shows the trends in the total number of Shoprite and Pick n Pay stores for each year from 2014 to 2023 (ten years in total). On the graph, the Shoprite line starts at 1 581 stores in 2014 and only climbs above 2 000 stores from 2017 onwards, so Shoprite had fewer than 2 000 stores in three of the ten years shown (2014 to 2016). Determine, as a percentage, the probability of randomly selecting a year where the number of Shoprite stores is fewer than 2 000.

## Method

probability as percentage

## Memo working

Probability = favourable outcomes over total outcomes. The favourable outcomes are the years with fewer than 2 000 Shoprite stores — reading the graph, that is 3 years (2014, 2015 and 2016). The total outcomes are all 10 years shown on the graph. So P = 3/10 x 100% (1RT correct numerator, 1RT correct denominator) = 30% (1CA simplification). AO

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

30%

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2024, question Q4.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

A hotel has three smaller venues, each with a maximum number of guests per function: cinema-style venue 400 guests; sit-down venue without dancing space 250 guests; sit-down venue with dancing space 200 guests. TABLE 6 shows the actual number of guests per function during a specific month — 2023: 180, 350, 400, 200, 215, 90, 150, 230, 160; 2022: 360, 160, 300, 70, 160, 200, 240. Write, as a decimal, the probability that a cinema-style venue was chosen as a suitable function venue for all the functions held during 2022 and 2023.

## Method

probability as decimal

## Memo working

Only the cinema-style venue (maximum 400) can host a function with more than 250 guests, so count the functions that needed it: 350 and 400 in 2023, plus 360 and 300 in 2022, giving 4 functions. The total number of functions over both years is 9 + 7 = 16. So P = 4/16 (1A numerator, 1A denominator) = 0,25 (1CA simplification).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

0,25

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2025, question Q2.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

TABLE 4 shows Metrobus trip packages with fares per passenger category (adults 15-59 years, children 3-14 years, pensioners 60+ years). The weekly package of 12 trips is offered at an adult fare of R127,10 only — the table shows no child fare and no pensioner fare for it. Write down the probability of a 10-year old child purchasing a weekly package with 12 trips.

## Method

identify impossible event

## Memo working

A 10-year old falls in the children category (3-14 years), but the 12-trip weekly package has no child fare at all — a child cannot buy it. An event that cannot happen is an impossible event, and its probability is 0. (Memo: 2A correct probability; accepted forms: 0, 0%, impossible, and also 0/4 or 0/3.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

0 / 0% / impossible (Accept: 0/4 or 0/3)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P1, November 2025, question Q3.1.2.

## Question (3 marks)

TABLE 5 shows the use of six social media platforms categorised by gender, with users in millions (male | female): Facebook 1 732,8 | 1 307,2; Instagram 1 020 | 980; Snapchat (male users not shown, 46% of users male) | 405; X/Twitter 346,64 | 272,36; TikTok 645 | 855; YouTube 1 350 | 1 150. Determine, as a decimal, the probability of randomly selecting a social media platform where the female users were fewer than the male users.

## Method

probability as decimal

## Memo working

Count the favourable outcomes: platforms where female users are fewer than male users are Facebook, Instagram, X/Twitter and YouTube — 4 of the 6 platforms. (Snapchat and TikTok both have more female than male users.) Probability = favourable outcomes over total outcomes: P = 4/6 (1A numerator, 1A denominator) = 0,67 (1CA simplification).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

0,67

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q2.1.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

John and five other family members (a family of six) are camping at Baviaanskloof Uitspan. ANNEXURE A lists the 13 huts on the site with the number of campers each can hold (1: 6; 2A: 15, 2B: 4; 3A: 15, 3B: 4, 3C: 4; 4: 5; 5A: 15, 5B: 8; 6: 10; 7: 4-6; 8: 4-6; 9: 20). Calculate, as a percentage, the probability of John and his family randomly selecting a hut that can exactly accommodate the whole family.

## Method

probability as percentage

## Memo working

Probability = favourable outcomes over total outcomes. The family is 6 people (John plus five others). Count the huts that can accommodate exactly 6 campers: hut 1 takes 6, and huts 7 and 8 each take up to 6 (their range is 4 to 6) — that is 3 favourable huts out of 13 huts in total. So P = 3/13, and as a percentage: 3/13 x 100% = 23,076923...% which is about 23,08%. (Memo: 1A correct numerator; 1A correct denominator; 1CA simplification; no penalty for rounding.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

23,076923% (≈ 23,08%)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q3.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

There are 35 different coloured sweets in each birthday packet. TABLE 2 shows the number of sweets per colour: Blue 4; Purple 5; Pink 8; Orange 11; Yellow 7. Determine the probability, as a decimal, of randomly choosing a pink or a yellow sweet from the packet.

## Method

probability or events as decimal

## Memo working

Count the favourable sweets: pink and yellow together give 8 + 7 = 15 sweets out of the 35 in the packet. So P = 15/35 = 0,42857... which rounds to 0,43. (Memo alternative: add the two probabilities separately, P = 8/35 + 7/35 = 0,22857... + 0,2 = 0,43.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

0,43 (0,42857...)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q5.3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

TABLE 3 gives the area sizes of the mainland, islands and total for each Australian state or territory, with each state's percentage of the total area (Western Australia total 2 527 013 km^2, 32,9%; Queensland total 1 729 742 km^2, 22,5%; Northern Territory total 1 347 791 km^2, 17,5%; South Australia total 984 321 km^2, 12,8%; New South Wales total 801 150 km^2, 10,4%; Victoria total 227 444 km^2, 3,0%; Tasmania total 68 401 km^2, 0,9%; Australian Capital Territory total 2 358 km^2; TOTAL for Australia 7 688 220 km^2). A meteorite (rock from the sky) fell somewhere in Australia. Write down the probability that it randomly fell in Queensland.

## Method

probability from proportion

## Memo working

The probability that a random landing point is in Queensland equals Queensland's share of Australia's total area — which the table already gives as a percentage: P = 22,5%. (Memo alternative: compute it from the areas, P = 1 729 742 ÷ 7 688 220 = 0,224986..., which is 22,5%.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

22,5% (or 1 729 742 / 7 688 220 = 0,224986...)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025, question Q3.1.5.

## Question (4 marks)

Mrs Xulu placed all the coloured circles for her tree decoration in a container as she cut them out. TABLE 2 shows the number of circles per colour (Red 9; Green 7; Gold 28; Dark denim 8; Mixed colour 22). Determine, as a percentage, the probability of randomly choosing a green circle or a red circle from the container.

## Method

probability of either event as percentage

## Memo working

Total number of circles = 9 + 7 + 28 + 8 + 22 = 74. Favourable outcomes: green or red = 7 + 9 = 16. P(green or red) = 16/74 x 100% = 21,62%. (Memo option 2: add the separate percentages — P(red) + P(green) = 12,16% + 9,46% = 21,62%.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

21,62%

probability as fraction

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q4.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

FLOWERPOTS MANUFACTURERS: The business manufactures large concrete flowerpots. Their financial year ended on 29 February 2024. Refer to Information A. Calculate the direct/raw material cost. (Information A: 4 800 units were produced and sold during the financial year; each complete pot requires 1,4 packets of direct materials (concrete mix); the business allows for wastage of 10% of direct materials; the cost price of concrete mix was maintained at R125 per packet for the financial year.)

## Method

direct material cost with wastage

## Memo working

Packets needed for production: [4 800 x 1,4] = 6 720. Add the 10% wastage allowance: 6 720 x 1,1 = 7 392 packets (three marks). Cost at R125 per packet: 7 392 x R125 = 924 000. (Memo option 2: (6 720 (two marks) + 672 (one mark)) x R125. Memo option 3: 4 800 (one mark) x 1,54 (two marks) x R125, where 1,54 = 1,4 x 1,1 packets per pot including wastage. Workings in square brackets constitute one part, cannot be separated.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

924 000 (mark if x 125)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q4.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (7 marks)

Refer to Information B. Calculate the direct labour cost. (Information B: direct labour budgeted for the year amounted to R1 117 200; the business has 7 direct workers, each required to work 1 680 hours per year and paid the same hourly rate; not yet recorded — one worker resigned on 31 October 2023 (this worker did not work overtime), and three of the direct workers worked overtime of 60 hours each during the year at 1,6 times the normal hourly rate. The financial year ended on 29 February 2024.)

## Method

direct labour cost adjustments

## Memo working

Start from the budgeted direct labour of 1 117 200. Resigned worker: the year runs to 29 February 2024, so the worker who left on 31 October 2023 is unpaid for 4 of the 12 months. One worker-month is 1/84 of the budget (7 workers x 12 months), so subtract 1 117 200 x 4/84 = (53 200) (one part correct; ignore bracket). (Memo alternatives: per-worker budget [1 117 200 / 7] = 159 600, then 159 600 x 4/12; or 159 600 - 106 400 [159 600 x 8/12]; or hours [1 680 x 4/12] = 560 x the hourly rate of 95, where 95 = [1 117 200 / 1 680] / 7.) Overtime: 180 hours (3 x 60) x 95 (one mark + one method mark) x 1,6 = 27 360 (one part correct). (Memo option 2: (3 x 60 x 1,6) = 288 (two marks) x 95 (one method mark).) Total: 1 117 200 - 53 200 + 27 360 = 1 091 360.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1 091 360 (one part correct; check operation; resigned worker subtracted and overtime added; must include R1 117 200)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q4.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Refer to Information C. Complete the Factory Overhead Cost Note. (Information C: the bookkeeper calculated the factory overhead cost as R1 132 700. Adjustments — a clerk was paid a salary of R9 200 per month, recorded entirely as an administration cost, but 20% must be allocated to the office and the rest to production; rent of R126 000 was shared by the bookkeeper on floor areas of 600 m2 total, with factory 400 m2, office 80 m2, sales 120 m2 — however, since the beginning of the year the annual rent increased to R157 500 as the factory grew, with adjusted floor areas of 800 m2 total: factory 600 m2, office 80 m2, sales 120 m2, which the bookkeeper did not consider.)

## Method

factory overhead note adjustments

## Memo working

Start with the bookkeeper's (incorrect) factory overheads of 1 132 700. Factory indirect labour: the clerk's annual salary is (9 200 x 12) = 110 400, and 80% belongs to production: 110 400 x 80/100 = 88 320 to add. Factory rental correction: the correct factory share is [157 500 x 600/800] = 118 125, while the bookkeeper recorded [126 000 x 400/600] = 84 000, so add the difference of 34 125. Corrected total: 1 132 700 + 88 320 + 34 125 = 1 255 145.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1 255 145 (one part correct; should include R1 132 700)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q4.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

TIMEPIECE MANUFACTURERS: The business manufactures watches and is owned by Jabu Tallies. The financial year ended on 31 August 2024. (NOTE: Where comments or explanations are required, you should quote calculations, figures and/or trends and give an explanation or a reason in each case.) Comment on the level of production and break-even point on 31 August 2024. (Information, 2024 vs 2023: number of units produced and sold 3 640 vs 2 910; break-even point 6 868 vs 7 983; selling price per unit R1 020 vs R990; variable cost per unit R755 vs R762; total fixed cost R1 820 000 in both years.)

## Method

breakeven vs production comment

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) — Compare production to the break-even point in each year. In 2024 the business produced and sold 3 640 units, which is below the break-even point of 6 868 — it made a loss on the 3 228-unit shortfall. But the position improved against 2023, when the shortfall was 5 073 units (7 983 - 2 910): the gap narrowed by 1 845 units. Supporting trends: the break-even point fell by 1 115 units, from 7 983 to 6 868 (14%), while production rose by 730 units, from 2 910 to 3 640 (25%). The full four marks need the below-break-even observation plus the year-on-year improvement, each with figures.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

For FOUR marks: Produced and sold 3 640 units, below the BEP 6 868 / made a loss on 3 228 units; Loss on 3 228 units (1 845 fewer) has improved compared to 2023 loss on 5 073 units. For TWO marks (max): BEP decreased by 1 115 units / (from 7 983) to 6 868 / by 14%; Units produced increased by 730 units / (from 2 910) to 3 640 / by 25%.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q4.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Comment on the gross profit earned by the business and the price charged for the watches. In your opinion, explain if Jabu's customers found the 2024 price reasonable. Provide figures. (Information, 2024 vs 2023: gross profit R1 237 600 vs R960 300; total sales R3 712 800 vs R2 880 900; units produced and sold 3 640 vs 2 910; selling price per unit R1 020 vs R990.)

## Method

gross profit and price comment

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) — Link the three movements. Gross profit rose from 960 300 to 1 237 600, an increase of R277 300 or 28,9%. Volume rose too: units sold went from 2 910 to 3 640 (up 730, or 25%), and total sales from 2 880 900 to 3 712 800 (up R831 900, or 28,9%). Yet the selling price only moved from R990 to R1 020 — up R30, a modest 3% that sits within the inflation rate. Customers evidently found the price reasonable: despite the increase they bought 25% more watches, which is what drove the 28,9% gross profit growth.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Gross profit has increased (from R960 300) to R1 237 600 / by R277 300 / by 28,9%; Number of units sold increased (from 2 910) to 3 640 / by 730 units / by 25% / total sales increased (from R2 880 900) to R3 712 800 / by R831 900 / by 28,9%; Selling price increased (from R990) to R1 020 / by R30 / by 3%, which is reasonable for the customers and is within the inflation rate. For FOUR marks (be aware of comments being combined): Price increased with 3%, 25% more units sold, and GP increased with 28,9%.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q4.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

**Note (memo caveat):** The memo lists three acceptable cost rows (direct material cost, total fixed cost, selling and distribution cost) although the question asks for TWO main costs — any two of the three, each with a matching strategy, earn the marks. Direct material cost per unit decreased from R520 to R450, consistent with a positive effect on the selling price.

## Question (4 marks)

Identify the TWO main costs that would have a positive effect on the selling price. In each case, provide a strategy that Jabu would have implemented. (Information, cost per unit 2024 vs 2023: direct material cost R450 vs R520; direct labour cost R185 vs R132; selling and distribution cost R120 vs R110; total fixed cost R1 820 000 in both years while units produced rose from 2 910 to 3 640.)

## Method

cost control strategies

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) — Look for the costs that fell per unit or stayed flat while output grew, since those allow a keener selling price. Direct material cost dropped from R520 to R450 per unit — achievable strategies include switching to a cheaper or local supplier, bulk buying at lower prices, or cutting wastage through better supervision, better-trained workers or technology. Total fixed cost stayed at R1 820 000 even though more units were produced — economies of scale spread the same fixed cost over more watches. Selling and distribution cost (R110 to R120 per unit) qualifies where paired with a strategy such as more reliable distribution to increase customer satisfaction, or additional advertising / free delivery that contributed to increased sales.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Main costs (2 marks) with strategies (2 marks): Direct material cost — change to a cheaper supplier / local suppliers / bulk purchase at lower price; less wastage due to improved supervision / better trained workers / technology used. Total fixed cost — economies of scale, total fixed cost remained the same (R1 820 000) even though more units were produced. Selling and distribution cost — offer more reliable distribution systems to increase customer satisfaction; additional advertising / free delivery contributed to increased sales.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.2.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2024, question Q4.2.4.

## Question (4 marks)

Jabu wishes to increase his profit by R300 000 during the next financial year, while maintaining the costs. Calculate the price that he would have to charge his customers in order to produce 400 extra units. (Information: the variable cost per unit for 2024 is R755.)

## Method

required selling price for target profit

## Memo working

Each of the 400 extra units must carry its own variable cost of R755 plus its share of the extra profit target. The profit required per extra unit is [300 000 / 400] = 750 (two marks); add the variable cost per unit of 755 (one mark) to get the required price of R1 505. (Memo option 2: total amount the 400 units must bring in is (R300 000 (one mark) + R302 000 [400 x 755] (one mark)), divided by 400 (one mark) = R1 505. Workings in square brackets constitute one part, cannot be separated.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R1 505 (one part correct)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q3.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (16 marks)

LOCKSMITH MANUFACTURERS: The business manufactures security jackets. Their financial year ended on 28 February 2025. Complete the Factory Overhead Cost Note. (The ANSWER BOOK pre-prints the line: Other factory expenses 737 010.)

INFORMATION:

A. Extract from balances (columns: 28 Feb. 2025 (R) | 29 Feb. 2024 (R)): Factory equipment 5 400 000 | ?; Accumulated depreciation on factory equipment ? | 1 680 000; Work-in-progress stock 93 000 | 125 000.

B. Summary of totals for the year ended 28 February 2025 (R): Prime cost 6 025 000; Water and electricity 915 000; Insurance 78 000; Rent expense 240 400; Advertising 380 000; Other factory expenses 737 010.

C. Additional information and adjustments: 75% of the water and electricity must be allocated to the factory — the remainder must be shared equally between the other departments. Insurance includes an additional premium of R10 800 paid for the period of 1 December 2024 to 30 November 2025; this expense is allocated between the factory and the sales department in the ratio 3 : 2. Locksmith Manufacturers rent their premises from Dynamic Properties at a fixed rate per m2; due to expansion they had to rent additional space for the factory only, from 1 October 2024, at the same fixed rate per m2 — floor space for the year: 1 Mar. 2024 to 30 Sept. 2024: factory 200 m2, other departments 40 m2, total 240 m2; 1 Oct. 2024 to 28 Feb. 2025: factory 225 m2, other departments 40 m2, total 265 m2. Provide for depreciation on factory equipment at 20% p.a. on the diminishing-balance method. NOTE: New factory equipment costing R684 000 was installed on 1 November 2024; this was properly recorded.

## Method

factory overhead cost note

## Memo working

Take each overhead in turn and allocate the factory's share.

Water and electricity: (915 000 x 75%) = 686 250 (two marks).

Insurance: first remove the prepaid portion of the additional premium — R10 800 covers 1 December 2024 to 30 November 2025, so 9 months (1 March to 30 November 2025) are prepaid: 10 800 x 9/12 = 8 100. Insurance expense for the year: [78 000 - 8 100] = 69 900 (one mark + one mark); factory share 3/5 (one mark + one mark): 69 900 x 3/5 = 41 940 (one part correct). (Memo alternatives: 46 800 - 4 860, OR 69 900 - 27 960.)

Rent expense: the rate per m2 is fixed, so weight the floor space by months. Factory m2-months: 200 x 7 + 225 x 5 = 2 525 (two marks); total m2-months: 240 x 7 + 265 x 5 = 3 005 (two marks). Factory share: (240 400 x 2 525/3 005) = 202 000 (one part correct). (Memo alternatives: 112 000 + 90 000, OR 240 400 (one mark) - 38 400 (three marks).)

Depreciation on factory equipment (20% p.a. diminishing balance): new equipment, 4 months in use: 684 000 x 20/100 x 4/12 = 45 600; old equipment carrying value: (5 400 000 - 684 000) - 1 680 000 = 3 036 000, so 3 036 000 x 20/100 = 607 200. Total depreciation: 45 600 + 607 200 = 652 800 (one part correct).

Other factory expenses: 737 010 (given).

Total factory overhead cost: 686 250 + 41 940 + 202 000 + 652 800 + 737 010 = 2 320 000 (one part correct; must include other factory expenses; if advertising is included, lose the mark on the final total — advertising is a selling and distribution cost, not a factory overhead).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Water and electricity 686 250; Insurance 41 940; Rent expense 202 000; Depreciation: factory equipment 652 800; Other factory expenses 737 010; Total 2 320 000 (one part correct; must include other factory expenses)

## Question (4 marks)

Calculate the cost of production of finished goods for the year ended 28 February 2025. (From QUESTION 3.1, Locksmith Manufacturers: prime cost for the year R6 025 000; total factory overhead cost R2 320 000 as calculated in Q3.1.1; work-in-progress stock R125 000 on 29 February 2024 and R93 000 on 28 February 2025.)

## Method

cost of production of finished goods

## Memo working

Cost of production of finished goods is the total cost of goods completed in the factory this year: prime cost plus factory overhead cost, adjusted for the change in work-in-progress stock. Start with the prime cost of 6 025 000. Add the factory overhead cost of 2 320 000 (see 3.1.1) to get total manufacturing cost. Then adjust for work-in-progress: the stock still on the factory floor decreased from 125 000 to 93 000, so an extra 32 000 of earlier work was completed and released into finished goods this year — add it. 6 025 000 + 2 320 000 + 32 000 [125 000 - 93 000] = 8 377 000.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

R8 377 000 (one part correct)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q3.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Picaso Manufacturers produces cellphone screen covers and cases; the financial year ends on 31 August each year. CELLPHONE CASES: Calculate the break-even point on 31 August 2025. (From the information table, cellphone cases for the year ended 31 August 2025: 28 750 units produced and sold; selling price R265 per unit; total fixed cost R80 per unit; total variable cost R146 per unit.)

## Method

break even point

## Memo working

Break-even point = total fixed costs divided by contribution per unit. First convert the fixed cost per unit into total fixed costs: 28 750 units x R80 = 2 300 000. Then find the contribution each unit makes towards covering fixed costs: selling price minus variable cost per unit = 265 - 146 = 119. Break-even point = 2 300 000 / 119 = 19 327,7, rounded up to 19 328 units. (Numerator and denominator must be marked as such.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

19 328 units (one part correct; do not accept less than 1; accept 19 327,7)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Accounting P2, November 2025, question Q3.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Comment on whether Dawn should be satisfied with the number of units produced and sold. Provide ONE point, with figures. (From QUESTION 3.2, Picaso Manufacturers, cellphone cases: 28 750 units produced and sold in 2025 against a break-even point of 19 328 — see Q3.2.1; in 2024 the figures were 25 000 units against a break-even point of 20 000.)

## Method

units vs breakeven comment

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) — Compare the units produced and sold with the break-even point: 28 750 - 19 328 = 9 422 units above break-even, each earning the full contribution of R119, so profit is made on 9 422 units (9 422 x 119 = R1 121 218). In 2024 the margin was only 25 000 - 20 000 = 5 000 units, so the position improved.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Valid explanation with comparison of units produced and break-even point, with figures (2 marks). Yes, Dawn should be satisfied — any ONE of:

- Units produced (28 750) are above the break-even point of 19 328 (see 3.2.1) / exceed the break-even point by 9 422 units / the business makes a profit on 9 422 units (R1 121 218).
- More units were produced and sold, resulting in a higher profit: 9 422 units above break-even in 2025 compared to 5 000 units in 2024.

For ONE mark only: units produced increased (from 25 000) to 28 750 / by 3 750 units; or the break-even point decreased (from 20 000) to 19 328 (see 3.2.1) / by 672 units.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2024, question Q10.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

In the diagram, triangle RST is drawn. Line AB intersects RS and RT at A and B respectively such that AB || ST. (Diagram: triangle RST with apex R; line AB inside the triangle parallel to base ST, with A on RS and B on RT.) Prove the theorem which states that a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally, i.e. RA/AS = RB/BT.

## Method

proportionality theorem proof

## Memo working

Construction: join SB and TA; draw h1 from B ⊥ AR and h2 from A ⊥ RB. area ΔRAB/area ΔASB = (½RA·h1)/(½AS·h1) = RA/AS; area ΔRAB/area ΔABT = (½RB·h2)/(½BT·h2) = RB/BT; area ΔASB = area ΔABT [same base AB, same height, AB || ST]; therefore RA/AS = RB/BT

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

RA/AS = RB/BT

midpoint theorem

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

OR : WS = 1 : 2

In the diagram, ΔABC is drawn. BA is produced to E. F and D are points on BC such that AD || EF. AC and EF intersect at G. CF/FB = 2/5 and CG/GA = 3/2. (In the figure, B is top right and C at the bottom; E lies to the left of A on BA produced; D is on BC between the foot of A and B; EF runs from E through G on AC to F on BC below D; AD || EF is marked.) Calculate, with reasons, the value of: FD/CF

## Method

proportionality theorem

## Memo working

Look at triangle CDA: the line GF is parallel to side AD (given AD || EF) and cuts the other two sides at G and F. By the proportionality theorem (a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio), FD/CF = GA/CG. Since CG/GA = 3/2, the reciprocal gives GA/CG = 2/3, so FD/CF = 2/3.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q11.1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q11.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Calculate, with reasons, the value of: BA/EA (From QUESTION 11.1: in ΔABC, BA is produced to E; F and D lie on BC with AD || EF; AC and EF intersect at G; CF/FB = 2/5 and CG/GA = 3/2; from QUESTION 11.1.1: FD/CF = 2/3.)

## Method

proportionality theorem combined ratios

## Memo working

Introduce a variable to combine the two ratios along BC. Let CF = 2x and FB = 5x (from CF/FB = 2/5). From QUESTION 11.1.1, FD = (2/3)CF = (2/3)(2x) = (4/3)x. Now use triangle BEF: A lies on BE and D lies on BF, with AD || EF, so by the proportionality theorem BA/EA = BD/FD. Compute BD = FB - FD = 5x - (4/3)x = (11/3)x. Therefore BA/EA = (11/3)x ÷ (4/3)x = 11/4.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

BA/EA = 11/4

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q11.1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q11.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Calculate, with reasons, the value of: Area of ΔGCF / Area of GFDA (From QUESTION 11.1: in ΔABC, F and D lie on BC with AD || EF; AC and EF intersect at G; CF/FB = 2/5 and CG/GA = 3/2; from QUESTION 11.1.1: FD/CF = 2/3.)

## Method

area ratio sine formula

## Memo working

Quadrilateral GFDA is what remains of triangle CDA after triangle GCF is removed, so Area GFDA = Area ΔCDA - Area ΔGCF. Express the sides from C in parts: CG/GA = 3/2 gives CG = 3k and CA = 5k; FD/CF = 2/3 gives CF = 3p and CD = CF + FD = 5p. Both triangles share the angle Ĉ, so use the sine area formula: Area ΔGCF = (1/2)(3k)(3p)sin Ĉ and Area ΔCDA = (1/2)(5k)(5p)sin Ĉ. Then the ratio = (1/2)(3k)(3p)sin Ĉ / [(1/2)(5k)(5p)sin Ĉ - (1/2)(3k)(3p)sin Ĉ] = 9kp/(25kp - 9kp) = 9/16.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Area ΔGCF / Area GFDA = 9/16

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q11.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q11.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

In the diagram, WVZR is a cyclic quadrilateral. RZ is produced to Q. A tangent is drawn from Q to touch the circle at S. WV is produced to E, a point on ZQ. RW produced meets ZV produced in P. PQ || WE. RS and ZS are drawn. (In the figure the circle passes through W at the top, V on the left, Z lower left and R on the right; P lies outside the circle above left where RW and ZV produced meet; Q lies outside at bottom left; E is on ZQ; S is at the bottom of the circle with tangent QS.) Prove, with reasons, that: PR = PW.QR/QE

## Method

proportionality theorem

## Memo working

Work in triangle PQR (or equivalently triangle RQP): W lies on side RP and E lies on side RQ, and WE || PQ is given. By the proportionality theorem (a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally), QE/QR = PW/PR. Cross-multiply: PR.QE = PW.QR, and divide both sides by QE to get PR = PW.QR/QE.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

PR = PW.QR/QE

## Question (1 mark)

Prove, with reasons, that: If ΔPQZ ||| ΔRQP, then PQ^2 = RQ.QZ (From QUESTION 11.2: WVZR is a cyclic quadrilateral, RZ is produced to Q, and P lies where RW produced meets ZV produced.)

## Method

similar triangles ratio

## Memo working

Similar triangles have their corresponding sides in proportion, matching the order of the letters: ΔPQZ ||| ΔRQP gives PQ/RQ = QZ/QP. Cross-multiplying yields PQ.QP = RQ.QZ, that is PQ^2 = RQ.QZ.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

PQ^2 = RQ.QZ

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q11.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q11.2.3.

## Question (3 marks)

Prove, with reasons, that: ΔQSZ ||| ΔQRS (From QUESTION 11.2: WVZR is a cyclic quadrilateral, RZ is produced to Q, and QS is a tangent touching the circle at S; RS and ZS are drawn.)

## Method

similar triangles aaa

## Memo working

Compare the two triangles angle by angle. First, Q̂2 = Q̂2: the angle at Q is common to both triangles, since Z lies on the line QR. Second, Ŝ1 = R̂2 by the tan-chord theorem — the angle between tangent QS and chord SZ equals the angle that SZ subtends in the alternate segment, which is the angle at R. Third, the remaining angles must be equal because the angles of a triangle sum to 180°: Ẑ1 = QŜR (third angle of the triangle). With three pairs of equal angles, ΔQSZ ||| ΔQRS (AAA).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

ΔQSZ ||| ΔQRS

## Question (3 marks)

Prove, with reasons, that: PQ = QS (From QUESTIONS 11.2.2 and 11.2.3: PQ^2 = RQ.QZ, and ΔQSZ ||| ΔQRS.)

## Method

combine similarity results

## Memo working

From the similarity ΔQSZ ||| ΔQRS, corresponding sides are proportional: QS/QR = QZ/QS. Cross-multiplying gives QS^2 = QZ.QR. But QUESTION 11.2.2 established PQ^2 = RQ.QZ — the same product. So PQ^2 = QS^2, and since both are lengths (positive), PQ = QS.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

PQ = QS

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q11.2.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q11.2.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Prove, with reasons, that: PW = QE.PZ/sqrt(QR.QZ) (From QUESTIONS 11.2.1 and 11.2.2: PR = PW.QR/QE, PQ^2 = RQ.QZ, and ΔPQZ ||| ΔRQP.)

## Method

combine similar triangles

## Memo working

From the similarity ΔPQZ ||| ΔRQP, corresponding sides give PQ/RQ = PZ/PR, so PR = QR.PZ/PQ. But QUESTION 11.2.1 proved PR = PW.QR/QE. Set the two expressions for PR equal: PW.QR/QE = QR.PZ/PQ. Cancel QR from both sides and solve for PW: PW = QE.PZ/PQ. Finally, from QUESTION 11.2.2, PQ^2 = RQ.QZ, so PQ = sqrt(RQ.QZ). Substituting gives PW = QE.PZ/sqrt(QR.QZ).

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

PW = QE.PZ/sqrt(QR.QZ)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2024, question Q3.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Discuss the advantages of import substitution for the South African economy. (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Tariffs and quotas encourage local employment as more workers get jobs in industries that produce previously imported goods.
- Expansion of domestic industries to meet the demand for goods that were previously imported may promote economic development.
- Reduced imports have a positive effect on the balance of payment as it reduces the current account/trade deficit.
- A wide variety of goods is produced which expands the industrial base.
- The increase in tax base for the state will lead to more tax revenue.
- Tariffs and quotas are easy and effective import control measures which ensure that domestic production is compromised.
- The country will be less vulnerable to foreign actions and conditions, such as price increases, because goods are produced locally.
- The available foreign exchange can be used to import other goods and services thereby increasing consumers' choice.
- It promotes diversification of the economy by producing a wider range of goods and services locally.
- Reducing dependence on imports may improve the balance of payments and this can contribute to a more stable economic environment.

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

**Note on a source anomaly:** the official memo bullet "Tariffs and quotas are easy and effective import control measures which ensure that domestic production is compromised" appears to contain a misprint — contextually it should read "is NOT compromised". It is transcribed verbatim above.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2025, question Q4.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Briefly discuss specialisation and innovation as arguments in favour of free trade. (2 x 4)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: two headings, four marks each. Specialisation: comparative advantage shows that world output and consumption rise when each country specialises where its opportunity cost is lowest; resources are used efficiently, waste is prevented and living standards rise as more goods and services are traded. Innovation: free trade intensifies competition, which is a powerful incentive to innovate — introducing new products for export markets, finding production methods that cut costs and lift quality, and continuously adopting the latest technology.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

**Specialisation**

- Comparative advantage shows that world output can be increased if countries specialise in what they are relatively best at producing.
- If countries specialise the goods for which they have a comparative advantage world trade and consumption will be maximised.
- The effect of increasing living standards results in the trading of more goods and services.
- Allows industries that have a comparative advantage with a lower opportunity cost.
- Specialisation increases economic efficiency and prevents the wasting of resources.
- Each country that is best suited for specific goods and services will engage in producing more of those goods or services.

**Innovation**

- Free trade leads to increased competition, which provides a powerful incentive for innovation.
- Free trade allows countries to introduce new products that can be exported to foreign markets
- Enterprises compete to find production methods that cut costs and improve quality and reliability of goods.
- Competition on international markets may force businesses to implement the latest technology and continuously improve their systems.

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

## Question (3 marks)

The sequence of the first differences of a quadratic pattern is: 1 ; 3 ; 5 ; ... If T99 of this quadratic pattern is 9 632, calculate the value of T98.

## Method

first differences

## Memo working

The first differences themselves form the linear pattern Tn = 2n - 1. The difference between T98 and T99 of the quadratic pattern is the 98th first difference: 2(98) - 1 = 195. Step back from T99: T98 = 9 632 - 195 = 9 437

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

T98 = 9 437

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.2

## Question (5 marks)

If it is further given that the third term of the quadratic pattern (with first differences 1 ; 3 ; 5 ; ...) is 32, determine the general term, Tn, of the quadratic pattern.

## Method

quadratic pattern general term

## Memo working

The pattern is 28 ; 29 ; 32 ; ... with first differences 1 ; 3 ; 5 ; 7 and constant second difference 2. For Tn = an^2 + bn + c: 2a = 2 -> a = 1; 3a + b = 1 -> b = -2; use T3 = 32: 9a + 3b + c = 32 -> 9 - 6 + c = 32 -> c = 29 (or from T1: 1 - 2 + c = 28 -> c = 29). So Tn = n^2 - 2n + 29

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Tn = n^2 - 2n + 29

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q3.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

The depth of a torpedo below sea level forms a quadratic pattern, where 0 metres is at sea level. A submarine tracked a torpedo in one-second intervals. (Figure: drawing of a submarine with a torpedo below it.) The depth (in metres) that the torpedo reached is given in the table below. At the end of the first second: 36; At the end of the first 2 seconds: 71; At the end of the first 3 seconds: 104. Calculate the depth of the torpedo at the end of the first 5 seconds.

## Method

extend quadratic pattern

## Memo working

The first differences of 36 ; 71 ; 104 are 35 and 33, so the second difference is -2. Each new first difference drops by 2: the next differences are 31 and 29. Extend the pattern: T4 = 104 + 31 = 135 and T5 = 135 + 29 = 164.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

T5 = 164 (metres)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Show that the depth of the torpedo at the end of n seconds was Tn = -n^2 + 38n - 1  (Quadratic pattern of depths: 36 ; 71 ; 104 ; ... at the end of 1, 2, 3, ... seconds)

## Method

quadratic pattern general term

## Memo working

For a quadratic pattern Tn = an^2 + bn + c, the second difference equals 2a. Here the second difference is -2, so 2a = -2 -> a = -1. The first first-difference equals 3a + b: 3(-1) + b = 35 -> b = 38. The first term equals a + b + c: -1 + 38 + c = 36 -> c = -1. Therefore Tn = -n^2 + 38n - 1. (Check: T2 = -4 + 76 - 1 = 71 and T3 = -9 + 114 - 1 = 104.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Tn = -n^2 + 38n - 1

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q3.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

Calculate the maximum depth that the torpedo reached. (Depth after n seconds: Tn = -n^2 + 38n - 1)

## Method

quadratic turning point

## Memo working

The general term Tn = -n^2 + 38n - 1 is a concave-down quadratic, so the maximum is at the turning point n = -b/(2a) = -38/(2(-1)) = 19. Substitute back: T19 = -(19)^2 + 38(19) - 1 = -361 + 722 - 1 = 360. (Memo alternative: set the derivative T'n = -2n + 38 = 0 -> n = 19.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

360 (metres, at n = 19)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q3.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

After how many seconds was the torpedo at 104 m below sea level for the second time? (Depth after n seconds: Tn = -n^2 + 38n - 1, maximum at n = 19)

## Method

quadratic pattern symmetry

## Memo working

The depth was 104 m at n = 3 (from the table). A quadratic pattern is symmetric about its turning point at n = 19, so the second time at the same depth satisfies (n + 3)/2 = 19, giving n + 3 = 38, so n = 35. (Memo alternative: solve -n^2 + 38n - 1 = 104 directly: n^2 - 38n + 105 = 0; (n - 35)(n - 3) = 0; n = 35.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

n = 35 (seconds)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q1.1.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Solve for x:  sqrt(-2x + 4) - x = 2

## Method

surd equation squaring

## Memo working

Isolate the surd: sqrt(-2x + 4) = 2 + x. Square both sides: -2x + 4 = 4 + 4x + x^2. Rearrange: x^2 + 6x = 0, and factorise: x(x + 6) = 0 -> x = 0 or x = -6. Check both in the original equation: x = 0 gives sqrt(4) - 0 = 2 (valid); x = -6 gives sqrt(16) + 6 = 10 ≠ 2, so x = -6 is rejected.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = 0 (x = -6 rejected)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Solve for x and y simultaneously:  2x + y = 3  and  y^2 + xy = 2

## Method

simultaneous substitution

## Memo working

From the linear equation: y = 3 - 2x. Substitute into the second equation: (3 - 2x)^2 + (3 - 2x)x = 2. Expand and simplify: 2x^2 - 9x + 7 = 0. Factorise: (2x - 7)(x - 1) = 0 -> x = 7/2 or x = 1. Substitute back: y = 3 - 2(7/2) = -4 or y = 3 - 2(1) = 1. (Memo alternative: solve for y first via y^2 + 3y - 4 = 0, giving y = -4 or y = 1.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = 7/2 or x = 1; y = -4 or y = 1

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q1.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Solve for x:  8x^2 > 2x

## Method

quadratic inequality

## Memo working

Bring everything to one side: 8x^2 - 2x > 0. Factorise: 2x(4x - 1) > 0. The critical values are x = 0 and x = 1/4. The expression is a concave-up parabola in x, so it is positive outside its roots and negative between them. Sign analysis: for x < 0 both factors are negative, so the product is positive; between 0 and 1/4 the product is negative; for x > 1/4 both factors are positive, so the product is positive. Therefore x < 0 or x > 1/4.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x < 0 or x > 1/4

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q1.1.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Solve for x:  sqrt( sqrt(1/x) + 2 ) = 1/sqrt(x)

## Method

surd equation squaring twice

## Memo working

Square both sides: sqrt(1/x) + 2 = 1/x. Isolate the remaining surd: sqrt(1/x) = 1/x - 2, and square again: 1/x = 1/x^2 - 4/x + 4. Bring everything to one side: 1/x^2 - 5/x + 4 = 0, and multiply through by x^2: 4x^2 - 5x + 1 = 0. Factorise: (4x - 1)(x - 1) = 0, so x = 1/4 or x = 1. Check both in the original equation: x = 1/4 gives sqrt(sqrt(4) + 2) = sqrt(4) = 2 and 1/sqrt(1/4) = 2, which is valid; x = 1 gives sqrt(3) on the left but 1 on the right, so x = 1 is rejected. (Memo alternative: substitute k = sqrt(1/x), so sqrt(k + 2) = k; k^2 - k - 2 = 0; (k - 2)(k + 1) = 0; k = 2 with k = -1 rejected; then sqrt(1/x) = 2 -> x = 1/4.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = 1/4 (x = 1 rejected)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Calculate the values of x and y if: x is the sum of 2 and y; Five times the product of x and y, is 6 more than the square of x

## Method

simultaneous substitution

## Memo working

Translate the sentences into equations: x = y + 2 ...(1) and 5xy = x^2 + 6 ...(2). Substitute (1) into (2): 5(y + 2)y = (y + 2)^2 + 6. Expand both sides: 5y^2 + 10y = y^2 + 4y + 4 + 6, so 4y^2 + 6y - 10 = 0, which divides by 2 to give 2y^2 + 3y - 5 = 0. Factorise: (2y + 5)(y - 1) = 0, so y = -5/2 or y = 1. Substitute back into (1): y = -5/2 gives x = -1/2, and y = 1 gives x = 3. (Memo alternative: substitute y = x - 2 into 5xy - 6 = x^2 to get 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0; (2x + 1)(x - 3) = 0.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = -1/2 or x = 3; y = -5/2 or y = 1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q1.1.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Solve for x:  2^(2x) - 2^(x+2) - 32 = 0

## Method

exponential equation substitution

## Memo working

Rewrite using exponent laws: 2^(2x) - 2^2·2^x - 32 = 0, a quadratic in 2^x. Factorise: (2^x - 8)(2^x + 4) = 0, so 2^x = 8 or 2^x = -4. An exponential is never negative, so 2^x = -4 has no solution. From 2^x = 8: 2^x = 2^3 -> x = 3

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = 3

exponential equation factorise

This is a quadratic in 2^x. Factorise directly: (2.2^x - 1)(2^x - 4) = 0, so 2^x = 1/2 or 2^x = 4. Write each side with base 2: 2^x = 2^(-1) or 2^x = 2^2. Equate exponents: x = -1 or x = 2. ## Answer (per marking guidelines)

x = -1 or x = 2

## Question (2 marks)

The reaction between pure aluminium, Aℓ(s), and EXCESS hydrochloric acid, HCℓ(aq), is used to investigate the factors that affect the rate of a reaction. The balanced equation for the reaction is: 2Aℓ(s) + 6HCℓ(aq) → 2AℓCℓ3(aq) + 3H2(g). Define the term reaction rate.

define reaction rate

Any one of the memo's formulations earns both marks. (Memo note: give the mark for 'per unit time' only if in context of reaction rate.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

ANY ONE: Change in concentration of products/reactants per (unit) time. Change in amount/number of moles/volume/mass of products or reactants per (unit) time. Amount/number of moles/volume/mass of products formed/reactants used per (unit) time. Rate of change in concentration/amount/number of moles/volume/mass. (2 or 0)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q5.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

EXPERIMENT I: 1 mol·dm⁻³ HCℓ solution reacts with a 0,5 g Aℓ strip from an aluminium roll at room temperature. (Graph: volume of H2 in dm³ versus time in minutes, not drawn to scale; the curve rises steeply then levels off; the time axis is marked at 5 minutes. Balanced equation: 2Aℓ(s) + 6HCℓ(aq) → 2AℓCℓ3(aq) + 3H2(g).) For the time interval t = 0 to t = 5 minutes, the average reaction rate for the formation of H2(g) is 0,033 dm³·min⁻¹. Calculate the mass of Aℓ present in the container at t = 5 minutes. Take the molar gas volume as 24,5 dm³·mol⁻¹.

## Method

reaction rate stoichiometry

## Memo working

Rate = ΔV(H2)/Δt: 0,033 = ΔV(H2)/5; V(H2) = 0,165 dm³. n(H2) = V/Vm = 0,165/24,5 = 6,74 x 10⁻³ mol. n(Aℓ) = (2/3)n(H2) = (2/3)(6,74 x 10⁻³) = 4,49 x 10⁻³ mol. OPTION 1: m(Aℓ) reacted = nM = (4,49 x 10⁻³)(27) = 0,12 g (0,121); Δm(Aℓ) = 0,5 – 0,12 = 0,38 g. OPTION 2: n(Aℓ)initial = 0,5/27 = 0,0185 mol; Δn(Aℓ) = 0,0185 – 4,49 x 10⁻³ = 0,014 mol; m(Aℓ) = 0,014 x 27 = 0,38 g. Step by step: first use the average rate to find the volume of hydrogen made in the first 5 minutes (rate times time gives 0,165 dm³). Convert that volume to moles with the molar gas volume. Then use the 2:3 mole ratio of Aℓ to H2 from the balanced equation to find the moles of aluminium that reacted, convert to mass with M = 27 g·mol⁻¹, and subtract the reacted mass from the 0,5 g you started with — what is left in the container is the answer.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

0,38 g (0,379 g) (accepted range 0,365 – 0,42 g)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q5.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Assume that the concentration of the HCℓ(aq) stays constant for the duration of the reaction. Use the collision theory to explain the change in the reaction rate from t = 0 to t = 5 minutes. (Context: a 0,5 g Aℓ strip reacting with HCℓ(aq); the volume-of-H2 curve rises steeply at first and then flattens.)

## Method

collision theory explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The graph flattens, so the rate is dropping — and with the acid concentration held constant, the cause must be the aluminium. The four mark points form a chain: as the strip reacts away, its surface area (mass/size) decreases; fewer aluminium particles are exposed to the acid; therefore there are fewer effective collisions per unit time between acid particles and the metal surface; and fewer effective collisions per unit time means the reaction rate decreases.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The surface area/contact area/mass/size of aluminium decreases. Less particles exposed. Less effective collisions per unit time/second (OR lower frequency of effective collisions). Reaction rate decreases / lower reaction rate / reaction slows down.

rate graph sketch

[Sketch: volume of H2 (dm³) versus time; curve B starts at the origin, has a steeper gradient than curve A for the whole duration, and ends (levels off) at the same final volume as curve A.] Marking criteria: curve B starts at the origin and ends at the same point as curve A; gradient of curve B steeper for the whole duration. **Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q5.1.5.

## Question (1 mark)

EXPERIMENT III: Experiment I is repeated using 0,5 g pure powdered Aℓ. How will the volume of H2(g) produced in Experiment III compare to that in Experiment I? Choose from GREATER THAN, LESS THAN or EQUAL TO. (Context: Experiment I used a 0,5 g Aℓ strip in excess HCℓ(aq).)

## Method

surface area yield reasoning

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Powdering the aluminium increases its surface area, which speeds the reaction up — but rate and yield are different things. The same 0,5 g of aluminium reacts with the same excess of acid, so exactly the same amount of hydrogen is produced in the end; it just forms faster.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Equal to.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.2.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2024, question Q5.2.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Curve X is the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve for a reaction under a set of reaction conditions. A change was made to one of the reaction conditions to obtain curve Y. (Graph: number of particles versus kinetic energy; curve X has a higher, earlier peak; curve Y is lower and shifted to higher kinetic energy.) What change was made to obtain curve Y?

## Method

maxwell boltzmann interpretation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Read the shape change: curve Y's peak is lower and sits at a higher kinetic energy than curve X's, with the distribution spread further to the right. That is the signature of raising the temperature — the same number of particles is redistributed towards higher kinetic energies. (A catalyst would not move the distribution at all; it only lowers the activation energy.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

An increase in temperature.

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: Magnesium ribbon of mass 2 g reacts with excess hydrochloric acid of concentration 0,1 mol·dm⁻³ at 20 °C: Mg(s) + 2HCℓ(aq) → MgCℓ2(aq) + H2(g). Which ONE of the following changes will NOT increase the initial rate of the reaction? A Using 2 g of powdered magnesium B Increasing the temperature of HCℓ to 30 °C C Using a longer piece of the magnesium ribbon D Doubling the volume of the hydrochloric acid used

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Work through the collision-theory factors one by one. Powdering the same 2 g of magnesium (A) increases the surface area, so more effective collisions per second — rate increases. Raising the temperature to 30 °C (B) increases the kinetic energy of the particles and the fraction with energy above the activation energy — rate increases. A longer piece of ribbon of the same mass (C) is a thinner, more spread-out piece, which also exposes more surface area — rate increases. Doubling the volume of the acid (D) changes neither its concentration (still 0,1 mol·dm⁻³) nor any other rate factor, and the acid was already in excess — so the initial rate stays the same.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

D

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q1.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Multiple choice: A hypothetical endothermic reaction is given below: A(g) + B(g) ⇌ AB(g). The activation energy for the reverse reaction is 50 kJ·mol⁻¹. Which ONE of the following is possible for the reaction above? A The heat of the reaction is +70 kJ·mol⁻¹. B The activation energy for the forward reaction is 50 kJ·mol⁻¹. C The energy of the activated complex is 40 kJ·mol⁻¹. D The activation energy for the forward reaction is 40 kJ·mol⁻¹.

## Method

multiple choice

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Use the key relationship ΔH = EA(forward) − EA(reverse). The reaction is endothermic, so ΔH must be positive, which forces EA(forward) to be GREATER than EA(reverse) = 50 kJ·mol⁻¹. Option A: ΔH = +70 kJ·mol⁻¹ gives EA(forward) = 50 + 70 = 120 kJ·mol⁻¹ — perfectly possible. Option B: EA(forward) = 50 would make ΔH = 0, not endothermic. Option D: EA(forward) = 40 would make ΔH = 40 − 50 = −10 kJ·mol⁻¹, exothermic. Option C: the activated complex sits 50 kJ·mol⁻¹ above the products and more than 50 kJ·mol⁻¹ above the reactants, so an energy of only 40 kJ·mol⁻¹ is inconsistent with the diagram. Only A is possible.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A
