# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q5.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Carbon monoxide, CO(g), reacts with oxygen, O2(g), to form carbon dioxide, CO2(g), in a sealed container according to the balanced equation: 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). The graph shows the concentration of O2(g) versus time. (Graph of concentration of O2(g) in mol·dm⁻³ versus time in s: the curve starts at 0,27 mol·dm⁻³ at t = 0, falls steeply to 0,15 mol·dm⁻³ at 10 s, continues falling less steeply and flattens to 0,05 mol·dm⁻³ from about 40 s to 60 s.) The reaction takes place in a 3 dm³ container. Calculate the average rate (in mol·s⁻¹) at which CO2(g) is formed in the first 10 s.

## Method

average rate calculation

## Memo working

Step 1 — read the change in oxygen concentration off the graph over the first 10 s: [O2] falls from 0,27 mol·dm⁻³ at t = 0 to 0,15 mol·dm⁻³ at t = 10 s. Rate = −Δc(O2)/Δt = −(0,15 − 0,27)/(10 − 0) = 0,012 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.

Step 2 — convert from concentration per second to moles per second using the container volume: rate(O2) = cV per second = (0,012)(3) = 0,036 mol·s⁻¹.

Step 3 — use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, n(O2) : n(CO2) = 1 : 2, so CO2 forms twice as fast as O2 is used: rate(CO2) = 2 x 0,036 = 0,072 mol·s⁻¹.

Marking criteria: (a) calculate the change [O2]final − [O2]initial (accept 0,265 to 0,27 for [O2]initial); (b) substitute 10 s in rate formula; (c) multiply rate/concentration of O2 by 3 dm³; (d) use mole ratio n(O2) : n(CO2) = 1 : 2; (e) final correct answer 0,072 mol·s⁻¹.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Rate(CO2) = 0,072 mol·s⁻¹ [accepted RANGE: 0,06 - 0,072]

## Method

rate concentration reasoning

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The same amounts of gas in a smaller container mean higher concentrations (and higher pressure). Higher reactant concentration gives more effective collisions per unit time, so the initial reaction rate is higher — and the gradient of the concentration-time graph at the start, which represents that rate, is steeper in magnitude.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Increases. Higher reaction rate / concentration of reactants is higher. (ACCEPT: pressure increased.)

exothermic endothermic reasoning

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5.3.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P2, November 2025, question Q5.3.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (3 marks)

The reaction between sulphur dioxide, SO2(g), and oxygen, O2(g), takes place in a sealed container according to the balanced equation: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), ΔH = −196 kJ·mol⁻¹. A catalyst, vanadium pentoxide, is added to the reaction. Explain, in terms of the collision theory, why the rate of the reaction will increase.

## Method

collision theory catalyst explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) Build the explanation in three linked steps. First, the catalyst provides an alternative reaction path with a lower activation energy. Second, because the energy barrier is lower, more particles now have kinetic energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. Third, more of the collisions are therefore effective per unit time, so the reaction rate increases.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The catalyst provides an alternative path with lower activation energy / lowers the activation energy; more particles have sufficient (kinetic) energy / kinetic energy greater than (or equal to) the activation energy; more effective collisions per unit time/second (OR higher frequency of effective collisions).

## Question (1 mark)

The reaction between sulphur dioxide, SO2(g), and oxygen, O2(g), takes place in a sealed container according to the balanced equation: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), ΔH = −196 kJ·mol⁻¹. Curve X is the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve for the reaction above. (Graph: number of particles versus kinetic energy; single distribution curve labelled X starting at the origin, rising to a peak and tailing off.) More SO2(g) is now added to the container at constant temperature. How will this change affect the heat of the reaction? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.

## Method

heat of reaction reasoning

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The heat of reaction, ΔH, is a fixed property of the reaction itself — the energy difference between products and reactants per mole. Adding more of a reactant changes how much reacts, and adding it at constant temperature does not change the energy of the particles, so ΔH stays −196 kJ·mol⁻¹: it remains the same.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Remains the same

Curve Y: same shape as curve X, starting at the origin, with its peak HIGHER than curve X and at the SAME kinetic energy (more particles, same temperature).

The physical (natural) impact of river capture on the captor stream is that the … and …  (i) drainage basin decreases  (ii) river rejuvenation takes place  (iii) deposition increases  (iv) water flows faster  A (i) and (iv)  B (i) and (iii)  C (ii) and (iv)  D (ii) and (iii)  (Two block diagrams on river capture. fluvial mcq

The captor stream gains water and energy: its erosive power is renewed (river rejuvenation takes place) and the extra volume makes the water flow faster. Its drainage basin grows rather than decreases, and erosion, not deposition, increases - so (ii) and (iv) are correct. Answer C.

C ((ii) river rejuvenation takes place and (iv) water flows faster)

## Question (4 marks)

Refer to photograph B and cross-section E-F. How does the process of river rejuvenation lead to the formation of incised meanders? (2 x 2)

(Photograph B shows an incised meander: a river loops around a high, steep-sided wooded spur in a deep gorge; the cross-section E-F drawn across the valley shows a deep valley with steep sides and a relatively flat floor.)

## Method

process explanation

## Memo working

Rejuvenation gives the river renewed erosive energy, so it starts cutting downwards again. This vertical (downward) erosion happens while the river keeps its existing meandering course, so the meander loops are cut deeper and deeper into the landscape. The result is the deep, steep-sided channel seen in cross-section E-F: the meander has become incised into a gorge-like valley.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

River rejuvenation results in vertical (downward) erosion (2); Results in a deeper stream channel/valley (due to vertical erosion) (2)

- Older/younger community members vulnerable to social ills (accept examples) (2)
- Gender structure changes (2)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2024, question Q1.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Suggest strategies that can be introduced in rural areas to reduce the movement of young adults to urban areas. (3 x 2)

## Method

suggest strategies

Ask what pulls young adults to the city — jobs, services, opportunity — and then propose ways of providing those same things in the rural area itself: attract investment and create employment, develop skills and entrepreneurship, improve services and infrastructure, promote tourism, and support young farmers through land reform and financial assistance. Three workable strategies at two marks each give the six marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Create opportunities for investments (accept examples) (2)
- Increase employment opportunities (accept examples) (2)
- Skills development programmes (accept examples) (2)
- Promote entrepreneurship (2)
- Develop community projects (2)
- Make services more accessible (accept examples) (2)
- Improve the quality of services (accept examples) (2)
- Improve infrastructure (accept examples) (2)
- Increase recreational/cultural activities (accept examples) (2)
- Promote tourism (accept examples) (2)
- Subsidising education (2)
- Land reform programmes (accept examples) (2)
- Young farmers receive financial assistance (accept examples) (2)
- Provide market-related salaries/bonuses (accept examples) (2)

[ANY THREE]

graph reading

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Refer to the bar graph showing the percentage of rural population in South Africa from 2017 to 2024 (values: 2017 — 34,66; 2018 — 34,16; 2019 — 33,65; 2020 — 33,14; 2021 — 32,65; 2022 — 32,15; 2023 — 31,67; 2024 — 31,18).

Give the general trend in the rural population (percentages) as depicted between 2017 and 2024 in the graph. (1 x 1)

## Method

trend identification

## Memo working

Compare the first and last bars: the rural population percentage falls from 34,66 in 2017 to 31,18 in 2024, and every year in between is lower than the year before. A steady fall like this is described as a downward or decreasing trend — one describing word is all the mark needs.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Downward (Decreases) (1) (Accept: from 34,66 to 31,18) (1)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.3.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Explain the social impact that the general trend (answer to QUESTION 1.3.2 — the decreasing rural population) will have on the rural community. (2 x 2)

## Method

impact explanation

## Memo working

The trend is rural depopulation: people, especially the young and economically active, are leaving the countryside. Reason from that loss of people to what happens socially to those who stay behind. Fewer people means shops, schools and clinics lose support, so facilities and services decline; with fewer workers and customers, employment opportunities shrink and poverty deepens; the population becomes unbalanced (mostly the elderly and children remain), family ties are broken and there is less social interaction; quality of life and infrastructure deteriorate, and crime and other social ills can increase. Give any TWO impacts, each explained for 2 marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Decrease in employment opportunities (accept examples) (2)
- Lack of facilities (accept examples) (2)
- Lack of services (accept examples) (2)
- Quality of life/standard of living will deteriorate (accept examples) (2)
- It will increase poverty (accept examples) (2)
- Infrastructure will deteriorate (accept examples) (2)
- Increase in crime/social ills (accept examples) (2)
- Population imbalance (accept examples) (2)
- Family ties are broken (accept examples) (2)
- Less social interaction (2)
- Loss of community identity (accept examples) (2)

[ANY TWO]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.3.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Refer to the extract on land restitution (the Moletele community's citrus farm at Hoedspruit, a successful land restitution programme in Limpopo). What is land restitution? (1 x 2)

## Method

definition

## Memo working

"Restitution" means giving back. Land restitution is the land-reform programme that returns land to the people it was forcefully taken from — either the land itself goes back to its rightful owners, or the dispossessed are compensated for it. Either formulation, stated as a full definition, earns the concept mark.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Returning the land to its rightful owners (2); Compensation for people for land forcefully taken away (2) [ANY ONE]

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Refer to the extract on land restitution: the Moletele community's lime-producing farm at Hoedspruit, Limpopo — "The Moletele community opted to take their land back and this has resulted in a successful land restitution programme … a joint venture project of the Moletele communal property association (holding a 51% stake) and the established commercial fruit producer Komati Fruit Group."

According to the extract, which option (model) of land restitution applied to the Moletele community? (1 x 1)

## Method

extract reading

## Memo working

Land restitution offers claimants a choice: take the land itself back, or accept financial compensation instead. The extract answers this directly in its opening line — "The Moletele community opted to take their land back". Quote that option; the community chose the return of the land, not a payout.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

They opted to take their land back (1)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.3.6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.3.6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

Suggest strategies that can be implemented after land restitution has taken place to reduce rural depopulation (as indicated in the graph of the falling rural population percentage). (3 x 2)

## Method

suggest strategies

## Memo working

The question links the two stimuli: land has been returned (as at Moletele), so what would keep people in the rural area instead of leaving? Any THREE strategies, each for 2 marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Facilitate skills training/education (accept examples) (2)
- Provide technical support (accept examples) (2)
- Provide financial training (2)
- Promote commercial farming (2)
- Create employment opportunities (accept examples) (2)
- Form business partnerships (accept examples) (2)
- Involve all stakeholders in decision making (accept examples) (2)
- Improve infrastructure (accept examples) (2)
- Improve services (accept examples) (2)
- Making financial subsidies available (2)

[ANY THREE]

## Question (1 mark)

(Match the statement in COLUMN A with the correct option in COLUMN B; write only the letter Y or Z.) Exact piece of land that a settlement is built on  [Y situation / Z site]

## Method

column matching

Separate the two paired concepts: the site is the actual, physical piece of land a settlement occupies — its soil, slope, drainage. The situation is the settlement's position relative to its surroundings, such as routes, markets or other towns. "Exact piece of land" points to the physical ground itself, so it is the site.

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Z (site)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2024, question Q1.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

(Match the statement in COLUMN A with the correct option in COLUMN B; write only the letter Y or Z.) Settlements located close to a water source in arid areas  [Y wet-point / Z dry-point]

## Method

column matching

A wet-point settlement is deliberately placed close to water where water is scarce — for example around a spring, well or river in a dry region. A dry-point settlement is the opposite: it is placed on land that stays dry where water is abundant or flooding threatens. In an arid area, locating close to a water source makes it a wet-point settlement.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Y (wet-point)

column matching

column matching

A dispersed pattern means farmsteads stand far apart, each on its own large piece of land — typical of large commercial farms. A nucleated pattern, with dwellings clustered together, is linked to smaller plots and more subsistence-style farming.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q1.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Complete the statement in COLUMN A with the correct option from COLUMN B. Write only the letter (Y or Z).

Settlements are classified as rural, based on …  [Y the number of functions / Z the total population]

## Method

column matching

## Memo working

Geographers separate rural from urban settlements by function, not by headcount. A rural settlement offers only a small number of functions, and those functions are dominated by primary activities such as farming. Total population cannot be the classifier: a small place can still be urban if its functions are urban, and a large farming area remains rural. So the number of functions, option Y, completes the statement.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Y (the number of functions)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.1.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Complete the statement in COLUMN A with the correct option from COLUMN B. Write only the letter (Y or Z).

A loose grouping of farmsteads is called a …  [Y town / Z hamlet]

## Method

column matching

## Memo working

Work up the rural settlement hierarchy: a single farmstead is one farm dwelling; a loose grouping of a few farmsteads with almost no functions is a hamlet; a village is bigger and adds some urban functions; a town is already an urban settlement. "A loose grouping of farmsteads" therefore describes a hamlet, option Z — a town is far too high up the hierarchy.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Z (hamlet)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.1.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

Complete the statement in COLUMN A with the correct option from COLUMN B. Write only the letter (Y or Z).

A … has mostly rural functions and some urban functions.  [Y farmstead / Z village]

## Method

column matching

## Memo working

A farmstead is a single farm dwelling with purely rural (farming) functions — it has no urban functions at all. A village is the step in the rural hierarchy where urban functions first appear: it is still mostly rural, but adds a few urban functions such as a school, a shop or a church. "Mostly rural functions and some urban functions" is exactly the village, option Z.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Z (village)

## Question (1 mark)

Complete the statement in COLUMN A with the correct option from COLUMN B. Write only the letter (Y or Z).

The pattern of the settlement below is …  [Y nucleated / Z dispersed]  (Examiner's sketch, scale 1 : 30 000, key: square = settlement, line = road — a few isolated settlement squares spread far apart, each connected by roads that meet at a central junction.)

## Method

column matching

## Memo working

Ask what the buildings are doing relative to each other. In a nucleated pattern the buildings cluster tightly together around a point. In the sketch the opposite is happening: only a few settlement squares appear, and they are spread far apart from one another, each standing on its own and linked to the others only by roads. Isolated, spread-out dwellings define a dispersed pattern, option Z.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Z (dispersed)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025, question Q1.1.6.

## Question (1 mark)

Complete the statement in COLUMN A with the correct option from COLUMN B. Write only the letter (Y or Z).

The sketch below depicts a … settlement.  [Y wet-point / Z dry-point]  (Examiner's sketch, key: bold line = river, square = settlement, thin line = contour line — contour lines labelled 60 and 80 run parallel to a river, and the settlement squares are clustered right along both banks of the river.)

## Method

column matching

## Memo working

A wet-point settlement is sited to be near water, typically right at a river or spring; a dry-point settlement is sited to stay away from water, for example on higher ground above a floodplain. In the sketch the settlement squares hug both banks of the river rather than sitting up on the higher contours at 60 and 80 — the site was clearly chosen for access to the water. That is a wet-point settlement, option Y.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Y (wet-point)

The shape of the settlement below is …  [Y linear / Z round]  (Examiner's sketch, key: bold line = river, square = settlement — settlement squares strung out in a line following the winding course of the river on both banks.)

column matching

## Memo working

Shape describes the outline the settlement makes on the landscape. A round settlement grows evenly outwards from a centre. Here the settlement squares do not spread outwards — they are strung out one after another along the winding river, so the settlement is long and narrow, following a line feature. A settlement stretched along a river, road or railway is linear in shape, option Y.

Y (linear)

## Question (2 marks)

TABLE 1 contains a list of explanations and definitions of concepts used in Mathematical Literacy (A: a measuring system using metres, litres and kilograms; B: the amount of space occupied by an object; C: a system measuring in inches, gallons and pounds; D: the amount of space available to hold something; E: the side of a building you see when you are facing south; F: the side of a building you see when you are facing north; G: the amount of space that is enclosed by the perimeter of an object). Use TABLE 1 and match an explanation or a definition with the concept below. Write only the letter (A-G). QUESTION: North elevation

## Method

match definition

## Memo working

The north elevation is the side of a building that faces north. To look at that side you must stand to the north of the building and look back towards it — which means you, the observer, are facing south. That matches option E, "the side of a building you see when you are facing south". Option F is the trap: facing north shows you the south elevation. (Memo: 2A correct option.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

E

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.6b

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024, question Q2.1.6b.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

The layout plan of the ablution facilities shows a rectangle whose actual length is 8,2 metres; on the printed paper the plan's length measures 90 mm. (b) Determine, rounded to the nearest whole number, the scale of the plan.

## Method

calculate scale from measurement

## Memo working

A number scale compares a measured length on the plan with the real length, in the SAME units. Measure the plan's length with a ruler: 90 mm. The real length is 8,2 m, which is 8,2 x 1 000 = 8 200 mm. The scale is then 90 : 8 200; divide both sides by 90 to get the form 1 : n, so n = 8 200 ÷ 90 = 91,11..., which rounds to 91. The scale of the plan is 1 : 91. (Memo option 2: work in centimetres — 9 cm : 8,2 m = 9 cm : 820 cm = 1 : 91,11 = 1 : 91.) The memo accepts a deviation of ± 1 mm on the ruler measurement, since it is taken on the printed paper. (Memo: 1A measured distance; 1C convert to mm; 1M divide by 90; 1R rounded answer.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

1 : 91

The scale on this map is not written as a number ratio like 1 : 50 000. Instead it is drawn as a marked line segment labelled with the real distance that length represents (a measured 13 mm on the printed scale stands for 500 m). A scale drawn as a labelled line is called a bar scale — also known as a line scale, linear scale or graphic scale. (Memo: 2RT correct scale.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Bar scale / Line scale / Linear scale / Graphic scale

The distance of a round trip is 19,2 km. Use the given scale on the map to determine the map distance.

## Method

real distance to map distance via bar scale

## Memo working

Measure the bar scale: 13 mm = 500 m (1A measured distance, 1RT correct ratio). Put the real distance into the same unit as the scale: 19,2 km = 19 200 m (1C convert to m). Work out how many 500 m blocks fit into the trip and give each block 13 mm on the map: map distance = 19 200 ÷ 500 x 13 (1MCA divide and multiply) = 499,2 mm (1CA simplification). (Memo option 2: 1,3 cm = 500 m = 0,5 km; map distance = 19,2 x 1,3/0,5 = 49,92 cm. Accept measurements of 12 mm - 13 mm, so 460,8 mm is also accepted for a 12 mm reading. The bar-scale measurement comes from ANNEXURE A in the Special Answer Book; the scaling arithmetic 19 200/500 x 13 = 499,2 is verified.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

499,2 mm OR 49,92 cm (Accept 460,8 mm for a 12 mm bar-scale measurement)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q2.1.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

The first term of an arithmetic series is 7. The common difference of this series is 5 and the series contains 20 terms. Calculate the sum of this series.

## Method

arithmetic series sum

## Memo working

Use the arithmetic sum formula Sn = n/2[2a + (n-1)d] with a = 7, d = 5, n = 20: S20 = 20/2[2(7) + (20-1)(5)] = 10[14 + 95] = 1 090

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

S20 = 1 090

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.1.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2024, question Q2.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

The original arithmetic series (first term 7, common difference 5, 20 terms) is extended to 75 terms. The sum of these 75 terms is 14 400. Using sigma notation, write down an equation for the sum of the terms added to the original series.

## Method

sigma notation

## Memo working

General term: Tn = 7 + (n-1)(5) = 5n + 2. The added terms run from term 21 to term 75, and their sum is S75 - S20 = 14 400 - 1 090 = 13 310. Therefore Σ_{n=21}^{75} (5n + 2) = 13 310. (Memo alternative: Σ_{n=1}^{55} (5n + 102) = 13 310, using Tn = 102 + 5n for the added terms.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Sum from n=21 to 75 of (5n + 2) = 13 310

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.2.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P1, November 2025, question Q2.2.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Calculate the value of k. (Given: Sum from p=k to 117 of (4p - 1) = 26 675)

## Method

arithmetic series solve first index

## Memo working

The sum runs from p = k to p = 117, so the number of terms is n = 118 - k. The first term is 4k - 1 and the last term is T117 = 4(117) - 1 = 467. Using S = n/2 (first + last): (118 - k)/2 [4k - 1 + 467] = 26 675, so 26 675 = (118 - k)(2k + 233). Expand and simplify: 2k^2 - 3k - 819 = 0. Factorise: (k - 21)(2k + 39) = 0, so k = 21 (k = -39/2 rejected because k must be a positive integer index). (Memo alternatives: (118-k)/2 [2(4k-1) + (118-k-1)(4)] = 26 675; or S117 = 27 495 and S_(k-1) = 27 495 - 26 675 = 820 -> 2n^2 + n - 820 = 0 -> n = 20, so k - 1 = 20 -> k = 21.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

k = 21 (k = -39/2 rejected)

right triangle trig ratio

DE = 10,81 m

The main conditions for the formation of the wind at A are … and …  (i) terrestrial radiation  (ii) solar radiation  (iii) low temperatures  (iv) high temperatures  A (i) and (iii)  B (i) and (iv)  C (ii) and (iii)  D (ii) and (iv)

## Method

photo mcq

A katabatic wind forms at night. The ground loses the day's heat through terrestrial radiation, so temperatures on the slopes drop. The cold, dense air next to the slopes then sinks and drains down to the valley floor. The two required conditions are therefore terrestrial radiation and low temperatures — options (i) and (iii). Solar radiation and high temperatures drive the opposite, daytime anabatic wind.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

A ((i) terrestrial radiation and (iii) low temperatures)

## Question (1 mark)

(Valley climates. Choose the answer and write only the letter A-D.) … forms when the dew point temperature of air is below freezing point on the valley floor.  A Mist  B Fog  C Frost  D Smog

## Method

photo mcq

The deciding phrase is "below freezing point". Cold katabatic air ponds on the valley floor at night; when the air is cooled to its dew point and that dew point is below zero degrees Celsius, the water vapour is deposited directly as ice crystals on the ground and on plants — that is frost. Mist and fog are droplets of liquid water in the air, and smog is fog mixed with pollution, so none of them require freezing temperatures.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

C (Frost)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q6.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (40 marks)

QUESTION 6: CONTEMPORARY ECONOMIC ISSUES.

- Discuss in detail how the government can ensure sustainable development or environmental sustainability. (26 marks)
- Analyse the international measures taken to reduce environmental problems. (10 marks)

(Section C essay: answer ONE of two essay questions. Rubric: Introduction max 2 — define the main concept, do not include any part of the question or announce what will be discussed; Body main part max 26 — a maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples; Body additional part max 10 — a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; Conclusion max 2 — a higher-order summary, opinion or recommendation without repeating facts. Total 40.)

## Method

essay

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: open by defining environmental sustainability or sustainable development. In the main body, discuss the government's toolkit measure by measure, each under its own heading: granting property rights (ownership breeds conservation), charging for the use of the environment (garbage, sewage and emission charges), levying environmental taxes (such as carbon tax, set against the marginal external cost), paying environmental subsidies (for green technology, substitutes, recycling and clean energy), issuing marketable permits (tradeable pollution licences), command and control regulation (limits, inspectors, quantity/quality/social-impact standards), voluntary agreements with businesses, and education to change attitudes. In the additional part, analyse the international agreements — CITES, the Basel Convention, the Stockholm protocol, the Rotterdam Convention, the UN Declarations, the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement — each tied to the environmental problem it tackles. Close with a brief higher-order conclusion.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):

Environmental sustainability refers to the ability of the environment to survive its use for economic activity. / Sustainable development refers development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

BODY MAIN PART (Max 26) — GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ENSURE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT:

- Granting property rights: Property rights have a conservationist effect whereby people will take care of resources that belong to them. Property rights promote collective responsibility towards the environment while at the same time preventing over-exploitation. People are granted property rights if they agree to preserve the flora and fauna to prevent extinction. Property rights can be expanded to common resources such as clean air.
- Charging for the use of the environment: The government levies fees for waste produced and disposed to the environment. In South Africa, local authorities levy charges on garbage collection and sewage disposal. The best results are achieved when charges are proportional (related to) to waste produced. Emission charges are used when the government sets a price per unit of pollution.
- Levy environmental tax: Environmental taxes are imposed on the output of goods that generate external environmental costs such as pollution. Environmental taxes ensure that practices that are harmful to the environment are reduced. The government can use the income generated through environmental taxes to plough back into environmental issues. In South Africa, carbon tax is levied on carbon emissions from industrial processes, fuel burning and vehicle tyres. The rate of environmental tax should be equal to the marginal external cost.
- Pay environmental subsidies: Environmental subsidies refer to the payment made by the government to businesses to reduce activities that negatively affect the environment. Subsidies are granted to: encourage businesses to develop new technologies or equipment such as LED light bulbs and solar geysers; promote production of environmentally-friendly substitutes such as reusable shopping bags and rechargeable batteries; encourage recycling waste material such as bottles and cans; encourage businesses to use environmentally-friendly sources of energy such as solar and wind. Environmental subsidies can be recovered from the levying of taxation.
- Issue marketable permits: Marketable permits are licenses that are sold by the government to businesses which allow them to pollute to a certain degree. The government decides on a maximum desired level of pollution in a particular area. Businesses with low levels of pollution can sell part of their permits to firms with high levels of pollution. In South Africa, marketable permits are granted by the Department of Minerals and Energy.
- Command and Control (CAC): CAC refers to regulations set by the government to enforce environmental limits and standards. The government enforces policy by setting maximum levels of the emission of pollution. The Department of Environmental Affairs assigns inspectors to monitor the environmental activities of businesses and impose fines if the legal limits are not adhered to. Most developed countries have regulations that control air and water pollution. There are 3 approaches in CAC systems: Quantity standards that focus on the amount of pollution emitted; Quality standards that focus on the environmental impact of the pollution emitted; Social impact standards that focus on the effect of the pollution emitted on people.
- Voluntary agreements: Voluntary agreements refer to formal and informal arrangements between the government and businesses to reduce pollution. Businesses are empowered to negotiate arrangements that suit their own circumstances and create better opportunity for planning. Voluntary agreements ensure commitment by businesses as they support agreements that they have negotiated.
- Education: Education refers to methods used to create awareness and change people's attitudes towards the environment. Awareness of environmental issues ensures better decision making when interacting with the environment. Educating children on the effects of their actions on the environment helps them to become more environmentally empowered adults. Setting up community wildlife reserves educate people about the importance of protecting the environment.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for mere listing of facts/examples)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10):

- The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) bans commercial international trade in a list of endangered species to reduce biodiversity loss. CITES uses permits and quotas to regulate and monitor trade in other species that may become endangered.
- The Basel Convention controls the disposal of hazardous waste by allowing their export only to parties that have not banned its import. Countries are obliged to prevent the import or export of hazardous waste if they have reason to believe that it will not be treated in an environmentally sound manner.
- The Stockholm protocol bans some of the deadliest manufactured substances such as DDT, which is a highly toxic insecticide to reduce the effects of chemical waste.
- The Rotterdam Convention protects countries that lack adequate infrastructure to monitor the import and export of dangerous chemicals. Prior Informed Consent insures that governments have all information they need for assessing risks and taking informed decisions on chemical waste imports.
- The UN's Declarations requires indigenous capacity building to use alternative ways to manage resources.
- The Kyoto Protocol sets binding targets for developed countries to limit the production of greenhouse gases, which helps to reduce the effects of climate change. The Kyoto Protocol is an international agreement whereby developed countries pay developing countries for their right to pollute.
- The Paris Agreement limits the increase in global average temperature to below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. Paris Agreement pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. The agreement aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions to the same levels that trees, soil, and oceans can absorb naturally. Paris Agreement aims to provide financing to developing countries to reduce and adapt to climate change.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):

Environmental problems are complex, hence solutions must involve market-based environmental policies, government regulations and international measures to sustain the available resources of the country. (Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q3.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Why do markets fail to ensure environmental sustainability? (2 x 2)

(Refers to the INTERNATIONAL PROTOCOLS AND AGREEMENTS ON ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY cartoon in Q3.3.1.)

## Method

explanation

The failures all trace back to prices and ownership. The air and the seas are common resources nobody owns, and most environmental resources carry no price — so there is no economic incentive to economise on them. Producers do not bear the external costs of pollution, so they overproduce goods with negative externalities, and the profit motive pushes firms to cut costs at the environment's expense. Any two of these chains, fully explained, earn the 4 marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- The market views the environment as a common resource where many parts of the environment are not privately owned, such as the air and the seas.
- Most of the resources provided by the environment do not have a price, so there is no economic incentive to economise on their use.
- Markets may cause environmental damage due to lack of knowledge even if they would like to be more environmentally friendly in their activities.
- Consumers and businesses show carelessness as they continue with various harmful practices and leave future generations to worry about their environmental consequences.
- Businesses overproduce goods that cause negative externalities because they do not bear the external costs which result in environmental degradation.
- Markets are driven by the profit motive and they may reduce their cost of production at the expense of the environment.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

Analyse the various international measures in reducing climate change. (4 x 2)

## Method

analysis

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: organise the analysis chronologically around the three big agreements, and for each one say what it tried to do and how well it worked. The UNFCCC set out to reduce greenhouse gas emissions but failed because participation was voluntary. The Kyoto Protocol improved on it with binding targets for industrialised countries, but excluded developing countries, imposed no penalties for missed targets, and lost major polluters like the USA. The Paris Agreement improved on Kyoto by aiming to keep global warming well below 2 °C — preferably 1,5 °C — with subsidy pledges to developing countries, but targets are still being missed and there is no strict enforcement. Four analysed points earn the 8 marks. **Marking note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was established to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere.
- Most countries agree on taking measures to protect the environment, but they differ on who is most responsible for the damage and how to set emissions-reduction goals.
- The UNFCCC did not succeed because it was voluntary for individual countries.
- The Kyoto Protocol was an improvement on the UNFCCC as it attempted to get developed countries to commit to reducing their emission of greenhouse gases.
- The Kyoto Protocol established binding targets whereby industrialised countries agreed to reduce their emissions.
- The major shortcoming of the Kyoto Protocol was its focus on developed countries only and developing countries were excluded from the agreement.
- Kyoto Protocol failed as countries that did not meet targets were not penalised.
- Big polluters (like the USA) failed to meet the targets set by Kyoto Protocol and still contribute to global warming and are less interested in solving the crises due to expensive technology to reduce pollution.
- Major polluters like the USA pulled out and this impacted negatively on the success of the agreement.
- The Paris Agreement was an improvement on the Kyoto Protocol as its goal is to limit global warming to well below 2 °C, preferably to 1,5 °C, compared to pre-industrial levels.
- Assistance in the form of subsidies was pledged to developing countries to reduce greenhouse emissions.
- The success of Paris Agreement will be determined by the financial, technical and capacity-building support offered to countries who need it.
- Global warming targets are not met as we are fast approaching an increase in global temperatures of 2 °C.
- There was a lack of strict law enforcement because penalties were not imposed on those who did not meet the targets.

(Accept any other relevant response)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q4.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

How can the Basel Convention help to manage hazardous waste? (2 x 2)

(Refers to the MANAGING WASTE extract in Q4.3.1.)

## Method

explanation

The Basel Convention controls the movement of hazardous waste across borders. Its rules work as gates: exports may only go to fellow parties that have not banned such imports, trade with non-parties is prohibited, and shipments must be blocked whenever there is reason to believe the waste will not be treated in an environmentally friendly way at its destination. Two fully explained rules earn the 4 marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- The Basel Convention allows parties to the convention to only export a hazardous waste to other parties that have not banned imports of such waste.
- The Convention does not allow parties to import from or export to non-parties.
- Parties are obliged to prevent the import or export of hazardous wastes if they have reasons that the wastes will not be treated in an environmentally-friendly manner at their destination

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q8.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q8.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

If AB = BK, calculate the size of KÂC. (From QUESTIONS 8.1 to 8.3: the vertical rectangle ABCD has AB = 18 cm and diagonal AC = 18√5 cm; the base diagonal KC = 43,97 cm; the backdrop is vertical to the base, so AB ⊥ BK.)

## Method

cosine rule in 3d

## Memo working

First find AK. The backdrop stands vertical on the horizontal base, so AB is perpendicular to BK and triangle ABK is right-angled at B. With AB = BK = 18: AK^2 = AB^2 + BK^2 = 18^2 + 18^2 (Pythagoras), so AK = √648 = 18√2 = 25,46 cm. Now triangle AKC has all three sides known: AK = 18√2, AC = 18√5 and KC = 43,97. Apply the cosine rule with the angle at A: KC^2 = AK^2 + AC^2 - 2.AK.AC cos KÂC, so (43,97)^2 = (18√2)^2 + (18√5)^2 - 2(18√2)(18√5)cos KÂC. Solving: cos KÂC = 0,16..., so KÂC = 80,60°.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

KÂC = 80,60°

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q6.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (1 mark)

A stationary listener, standing on the roadside, records the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren of a police car travelling at a constant velocity. In the wavelength-time graph, NOT drawn to scale, λL is the wavelength of the sound recorded by the listener and λS is the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren. Take the speed of sound in air to be 343 m·s⁻¹. [Graph: two horizontal lines of wavelength versus time; λL = 0,40 m (upper line) and λS = 0,38 m (lower line).] 6.1 Name the phenomenon that explains why the wavelengths shown in the graph differ.

## Method

identify doppler effect

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines) The source of the sound (the siren) is moving relative to the stationary listener, so the wavelength the listener records differs from the wavelength the siren emits. The change in observed wavelength or frequency caused by relative motion between a sound source and an observer is the Doppler effect.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Doppler effect

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q6.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

A stationary listener, standing on the roadside, records the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren of a police car travelling at a constant velocity (wavelength-time graph: the wavelength recorded by the listener is λL = 0,40 m and the wavelength emitted by the siren is λS = 0,38 m; the speed of sound in air is 343 m·s⁻¹). Is the car moving TOWARDS or AWAY FROM the listener? Give a reason for the answer.

## Method

doppler direction reasoning

## Memo working

Compare the two wavelengths on the graph: the listener records λL = 0,40 m while the siren emits λS = 0,38 m, so the detected wavelength is longer than the emitted wavelength. A source moving away from a listener stretches the wavefronts, lengthening the detected wavelength and lowering the detected frequency.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Away from. Wavelength of sound detected/observed by the listener is longer than wavelength of sound emitted by the source OR frequency detected by the listener is lower than the frequency of the source OR λL > λS OR fL < fS.

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.3.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q6.3.1.

## Question (3 marks)

A stationary listener records the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren of a police car travelling at a constant velocity (the wavelength emitted by the siren is λS = 0,38 m; the speed of sound in air is 343 m·s⁻¹). Calculate the frequency of the sound emitted by the siren.

## Method

wave equation

## Memo working

Use the wave equation with the source wavelength: v = fλ, so 343 = f(0,38), giving f = 902,63 Hz. (Memo notes: if c = fλ is used, penalise 1 mark; if 340 m·s⁻¹ is used for the speed of sound, penalise 1 mark for the answer.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

f = 902,63 Hz

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.3.2

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q6.3.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

A stationary listener records the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren of a police car travelling at a constant velocity away from the listener (wavelength recorded by the listener λL = 0,40 m; wavelength emitted by the siren λS = 0,38 m; speed of sound in air 343 m·s⁻¹; from Question 6.3.1 the siren frequency is fS = 902,63 Hz). Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the car.

## Method

doppler equation moving source

## Memo working

POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 6.3.1. First convert the listener's wavelength to the frequency the listener hears: v = fλ, so 343 = f(0,4), giving fL = 857,5 Hz. Then apply the Doppler equation for a source moving away from a stationary listener: fL = v/(v + vs) × fS, so 857,5 = (343/(343 + vs))(902,63), giving vs = 18,05 m·s⁻¹. (Memo notes: if wavelengths are substituted instead of frequencies, max 2/6; if the wavelengths are swopped, max 3/6.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

vs = 18,05 m·s⁻¹ (accepted range 18,05 – 18,45 m·s⁻¹)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q6.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2025, question Q6.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (6 marks)

An ambulance siren produces sound with a constant frequency. The ambulance moves towards a stationary sound detector (Part A) and away from the stationary detector (Part B) at constant velocities. (Graph: detected frequency versus velocity of the ambulance; the Part A line passes through 1 298 Hz at 25 m·s⁻¹ and the Part B line passes through 1 115 Hz at 25 m·s⁻¹.)

Calculate the speed of sound in air.

## Method

doppler equation simultaneous

## Memo working

When the ambulance approaches the detector at 25 m·s⁻¹, the detected frequency is 1 298 Hz. The Doppler equation for a source moving towards a stationary listener is fL = v/(v − vs) × fs, which rearranges to vfs = 1 298(v − 25) ... equation (1).

When the ambulance moves away at 25 m·s⁻¹, the detected frequency is 1 115 Hz. For a source moving away, fL = v/(v + vs) × fs, which rearranges to vfs = 1 115(v + 25) ... equation (2).

The siren frequency fs and the speed of sound v are the same in both parts, so the left-hand sides are equal. Setting equation (1) equal to equation (2): 1 298(v − 25) = 1 115(v + 25). Expanding gives 183v = 60 325, so v = 329,64 m·s⁻¹.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

v = 329,64 m·s⁻¹

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2024, question Q4.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

How can an increase in injections contribute positively towards the South African economy? (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- A rise in injections, in the form of government expenditure, investment and export earnings, leads to a proportionately larger increase in national income through the multiplier process.
- Increase in investments may create new jobs, which helps to reduce unemployment in the economy.
- Households' income level may increase leading to higher demand for goods and services.
- More direct investments may increase production of goods and services which will increase/stimulate economic growth.
- Establishment of new businesses may help to expand the tax base of the government resulting in more tax revenue.
- Increase in foreign investments may create capital inflow which helps to increase the value of local currency.
- Increase in export earnings may help to reduce balance of payments problems in the economy.
- Increase in exports may increase local production of goods and services thereby stimulating economic growth.
- Increase in government expenditure on infrastructure helps to attract more direct investment across the country.
- Increase in welfare expenditure such as social grants may help to improve the standard of living for the people.

(Accept any other correct relevant response. Memo note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

## Question (2 marks)

The sum of marginal propensity to consume (mpc) and marginal propensity to save (mps) in a two-sector model is equal to …

A 2.
B 1.
C 0,5.
D 0,75.

## Method

multiple choice recall

In a two-sector model every extra rand of income can only go two ways: it is either spent (consumption) or not spent (saving). So the fraction consumed plus the fraction saved must account for the whole rand: mpc + mps = 1.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

B - 1

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2025, question Q5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (40 marks)

QUESTION 5: MACROECONOMICS.

- Discuss in detail the markets within the four-sector circular-flow model. (26 marks)
- Evaluate the contribution of the business sector to the development of the South African economy. (10 marks)

(Section C essay: answer ONE of two essay questions. Rubric: Introduction max 2 — define the main concept, do not include any part of the question or announce what will be discussed; Body main part max 26 — a maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples; Body additional part max 10 — a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts; Conclusion max 2 — a higher-order summary, opinion or recommendation without repeating facts. Total 40.)

## Method

essay

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: open by defining the circular flow or a market. In the main body, discuss the four markets each under its own heading. The goods (product/output) market, where goods and services are bought and sold — distinguish consumer goods (durable, semi-durable and non-durable) from capital goods. The factor (resource/input) market, where households sell labour, entrepreneurship, capital and land in exchange for wages, profit, interest and rent. The financial markets, which link savers with borrowers — the money market for short-term savings and loans, anchored by the South African Reserve Bank, and the capital market for long-term funds, anchored by the Johannesburg Securities Exchange. The foreign exchange market, where currencies such as the rand and the US dollar are exchanged and the rand's value is set by demand and supply. For the additional part, evaluate the business sector's contribution — jobs, skills development, GDP growth, research and innovation, corporate tax, infrastructure partnerships, export competitiveness and corporate social investment — balanced against negatives such as low wages, pollution and collusion. Close with a brief higher-order conclusion.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

**INTRODUCTION (Max 2):**

The circular flow is a simplified economic model that illustrates the inter-relationship between the economic participants. OR A market is a mechanism that brings buyers and sellers together to exchange different types of products. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

**BODY MAIN PART (Max 26) — FOUR TYPES OF MARKETS IN THE CIRCULAR FLOW.**

**(a) Goods market / Product market / Output market**

- Product market is where goods and services are bought and sold.
- Firms, government and foreign sector supply goods and services within the open economy which represents the real flow.
- Consumers, firms, government and foreign sector buy goods and services from the goods market and their payments represent money flow.
- Goods are defined as any tangible items such as food, clothing and cars that satisfy some human needs.
- Services are defined as non-tangible actions which include transportation, retailing and financial transactions.
- Consumer goods market involves the trading of durable consumer goods, semi-durable consumer goods and non-durable consumer goods.
- A further distinction is made between the following consumer goods: Non-durable goods are those items that are used up when they are consumed and cannot be re-used, such as petrol and beverages. Semi-durable goods last for a short period of time and can be used more than once, such as printer cartridge and a pen. Durable goods can be used over again and do not wear out very easily, such as vehicles and furniture.
- Capital goods are those goods which are purchased by businesses for use in the production process and they are purchased in the capital goods market.

**(b) Factor market / Resources market / Input market**

- Factor market is where factors of production are exchanged.
- The labour market, property market and the financial markets are part of the factor market.
- Households are the owners of factors of production and they sell them to firms to produce goods and services.
- The factors of production are labour, entrepreneurship, capital and land and they are exchanged for wages, profit, interest, and rent respectively.
- The factor market can be further subdivided into the following markets in which different factors of production are traded: A labour market where labour is traded, for example, the business done in employment agencies and labour brokers. A natural resource market where land and other natural resources are traded.
- Factor services are real flows and they are accompanied by counter flows of income on the factor market.

**(c) Financial markets**

- Financial markets are not directly involved in production of goods and services, but act as a link between households and businesses with surplus income and other participants who need funds
- Banks, insurance companies and pension funds form part of the financial market.
- Financial markets render financial services to the other participants in the economy by gathering surplus funds and lending them to those who needs funding

**Money market**

- The money market is the market for short-term savings and loans.
- Money market includes inter-bank lending for a period as short as overnight.
- The securities traded include short term deposits, short term debentures and treasury bills.
- The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) is a key institution in the money market.
- The SARB administers the function of legislating and managing the money market.

**Capital market**

- The capital market is the market for long-term savings and loans.
- The securities traded in this market are long term deposits, mortgage bonds and shares.
- The Johannesburg Securities Exchange (JSE) is a key institution in the capital market.

**(d) Foreign exchange market / Foreign currency market / Forex market**

- The foreign exchange market is where different currencies of all the countries are traded. e.g. The South African rand can be exchanged for the US dollar in this market.
- The foreign exchange market originates when one country imports goods from another country and domestic currency have to be exchanged in order to pay for such imports
- Foreign exchange can be bought and sold at the banks and foreign exchange agencies
- The South African rand is freely traded in the forex markets and its value is determined by the market forces of demand and supply.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (Allocate a max of 8 marks for headings/subheadings/examples)

**ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10):**

**POSITIVES:**

- Businesses create job opportunities directly and indirectly, helping to lower unemployment rates.
- The business sector offers skills development opportunities, such as in-service training and employee workshops, which improve workforce skills and enhance productivity.
- Businesses contribute largely to the gross domestic product (GDP) of a country through the production of goods and services as the main driver of economic growth.
- The sector invests in research and development, which encourages innovation and entrepreneurship.
- Businesses pay corporate tax to the government which is then used to fund public services and infrastructural projects.
- Businesses may work in partnership with the government to develop infrastructure, such as construction of roads, transportation and communication systems which promote economic activity and economic growth.
- Businesses participate in international trade activities enhancing competitiveness of the country's exports.
- Businesses engage in corporate social investment (CSI) projects which help to improve the welfare of communities.

**NEGATIVES:**

- The business sector widens inequality gap through paying low wages to workers.
- Businesses being profit driven, sometimes they fail to consider the negative impact of their activities to the environment such as pollution.
- The unfair business practices such as collusion, may result in consumer exploitation through high prices.

(Accept any other correct relevant response) (A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples)

**CONCLUSION (Max 2):**

Markets are critically important institutions in the economic system because they regulate the market, safeguard price stability and enhance both the business and consumer confidence. (Accept any other higher-order conclusion)

Two parallel upward-sloping expenditure lines: E = 20 + 0,5Y with vertical intercept 20, cutting E = Y at point e with income Y; and E1 = 30 + 0,5Y with vertical intercept 30, cutting E = Y at point e1 with income Y1. Arrows show the upward shift from E to E1 and the rightward movement from Y to Y1.)

Identify the value of the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) in the graph above.

## Method

data response identification

In an expenditure equation of the form E = a + bY, the intercept a is autonomous spending and the slope b — the coefficient of Y — is the marginal propensity to consume. Both lines on the graph, E = 20 + 0,5Y and E1 = 30 + 0,5Y, have slope 0,5, so the MPC is read straight off the equation as 0,5.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

0,5

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2024, question Q2.3.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Explain the relationship between marginal propensity to save (MPS) and the value of the multiplier (K). (Refers to the Q2.3.1 graph of the multiplier effect in a two-sector economy: expenditure lines E = 20 + 0,5Y and E1 = 30 + 0,5Y against the 45-degree line E = Y.)

## Method

explanation

Recall the formula K = 1/MPS (equivalently K = 1/(1 - MPC)). Because MPS sits in the denominator, the relationship is inverse: a bigger MPS means more of each rand leaks into saving, so the spending chain dies out sooner and the multiplier is smaller; a smaller MPS keeps more spending circulating, giving a bigger multiplier.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- There is an inverse or a negative relationship between marginal propensity to save (MPS) and the multiplier
- The bigger the MPS, the smaller the value of the multiplier / The smaller the MPS, the bigger the value of the multiplier

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q2.3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P1, November 2024, question Q2.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Use the information in the above graph to calculate the change in national income (ΔY). Show ALL calculations. (Graph titled MULTIPLIER EFFECT IN A TWO-SECTOR ECONOMY: expenditure on the vertical axis in billion rands, income on the horizontal axis, with a dashed 45-degree line E = Y. The expenditure line E = 20 + 0,5Y, with vertical intercept 20, cuts E = Y at income Y; it shifts up to the parallel line E1 = 30 + 0,5Y, with vertical intercept 30, which cuts E = Y at the higher income Y1.)

## Method

multiplier calculation

## Memo working

The memo accepts any of four routes; all give the same result.

Method 1 — multiplier times the change in injections: the autonomous spending injection rises from 20 to 30, so ΔJ = 30 - 20 = 10. The multiplier K = 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/(1 - 0,5) = 2. Therefore ΔY = ΔJ x K = 10 x 2 = 20.

Method 2 — compare the two equilibrium incomes directly: ΔY = Y1 - Y = (30/0,5) - (20/0,5) = 60 - 40 = 20.

Method 3 — start from the multiplier formula: K = 1/(1 - mpc) = 1/(1 - 0,5) = 2. Since K = ΔY/ΔJ, it follows that 2 = ΔY/(30 - 20), so ΔY = 20.

Method 4 — solve the equilibrium condition Y = E for each expenditure line: Y = 20 + 0,5Y gives Y = 40; Y = 30 + 0,5Y gives Y1 = 60; therefore ΔY = Y1 - Y = 60 - 40 = 20.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

ΔY = 20 (billion rand)

## Question (2 marks)

Red light, blue light and green light, each of a single frequency, are shone simultaneously on a sheet of potassium. ## Method

photoelectric explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Only green and blue light eject electrons / red light does not eject electrons. Green has a lower frequency than blue / green has longer wavelength than blue / photons of blue light have more energy than photons of green light, and therefore green ejects electrons with the lower kinetic energy. (fgreen < fblue / blue has a higher frequency than green.)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q10.2.3

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Physical Sciences P1, November 2024, question Q10.2.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (5 marks)

Light of different single frequencies is shone on a sheet of potassium. The electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 2,65 x 10⁻²⁰ J are ejected by light that has a frequency of 5,85 x 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the frequency of the light that ejected electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 6,96 x 10⁻²⁰ J.

## Method

photoelectric equation

## Memo working

OPTION 1: Apply the photoelectric equation E = W0 + Ek(max) twice — the work function of potassium is the same in both cases. First find W0 from the known frequency: hf = W0 + Ek(max), so (6,63 x 10⁻³⁴)(5,85 x 10¹⁴) = W0 + 2,65 x 10⁻²⁰, giving W0 = 3,61 x 10⁻¹⁹ J. Then use W0 with the larger kinetic energy: hf = W0 + Ek(max), so (6,63 x 10⁻³⁴)f = 3,61 x 10⁻¹⁹ + 6,96 x 10⁻²⁰, giving f = 6,5 x 10¹⁴ Hz. (Memo option 2: hf1 − Ek(max)1 = hf2 − Ek(max)2. Memo option 3: via the threshold frequency f0 = 5,45 x 10¹⁴ Hz.)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

f = 6,5 x 10¹⁴ Hz

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q8.1

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Maths P2, November 2025, question Q8.1.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

As part of a school project, learners are required to design a portable stage for a puppet show. The design must fulfil the following requirements: BKLC is a horizontal base having KB̂C = 104° and BK̂C = 52,6°; the rectangular backdrop, ABCD, is vertical to the horizontal base and must have an area of 648 cm^2; the sides of ABCD must be in the ratio AB : BC = 1 : 2; the stage must be partly enclosed with triangular sides ABK and DCL. (In the 3-D drawing, the vertical rectangle ABCD — A top-left, D top-right, B bottom-left, C bottom-right — stands on the shaded horizontal base BKLC, with K front-left, L front-right and diagonal KC drawn on the base.) Show that AB = 18 cm.

## Method

area ratio equation

## Memo working

The area of rectangle ABCD is length times breadth, BC × AB. The ratio AB : BC = 1 : 2 means BC = 2AB, so the area condition becomes 648 = 2AB × AB, that is 2AB^2 = 648. Then AB^2 = 324, and taking the positive square root gives AB = 18 cm.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

AB = 18 cm

pythagoras

AC is the diagonal of rectangle ABCD, so triangle ABC is right-angled at B. By Pythagoras: AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = 18^2 + 36^2 = 324 + 1296 = 1620. Therefore AC = √1620 = 18√5 = 40,25 cm.

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q3.3.3.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Briefly describe the term domestic tourism. (Refers to a bar graph titled REGIONAL CHANGES IN TOURIST ARRIVALS.)

## Method

definition

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: the defining feature is who travels where — residents of a country visiting places inside their own country's borders. Contrast it with inbound tourism (foreigners visiting) and outbound tourism (residents leaving), which is what makes "within the boundaries of their own country" the mark-earning phrase.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The activities of people visiting places within the boundaries of their own country.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3.4

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q3.3.4.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Explain the impact of a weaker rand on foreign tourist arrivals. (Refers to a bar graph titled REGIONAL CHANGES IN TOURIST ARRIVALS.)

## Method

explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: when the rand weakens, a foreign tourist's own currency buys more rand, so a South African holiday becomes cheaper for them. Cheaper travel and spending attracts more visitors, so foreign tourist arrivals tend to increase. State the direction of the effect and the reason to earn both marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Foreign tourist arrivals may increase as it becomes cheaper for them to visit or spend money in South Africa.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q3.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

How can the South African government ensure that tourists visit the various destinations across the country? (2 x 2) (Refers to a bar graph titled REGIONAL CHANGES IN TOURIST ARRIVALS.)

## Method

explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: the question is about spreading tourists beyond the famous spots. Think in two channels — information (marketing, representative bodies that publicise lesser-known destinations) and access (transport, accommodation and amenities in less developed areas). Give TWO developed measures for 2 marks each.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- The South African government may create representative bodies to provide information about all tourist attractions in the country.
- The Department of Tourism may improve marketing to provide accurate information about product descriptions and prices in less well-known tourist destinations.
- The government should improve supporting services such as transport, accommodation and other amenities in less developed tourist destinations.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (8 marks)

How can tourism activities negatively impact South Africa? (4 x 2)

## Method

discussion

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: group the negative impacts into environmental damage (permanent restructuring, waste, loss of wildlife, water shortages, noise), pressure on infrastructure and communities (congestion, overloaded facilities, displacement and relocation costs) and economic strain on locals (product shortages, price increases that worsen poverty). Choose FOUR distinct impacts and explain each consequence for 2 marks apiece. **Marking note: a maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.**

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Development of infrastructure and facilities for tourism can cause permanent environmental restructuring
- Transportation of tourists may cause traffic congestion in tourist areas during holiday seasons
- Tourism may lead to loss of wildlife species due to activities such as safari hunting
- Increase in tourists may lead to the use of water in large quantities may lead to water shortages especially in dry areas
- Use of aircrafts by tourists may lead to noise pollution to residents near airports
- Additional demand for goods and services by tourists may lead to product shortages on local market
- Local prices may increase resulting in local consumers failing to afford basic goods and services which may increase poverty
- Infrastructure at tourist sites can be under pressure to cater for a large number of tourists.
- Tourism activities may cause environmental damage at tourist sites through additional waste products
- Tourism may affect population dynamics due to migration and changes in population density to the needs of tourist sites
- People may incur relocation costs as they are displaced from their land to make way for tourism development

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

data response identification

Image A

Briefly describe the term paleo tourism. (Refers to two images titled SOUTH AFRICAN TOURISM.)

## Method

definition

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: "paleo" points to the ancient past — fossils and archaeology. Paleo tourism is travel to sites of great archaeological significance to learn about fossils, such as the Cradle of Humankind. The definition needs both the visiting of such sites and the fossil/archaeological focus.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

The activities of tourists visiting sites of great archaeological significance to learn about fossils

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q4.3.4.

## Question (2 marks)

Explain the impact of households' income levels on tourism. (Refers to two images titled SOUTH AFRICAN TOURISM.)

## Method

explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: tourism is a luxury bought out of disposable income. When disposable income rises, more households can afford to travel, so tourism participation increases; when it falls, leisure travel is among the first spending cut. Explaining either direction of the link earns the marks.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

Increase in households' disposable income may increase the number of people who participate in tourism activities / Decrease in disposable income reduces the number of people who travel for leisure and recreation

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

# Past-Paper Worked Example — Q4.3.5

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2024, question Q4.3.5.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2024. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (4 marks)

Why would South Africans be discouraged to visit tourist sites within the country? (2 x 2) (Refers to two images titled SOUTH AFRICAN TOURISM.)

## Method

explanation

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

Teachable steps: think of the barriers a domestic tourist actually faces — safety (crime and social unrest), health hazards (malaria, unsafe water), damage from natural disasters that destroy sites and infrastructure, and rising costs of entrance fees, accommodation and transport. Pick TWO and develop each into a discouraging effect for 2 marks apiece.

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Social unrests and high crime rate may discourage people from visiting tourist attractions in certain parts of the country.
- Health hazards, such as malaria and unsafe drinking water, may discourage people from visiting tourist sites in the affected areas.
- Natural disasters, such as floods, cyclones and heavy rains may destroy tourist sites and infrastructure which may disrupt tourism activities across the country.
- Increasing costs, such as entrance fees, accommodation and transport, may result in some people failing to afford visiting various sites across the countries.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q3.1.2.

**© Department of Basic Education, 2025. Reproduced for educational use with attribution.**

## Question (2 marks)

Why is the tourism industry regarded as labour-intensive? (1 x 2)

## Method

explanation

Labour-intensive means production relies more on people than on machines. Tourism is built on human interaction — guides, hospitality staff, drivers, cleaners — so it needs a large workforce, and for every unit of capital invested it creates more jobs, formal and informal, than most other industries. One fully explained reason earns the 2 marks.

## Memo working

(see marking guidelines)

## Answer (per marking guidelines)

- Tourism activities require a large workforce because the industry involves human interaction and personal services.
- Tourism creates more jobs opportunities, in both formal and informal sector, for every unit of capital invested compared to any other industry.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)

**Source:** Department of Basic Education — Grade 12 Economics P2, November 2025, question Q3.2.4.
